process_gridP processes, 1D or 2D layout per the underlying library's own convention (LiaoLLR21 uses 24 MPI ranks/node, one rank/core, no further grid structure disclosed in the extracted text); disclosed per run.
preprocessingone-shot: matrix generation (synthetic) or dense-to-tridiagonal reduction (real matrices, via ScaLAPACK or equivalent) happens once before the timed region and is reported separately, matching LiaoLLR21's own practice of calling ScaLAPACK's reduction routines as a distinct, unmeasured preprocessing step before invoking PSDC.
warmup1 full solve (a spec addition — LiaoLLR21's own protocol has no separate warmup, only the "twice per program invocation" inner loop described below).
reps6 (matches LiaoLLR21's own explicit protocol — "evaluated ... twice in the same program and called that program three times" = 2x3=6 total executions).
statisticmedian (report min and max alongside) — a DELIBERATE, explicit divergence from LiaoLLR21's own stated practice ("chose the BEST results among these six executions"), the most granular best-of-N structure found across this project's three dense-factorization- track surveys, per this project's general fairness principle.
timerwall-clock (matches LiaoLLR21's own timer choice, exact API not specified in the extracted text).
timing_scopekernel-only tridiagonal-eigensolve time; excludes matrix generation/reduction and any prior dense-to-tridiagonal step (that belongs to variant 1's scope if the pipeline is run end-to-end).
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once.
metric
primaryaggregate GFLOP/s (standard D&C tridiagonal-eigensolve FLOP count / time, summed across the run)
secondaryms; speedup vs. ScaLAPACK PDSTEDC (the literature's own primary baseline, 1.4x-1.6x per LiaoLLR21's own results) and vs. PHDC (a competing HSS-based D&C variant, with an explicit crossover at low process counts per LiaoLLR21's own finding — both comparisons kept, since the crossover itself is methodologically informative, not just a single winner/loser result)
correctnessTWO required, gating measurements, adopting LiaoLLR21's OWN explicit formulas verbatim (the most complete correctness disclosure found in this track, and one of the most complete across all three of this project's dense-factorization-track surveys) rather than substituting a different convention: (1) orthogonality, `||I - Q*Q^T||_max < 1e-12` (max absolute entry norm; LiaoLLR21's own reported values are all in the 2.5e-14 to 3.8e-14 range at every tested process count, so this spec's threshold is set well above the observed range, not arbitrarily); (2) backward-error residual, `||A - Q*Lambda*Q^*||_c / ||A||_2 < 1e-10` where `||X||_c` is the MAXIMUM Frobenius norm across X's individual columns and `||X||_2` is X's spectral norm (LiaoLLR21's own exact formula, adopted verbatim since it is this track's most concretely evidenced residual convention). A run failing either gate does not count toward reported throughput.
eigensolver-polynomial-filtered-partial-spectrum-kernelPARTIAL-spectrum eigensolve (only the k eigenpairs inside a disclosed interval [lambda_lo, lambda_hi]), via polynomial-filtered Krylov iteration, with the SEARCH INTERVAL and the underlying matrix-power- kernel POLYNOMIAL DEGREE both required, disclosed, spec-level parameters — this is the one variant in this track's spec that addresses the "partial spectrum" half of the task's own key axis, combining ShiLXSH21 (the application-level generalized-eigenproblem solve, interval-bounded) with YangNYLDXJ026 (the kernel-level matrix-power-kernel optimization that makes exactly this class of solve efficient) as complementary, not merely co-located, evidence.
inputs
suitetwo tiers matching this variant's two source papers exactly: (a) REAL/synthetic FEM operator pairs (A,B) from planetary normal-mode models, matches ShiLXSH21's own four shipped models (CONST, PREM, Mtopo, RTMDWAK); (b) any SuiteSparse-format sparse matrix for the underlying matrix-power-kernel microbenchmark (matches YangNYLDXJ026's own unrestricted `-in` input, this spec additionally requiring the SAME SuiteSparse selection criterion this project's `spmv`/`spmm` tracks already use, for cross-track matrix-suite consistency, since YangNYLDXJ026's own artifact enforces no selection criterion at all).
selectionfor tier (a): the four models shipped in ShiLXSH21's own artifact, spanning ~3k to ~100k mesh-derived DOFs; for tier (b): matrices matching this project's spmv-track SuiteSparse subset (for direct cross-track GFLOP/s comparability of the underlying MPK kernel).
recommended_subsettier (a): CONST3k, PREM3k, Mtopo100k (pOrder=1 only, per ShiLXSH21's own artifact note), RTMDWAK8k, each run at JOB=1 (no reference gravity, the simpler/faster operator) and, as a stretch point, JOB=2 (with reference gravity); tier (b): this project's existing spmv-track canonical SuiteSparse subset, reused rather than re-selected.
dense_operandN/A (sparse/FEM-generated); fp64 throughout, matches both source papers.
protocol
search_intervalREQUIRED, disclosed, swept parameter (tier a only): [lambda_lo, lambda_hi], reported in the problem's own natural units (mHz for ShiLXSH21's frequency-domain framing, converted internally via `(2*pi*freq*1e-3)^2` per the paper's own artifact README) — this is this variant's direct implementation of the task's "tolerance as part of the spec" requirement: a partial-spectrum solve's reported performance is MEANINGLESS without the interval that determines how many eigenpairs k actually fall inside it, since k (not N) governs cost.
polynomial_degreeREQUIRED, disclosed, swept parameter: the matrix-power-kernel degree `d` (tier b: matches YangNYLDXJ026's own `-d` CLI flag, default 20 in its README's own example; tier a: the filter polynomial's own degree, not directly exposed in ShiLXSH21's artifact materials read during this survey — flagged in open_questions, this spec requires it be disclosed once the underlying pEVSL configuration is inspected).
discretization_orderrequired, disclosed (tier a only): `pOrder` (1 or 2, FEM polynomial basis order), matches ShiLXSH21's own `demos/global_conf` parameter exactly — trades matrix size/accuracy, a genuinely different "tolerance" axis than a numerical convergence threshold, specific to this variant's PDE-discretization origin.
preprocessingone-shot: matrix/operator generation (tier a: FEM assembly of A,B from the mesh model; tier b: reading the .mtx file and CSR conversion) happens once before the timed region, reported separately, never amortized.
warmup1 full solve (a spec addition; neither source paper's artifact states a warmup practice).
repstier (a): 5 (a spec addition, matching this project's general convention; no repetition protocol found in ShiLXSH21's artifact materials); tier (b): 50 (matches YangNYLDXJ026's own hardcoded `iterations=50` exactly, the cleanest fixed-rep-count evidence found in this track).
statisticmedian (report min and max alongside) for tier (a), a spec default with no literature statistic to diverge from; MEDIAN for tier (b) too, DEVIATING from YangNYLDXJ022's own implicit mean-over-50- iterations (`total_time/iterations`), per this project's general fairness principle.
timerwall-clock (host-side, matches both source papers' own implicit choice, exact API not confirmed for ShiLXSH21).
timing_scopekernel-only solve time (tier a: the full polynomial-filtered Lanczos solve for the disclosed interval; tier b: the matrix-power- kernel `A^d*x` application only, matches YangNYLDXJ022's own separately-reported `DBMPK Setup Time` vs. solve-time split exactly — this spec REQUIRES that split be preserved, not combined, per this project's general preprocessing-reported-separately principle).
preprocessing_reportedtier (a): FEM assembly, reported separately, once; tier (b): DBMPK setup time (matches YangNYLDXJ022's own `setup_time` field exactly, already separately reported in the artifact's own output), reported separately, once.
metric
primaryfor tier (a): eigenpairs/second (k eigenpairs found inside the disclosed interval, divided by wall time) — NOT a FLOP-based metric, since k (not N) is the quantity that actually varies with the interval and matrix, matching how this variant's actual claim (partial-spectrum efficiency) should be measured; for tier (b): GFlop/s (2*d*iterations*nnz / time, matches YangNYLDXJ022's own formula exactly, kept separate from tier (a)'s metric since they measure genuinely different things - see notes_on_fairness)
secondaryms; k (realized eigenpair count, tier a); for tier (b), speedup vs. MKL sparse-BLAS baseline (matches YangNYLDXJ022's own comparison exactly)
correctnessPRIMARY (required) gate, tier (a): per-eigenpair relative residual, `||A*x - lambda*B*x|| / ||lambda|| < 1e-10` (matches ShiLXSH21's own artifact-documented metric exactly; the README states "typically around 1e-13" is achieved in practice, so this spec's 1e-10 threshold is set well above the literature-reported typical value, not arbitrarily, pending confirmation of the paper's own actual gating threshold — see open_questions). ADDITIONALLY required: completeness of the found spectrum inside [lambda_lo, lambda_hi] — no established numeric check for this exists in the surveyed literature (a polynomial-filtered method can, in principle, miss eigenpairs near the interval's edges), so this spec requires a documented cross-check (e.g. inertia-counting via a shift-and-count LDL^T factorization at lambda_lo and lambda_hi) be run at least once per configuration to validate k is not silently truncated — a spec addition not evidenced by either source paper, flagged as such. For tier (b), no correctness check exists in YangNYLDXJ022's own artifact (see survey.md); this spec requires the standard SpMV correctness convention already established by this project's `spmv` track (dense- reference comparison at a stated tolerance) be applied to the underlying `A^d*x` kernel's output, reusing that track's spec rather than inventing a new one for this variant.
Fairness notes
  • This spec covers SYMMETRIC (and symmetric-definite-generalized) eigenproblems only, since every one of this track's 5 papers is symmetric or symmetric-definite-generalized. This is a genuine, not superficial, gap in this track's own paper coverage (the direct eigensolver-track analogue of the `qr` track's TSQR/CAQR gap) and is disclosed here rather than filled with a fabricated nonsymmetric variant no surveyed paper evidences.
  • Full spectrum vs. partial (k eigenpairs) is treated as a genuinely different CLAIM, not a size variant of the same claim, following the task's own design brief directly: variants 1-2 report GFLOP/s (a quantity meaningful when the full N-sized problem is solved); variant 3 reports eigenpairs/second for its interval-bounded tier, since reusing a FLOP-based metric there would silently reward a wider interval (more eigenpairs, more real work) and a narrower one (less work, but also "less achieved") with the SAME apparent GFLOP/s if the per-eigenpair cost happened to be similar — the metric itself must change with the claim, not just the input size.
  • Residual/orthogonality normalization is standardized PER VARIANT to whichever surveyed paper's own convention is most concretely evidenced for that variant (max-entrywise for the dense full-spectrum variant, per the ASE/cuEV successor's own test suite; column-wise-Frobenius- over-spectral-norm for the distributed tridiagonal variant, per LiaoLLR21's own explicit formula; per-eigenpair relative residual for the generalized partial-spectrum tier, per ShiLXSH21's own artifact) — RATHER than forcing one convention across all three variants, since survey.md documents FOUR distinct residual normalizations already in active use across just 3 of this track's 5 papers, and picking a single "winner" convention would misrepresent what each source paper's own artifact actually validates against.
  • Correctness checks are REQUIRED and ALWAYS RUN (not compile-time-gated or run in a separate, optional binary) in every variant of this spec — a direct response to this track being the FOURTH consecutive track across this project's three dense-factorization-track surveys where a correctness check exists in an artifact but is disabled or separated from the performance-measurement path by default (WangHZSJWDZ25's EVD4SC2025 `#if CHECH_EVD_RESULT_ENABLE` flag being this track's own instance). The ASE/cuEV successor artifact's own fix (correctness always-run in a separate but MANDATORY test suite, not an optional compile flag) is the model this spec's "always run, report separately from timing if needed" requirement follows.
  • Timing statistic is fixed to median (with min/max reported) across every variant, diverging from every stated statistic found in this track's own literature: best-of-6 (LiaoLLR21, the most granular best-of-N structure found across this entire project's surveys), best-of-3 (the ASE/cuEV successor artifact), and mean-over-50-fixed- iterations (YangNYLDXJ022) — no paper in this track states a median.
Open questions
  • ShiLXSH21's own paper fulltext (OA link is an OSTI landing page) was not read during this survey pass — the search-interval-polynomial- degree relationship (how the pEVSL filter's own polynomial degree is chosen or disclosed per interval/model) was not recoverable from the artifact's README/config alone and is required before eigensolver-polynomial-filtered-partial-spectrum-kernel's polynomial_degree parameter can be fully specified for tier (a).
  • The exact gating threshold ShiLXSH21's own paper uses for its stated "typically around 1e-13" relative-residual metric (as opposed to a typically-observed value) was not found — this spec's 1e-10 threshold is a conservative spec default pending confirmation.
  • WangHZSJWDZ25's EVD4SC2025 `CHECH_EVD_RESULT_ENABLE` flag's default state (on/off in the shipped build configuration) was not confirmed - needed to know whether this paper's own reported performance numbers were measured with or without its correctness check active.
  • The ASE/cuEV successor artifact's own `tol_eval`/`tol_evec` tolerance functions' exact formulas (referenced in `solve_test.cu` but not themselves fetched, likely in `ref.hpp`) were not extracted - this spec's 1e-10 thresholds for eigensolver-dense-symmetric-full-spectrum-kernel are conservative spec defaults pending confirmation against the actual size/scale-dependent formula the source artifact uses.
  • Whether YangNYLDXJ026's own paper (not read as fulltext) reports ANY correctness/accuracy check for the polynomial preconditioner's downstream effect on solver convergence, as opposed to the raw matrix-power-kernel's own performance, was not investigated - needed to know whether this spec's tier-(b) reuse of the `spmv` track's correctness convention is a reasonable substitute or misses something the paper itself actually validates.
  • Whether this track's 5-paper input set omitting a genuinely nonsymmetric eigensolver reflects a real corpus gap or a narrower selection within a broader available set was not investigated during this pass.
gemv5 papers4 variants

Dense and mixed/low-precision matrix-vector multiplication (including the batch=1..~32 "thin-GEMM" regime that dominates LLM autoregressive decode, and format-compressed variants where decompression cannot be factored out of the timed kernel); a fundamentally memory-bandwidth- bound operation, unlike GEMM, so GB/s and roofline fraction (not GFLOP/s) are this track's primary metric.

y[M] = alpha*A[M,K]*x[K] + beta*y[M] (beta=0 unless noted); A may be full-precision (fp64/fp32/fp16) or a packed low-bit format (INT4/INT3/ INT2, optionally nonuniform-bitwidth across columns as in QIGen) paired with per-group FP16 scale/zero-point tensors, in which case "A" in the byte-accounting below means the packed representation actually read, not a hypothetical dequantized dense array. The harness must record which of these representations was measured, since bandwidth is dominated almost entirely by how A is stored, not by x or y.

gemv-dense-kernelsteady-state kernel bandwidth on full-precision dense GEMV across a shape sweep spanning tall-skinny, short-fat, and square aspect ratios, with an explicit 3-state cache axis (see cache_state below) instead of a naive hot/cold binary — the common-denominator variant grounded directly in TLR-MVM's own dense-GEMV comparison harness (`benchmark/cuda/bench_mvm_cuda_fp32.cpp`), the only paper in this survey shipping a general-purpose, precision-parameterized dense-GEMV micro-benchmark rather than an application-embedded one.
inputs
suiteunion of shapes actually exercised across the surveyed papers, spanning three aspect-ratio classes plus a spec-added square sweep (no surveyed paper isolates a square-only GEMV sweep, so this class is this spec's own addition, flagged here rather than silently presented as literature-derived).
selectiontall-skinny: M >> K, sourced from GPU-DPF's table shapes (the only surveyed source with an explicit, extreme tall-skinny sweep) even though GPU-DPF's own kernel is compute- not memory-bound (see survey.md Divergences) — here the shapes are reused as a materialized dense-GEMV stress point, not as a reproduction of GPU-DPF's own (non-memory-bound) methodology. short-fat: K >> M, sourced from PackKV's KV-cache context-length sweep (context length = K, head_dim = M). square: M=K, a spec-added synthetic power-of-2 sweep for roofline-fraction baselining, mirroring how gemm-square-kernel's own sweep was constructed in benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml.
recommended_subsettall-skinny (M,K): (16384,16), (65536,16), (262144,16), (1048576,16) (GPU-DPF's table row-counts x entry_size, verbatim). short-fat (M,K): (128,32768), (128,131072) (head_dim=128 x context length 32K/128K, PackKV's own tested context lengths). square (M=K): 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 16384 (spec-added, power-of-2 roofline-fraction baseline). 11 shapes total.
dense_operandprecision in {fp64, fp32, fp16}; A, x initialized U(-1,1) (same convention as benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml, for cross-track consistency; no surveyed GEMV paper states an initialization range at all, so this is purely this spec's choice, not a correction of any stated practice).
protocol
cache_statethree explicit, separately-reported states (a deliberate refinement of a naive hot/cold binary — see survey.md Divergences, since none of this track's realistic shapes let the O(M*K) matrix be cache-resident across independent calls the way GEMM's LibShalom setup does): (1) "cold-matrix" — default state, matrix A freshly read from DRAM/HBM every call because it is always >> LLC/L2 at these shapes (no explicit eviction trick needed at this scale, unlike CPU GEMM); this matches TLR-MVM's own harness, which performs one H2D copy before the loop and relies on the matrix simply being too large for GPU L2 to matter. (2) "hot-vector-reuse" — x (and the y accumulator) are kept resident in L1/L2/shared memory for the duration of a single kernel invocation, exploiting that O(M+K) is always cache-sized; report whether the measured kernel achieves this (inspect vendor profiler L2 hit rate for x's address range) rather than assuming it — this is the axis MARLIN's own design targets (README: "activations are essentially always fetched from L2 cache"). (3) "sram-resident-extreme" — OPTIONAL, only reported when the target hardware supports whole-operand on-chip residency across many calls (e.g. Cerebras wafer-scale SRAM, or a matrix small enough to genuinely fit LLC); report as a separate, clearly-labeled number, never averaged with (1) or (2), matching how this spec treats TLR-MVM's 92.58 PB/s Cerebras headline result as a distinct data point.
preprocessingone-shot device-buffer allocation and H2D residency of A, x, y; excluded from the timed region and reported once, separately (matches TLR-MVM's own harness structure: cudaMemcpy happens once before the timed loop).
warmup20
reps200 (deliberately higher than benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml's 50-200 range, since GEMV calls at these shapes are typically microsecond-scale and memory-latency-dominated, hence noisier per-call than compute-bound GEMM of comparable wall time — this generalizes TLR-MVM's own unfixed `loopsize` CLI parameter into an explicit default)
statisticmedian (report min and max) — TLR-MVM's own harness already uses median (`std::sort` + middle element); this spec keeps that choice rather than switching to MARLIN's mean, for consistency with benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml's stated preference for median over mean/min across this benchmark suite
timerper platform class, same convention as benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml: GPU - device-side kernel time (CUDA events, matching TLR-MVM's own `cudaEventRecord`/ `cudaEventElapsedTime` + `cudaDeviceSynchronize`/ `cudaEventSynchronize` bracketing, which prevents the async-queue leakage risk noted for GPU-DPF in survey.md); CPU - monotonic wall clock (matches QIGen's likely AMD EPYC target, though its own timer API was not recoverable from the extracted text).
timing_scopekernel only; H2D/D2H excluded (one-shot, see preprocessing above)
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once, before the steady-state loop
metric
primaryGB/s = bytes_moved / time, where bytes_moved = M*K*sizeof(A_dtype) + K*sizeof(x_dtype) + M*sizeof(y_dtype) — TLR-MVM's own formula (`bench_mvm_cuda_fp32.cpp`: `m*n*sizeof(float) + (m+n)* sizeof(float)`), generalized here to arbitrary dtype widths so it also covers the packed-low-bit case in gemv-quantized-weight-kernel
secondaryGFLOP/s (2*M*K/time); roofline_fraction = achieved GB/s / device peak memory bandwidth (report whether peak is the vendor spec sheet or a locally STREAM-measured number — the two can differ by 10-15% per MARLIN's own README note about ECC overhead on A10)
correctnessmax relative error vs. a same-precision-family vendor BLAS reference (cuBLAS `Xgemv` on GPU, MKL/OpenBLAS `Xgemv` on CPU) at fp64: < 1e-6 for fp64, < 1e-3 for fp32, < 1e-2 for fp16 (identical tolerances to benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml for cross-track consistency). This is a deliberate departure from every surveyed paper's own practice: MARLIN and TLR-MVM both check *mean* (not max) relative error, and neither states a threshold as strict as what a max-based gate implies at fp32 — flagged explicitly here, not silently adopted, per the design instructions' fairness principles.
gemv-quantized-weight-kernelsteady-state kernel bandwidth for the batch=1 (single-token decode, the literal "vector" case) regime of mixed/low-precision LLM weight-matrix x FP16-activation GEMV — in scope for this track rather than split into a separate quantized-gemv track because 3 of this track's 5 input papers (QIGen, MARLIN, PackKV) are exactly this workload; unlike GEMM's quantized-gemm split (see benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml's summary), this track's own literature is dominated by the quantized case, so keeping it here reflects what the track's papers actually do rather than a policy choice made in advance.
inputs
suitereal LLM linear-layer shapes, MARLIN's `bench.py` `MODELS` dict, reproduced verbatim (the only surveyed source giving concrete per-layer M,K pairs, and QIGen's own LLaMA 7B/13B/30B target models overlap this family)
selectionall 4 linear-layer shapes per model (QKV-fused proj, O-proj, gate+up-fused MLP proj, down-proj) for Llama7B/13B/33B/65B, plus Falcon180B's 2 fused shapes (parallel-attention+FC layer fusion)
recommended_subsetLlama7B: (4096,3*4096), (4096,4096), (4096,2*10752), (10752,4096). Llama13B: (5120,3*5120), (5120,5120), (5120,2*13568), (13568,5120). Llama33B: (6656,3*6656), (6656,6656), (6656,2*17664), (17664,6656). Llama65B: (8192,3*8192), (8192,8192), (8192,2*21760), (21760,8192). Falcon180B: (14848,14848*5+1024), (14848*5,14848). 18 shapes total (M,K) — verbatim from MARLIN's own `bench.py`.
dense_operandweight precision in {INT4, INT3, INT2} (QIGen's 2/3/4-bit + MARLIN's INT4; nonuniform per-column bitwidth, QIGen's specific contribution, is an OPTIONAL sub-mode — report which columns use which bitwidth when exercised); activation/output FP16; quantization group size in {-1 (per-column/per-row), 16, 32, 64, 128} (union of MARLIN's {-1,128} and QIGen's {16,32,64,128})
protocol
batch1 (fixed; the multi-token/batched regime is gemv-batched-decode below)
preprocessingone-shot weight packing/reshuffling into the kernel's preferred on-disk layout (MARLIN's `Layer.pack(...)`) and scale-tensor layout; excluded from the timed region, reported once
warmup10 (MARLIN's own script uses warmup=1; this spec raises it to 10 to better stabilize GPU clocks before timing, consistent with every other single-device variant in this benchmark suite)
reps50 (MARLIN's own script uses 10; raised for a more stable median — see statistic below)
statisticmedian (report min and max) — a deliberate departure from MARLIN's own mean-based statistic, for the same reason given in gemv-dense-kernel and in benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml
timerdevice-side kernel time (CUDA events); MARLIN's own script uses a host-side `time.time()` bracket with `torch.cuda.synchronize()` calls, which is equivalent in effect but CUDA events are preferred per this suite's stated convention
anti_throttlingMARLIN's own script inserts a 1-second `time.sleep()` between successive benchmark configs specifically to avoid GPU clock throttling biasing later configurations in a sweep — this spec keeps that practice as an explicit protocol step (not optional), since it is the only anti-throttling measure found anywhere in this track's surveyed code and is cheap to keep
timing_scopekernel only; weight packing excluded (see preprocessing above)
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once
metric
primaryGB/s = (bits_per_weight/8)*M*K [packed weight] + 2*K [FP16 activation] + 2*M [FP16 output] + 2*(K/groupsize)*M [FP16 scales] bytes, divided by time — this is MARLIN's own `benchmark_quant` formula (`4*B.numel()` where `B.numel()=K*N/8` for INT4 packing = 0.5 byte/element), generalized to arbitrary bit-width
secondaryTFLOP/s (2*M*K/time); speedup vs. a dense FP16 GEMV of the same shape (MARLIN's own comparison baseline, `benchmark_dense` in the same script)
correctnessmean relative error vs. a dense FP16 GEMV computed from the SAME dequantized reference weights (not the pre-quantization original weights, isolating kernel bugs from quantization error) < 1e-3 — this is MARLIN's own tolerance and check construction (`test.py`: `torch.mean(torch.abs(C-C_ref))/torch.mean(torch.abs( C_ref)) < 0.001`), kept as-is here (unlike gemv-dense-kernel, which switches to a max-based gate) because quantization error is not i.i.d. across output elements the way floating-point rounding error roughly is, making a strict max-based gate liable to reject numerically-correct kernels at outlier-heavy elements — a real difference from the dense case, not an inconsistency for its own sake.
gemv-batched-decodethroughput across the batch-size sweep that crosses GEMV's memory-bound/compute-bound roofline knee — MARLIN's own central empirical claim (near-ideal 4x quantization speedup sustained up to batch ~16-32, degrading above that as the operation becomes compute-bound) is itself a benchmark-methodology finding, not just a result, so this variant makes the batch axis a first-class, always-swept dimension rather than a single fixed point.
inputs
suitesame LLM linear-layer shape list as gemv-quantized-weight-kernel
selectionsame 18 (M,K) shapes, INT4/groupsize=128 fixed (MARLIN's own default sweep configuration) as the representative precision for this variant, since batch behavior is the axis under test
recommended_subsetsame 18 shapes as gemv-quantized-weight-kernel; batch in {1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256,512,1024,2048} (MARLIN's own "ALL=True" full sweep, verbatim)
dense_operandINT4 weight (groupsize=128), FP16 activation/output (fixed; this is the one precision point MARLIN's own batch sweep was run at)
protocol
preprocessingsame as gemv-quantized-weight-kernel
warmup10
reps50
statisticmedian (report min and max)
timerdevice-side kernel time (CUDA events)
anti_throttlingsame 1-second inter-config sleep as gemv-quantized-weight-kernel
timing_scopekernel only
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once
required_outputa roofline-fraction-vs-batch curve (achieved GB/s / peak bandwidth, and achieved TFLOP/s / peak compute, both vs. batch size) is a REQUIRED reported artifact for this variant, not optional — the batch at which the curve crosses from bandwidth-bound to compute-bound IS the finding this variant is designed to surface, matching MARLIN's own headline plot
metric
primaryTFLOP/s (2*batch*M*K/time) — primary here (unlike the other three GEMV variants, which use GB/s) because at the large end of this variant's batch sweep the kernel is compute- not memory-bound, so GB/s alone would understate what changes across the sweep
secondaryGB/s (same formula as gemv-quantized-weight-kernel, with activation/output terms scaled by batch); speedup vs. dense FP16 GEMM of the same (batch,M,K) shape
correctnesssame as gemv-quantized-weight-kernel, checked at every swept batch size (not just batch=1)
gemv-e2e-compressed-formatend-to-end throughput for GEMV embedded in a compressed/structured storage format where decompression is NOT separable from the per-call kernel by the algorithm's own design (unlike this benchmark suite's usual "preprocessing excluded, reported separately" rule) — covers TLR-MVM's tile-low-rank compressed MVM and PackKV's fused decompression+GEMV, the two surveyed papers whose own methodology times decompression/decoding together with the arithmetic because there is no natural "already decoded" state to start a kernel-only clock from.
inputs
suiteTLR-MVM's seismic-redatuming and MAVIS adaptive-optics datasets (Zenodo-hosted, linked from the repo README; exact matrix dimensions not recoverable from available sources — open question) and PackKV's 6-model x 6-benchmark KV-cache sweep
selectionwhichever datasets/models are actually available to the harness (both source datasets require registration/download per their Zenodo pages); no independent inclusion criterion beyond "use the artifact's own shipped datasets/models", since this variant exists to reproduce two specific papers' own end-to-end numbers under a common protocol, not to define a new standard suite
recommended_subsetTLR-MVM: whichever TLR rank/tile-size configuration the artifact ships as its default test config (not specified in the README text extracted in this pass — open question). PackKV: the 6 models x {32K, 128K}-token context length points already listed in survey.md
dense_operandTLR-MVM: precision per its own build target (fp32/complex-fp32 shown in the benchmark dir; the paper's Cerebras run uses whatever precision the CS-2 SDK exposes, not confirmed here). PackKV: FP16/BF16.
protocol
preprocessingTLR-MVM: one-shot tile-rank decomposition (SVD-based low-rank factorization of the dense matrix into tiles) — this IS excludable and reported separately, since it happens once and the compressed representation is then reused across many GEMV calls (unlike PackKV below). PackKV: NONE excludable — decompression is fused into the per-call kernel by construction (see claim above); the entire fused kernel call is the timed unit.
warmup10
reps50
statisticmedian (report min and max), except where the artifact only exposes an aggregate number (flag explicitly if so, per the same caveat CA3DMM required in benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml's gemm-distributed-e2e variant)
timerdevice-side kernel time (CUDA events) for the GPU-only (PackKV) case; for TLR-MVM's own Cerebras run, whatever the CS-2 SDK's native timing mechanism is (not confirmed — open question)
timing_scopetwo numbers, both reported: "compressed/fused kernel" (the variant's headline number: TLR-MVM's compressed-format read + multiply, or PackKV's fused decompression+GEMV) and "dense baseline" (TLR-MVM's own dense cuBLAS/MKL comparison per gemv-dense-kernel's protocol; PackKV's own cuBLAS-on-uncompressed comparison) at the SAME shape, so the compression benefit is always reported as a ratio of two numbers measured under this spec's own protocol, not lifted from the papers' own (differently protocoled) baseline numbers
preprocessing_reportedTLR-MVM's tile-rank decomposition reported separately, once, as described above; PackKV has no separable preprocessing to report
metric
primaryGB/s (compressed/fused kernel) and GB/s (dense baseline), both reported, plus their ratio as "bandwidth amplification factor"
secondaryfor TLR-MVM's Cerebras-scale run specifically (not reproducible on commodity hardware): report the paper's own aggregate PB/s number as a separate, clearly-labeled reference point, not averaged into this variant's commodity-hardware numbers
correctnessTLR-MVM: mean relative error vs. dense reference (matches the artifact's own `checkcorrectness` function; no fixed threshold enforced in the shipped benchmark binary itself — this spec requires < 1e-2 be enforced as a pass/fail gate, since TLR compression is inherently lossy and 1e-2 matches this suite's own fp16-class tolerance). PackKV: accuracy-drop check against the paper's own stated "same and minimum accuracy drop as SOTA quantization" criterion (application-level, not a numeric per-kernel tolerance — an acknowledged gap, see open_questions).
Fairness notes
  • GEMV's cache-state axis does not transfer cleanly from GEMM: this spec replaces GEMM's LibShalom-derived hot/cold-whole-matrix binary with a 3-state axis (cold-matrix / hot-vector-reuse / sram-resident-extreme) in gemv-dense-kernel, because at every shape this track's own papers actually use, the O(M*K) matrix operand is far larger than any commodity cache level, making a literal "matrix-in-cache" hot state either unreachable or physically meaningless — while the O(M+K) vector operand is always cache-sized, and whether a kernel exploits that (MARLIN does, explicitly, by design) is the real cache-related axis this track's literature actually varies on.
  • Every surveyed paper's own correctness check uses either a *mean* relative-error statistic (MARLIN, TLR-MVM) or an application-level accuracy-drop check (QIGen, PackKV) rather than a *max* per-element tolerance; GPU-DPF is the sole exception with an exact-match check (meaningful only because its outputs are exact integers). This spec's gemv-dense-kernel variant uses max relative error anyway, for consistency with benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml and because a mean-based gate can hide a single catastrophically wrong output element behind many correct ones — the gemv-quantized-weight-kernel variant is the one deliberate exception (kept as mean-based, matching MARLIN's own practice), because quantization error's non-i.i.d. distribution across elements makes a strict max-based gate liable to reject a numerically-fine kernel over a small number of naturally higher-error outlier elements — see that variant's correctness field for the full reasoning.
  • MARLIN's own benchmark script inserts a 1-second sleep between configs specifically to prevent GPU clock throttling from biasing later runs in a sweep — the only anti-throttling protocol step found anywhere in this track's 5 surveyed papers/artifacts. This spec promotes it from an implementation detail of one paper's script to an explicit, required protocol field (`anti_throttling`) in both variants that inherit MARLIN's shape list, since a benchmark harness that silently drops it would produce numbers biased by whichever config happened to run first in a sweep.
  • GPU-DPF is included in this survey (it is in the track's own input list, `data/track_inputs/gemv.json`) but its own protocol is deliberately NOT used as a template for any variant above, because its kernel is compute- (PRF-evaluation-) bound rather than memory-bandwidth-bound, unlike every other paper in this track and unlike this spec's own primary-metric choice (GB/s / roofline fraction). Its table shapes ARE reused as a tall-skinny stress point in gemv-dense-kernel's inputs, but as a materialized dense-matrix stress test, not as a reproduction of GPU-DPF's own (non-memory-bound) methodology — this distinction is stated explicitly in that variant's `selection` field so it is not mistaken for endorsing GPU-DPF's own benchmark as directly comparable to the others.
  • Matrix/vector initialization range (U(-1,1)) is this spec's own choice, matching benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml for cross-track consistency; no surveyed GEMV paper states an initialization range at all (not even QIGen's `rand()`-based CPU generator, which is visible in TLR-MVM's benchmark source but not tied to a distribution statement in any paper text read in this pass).
Open questions
  • QIGen's and PackKV's exact timing protocol (warmup/repetition counts, timer API) could not be recovered from the extracted arXiv fulltext in this pass; QIGen's `generate.py` (55KB) and PackKV's `evaluation/evaluation.py` (53KB) were listed but not read line-by-line — either would likely resolve this.
  • TLR-MVM's SC'23 paper PDF text could not be extracted via WebFetch (both the ACM DL link and the eScholarship OA mirror returned undecodable binary/stream content to the fetch tool, and no local PDF-to-text utility — `pdftotext`/`pdftoppm` — was available in this environment). The paper's own stated protocol for the Cerebras-scale TLR-compressed run (as opposed to the dense cuBLAS comparison harness read directly from source) is therefore not confirmed from primary text, including the exact tile-rank/tile-size configuration and the seismic/MAVIS matrix dimensions — needed to fully specify gemv-e2e-compressed-format's `recommended_subset` for TLR-MVM.
  • Whether TLR-MVM's Cerebras CS-2 run uses a timing mechanism comparable to CUDA events (a native SDK profiling counter, a wall-clock wrapper, or something else) is unknown — needed before gemv-e2e-compressed-format's Cerebras-scale secondary metric can be treated as protocol-comparable to this spec's other numbers rather than a purely reference/context figure.
  • GPU-DPF's `dpf_cpp.BATCH_SIZE` compiled constant (the implicit batch size in its own `test_gpu_dpf_perf` default) is not visible from the Python source alone; would need to build the C++ extension or read its source to confirm — relevant only if a future revision of this spec decides to include a GPU-DPF-templated variant after all.
  • No surveyed paper gives a numeric max-relative-error tolerance for dense (non-quantized) GEMV; the 1e-6/1e-3/1e-2 values in gemv-dense-kernel are carried over from benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml for cross-track consistency, not derived from any GEMV-specific source, and should be revisited against real reproduction runs.
blas-level1-24 papers4 variants

Vector-vector (level-1: dot, axpy, nrm2, scal) and matrix-vector (level-2: gemv, symmetric symv, triangular trsv) BLAS operations, as produced by the compiler/DSL/generator systems this track's 4 papers actually are (only 1 of 4, fBLAS, benchmarks named BLAS routines directly against a reference library the other way this spec's other tracks do; the other 3 evaluate a generator whose output includes BLAS-L1/L2-shaped kernels among a broader kernel set — see survey.md Divergences). Overwhelmingly memory-bandwidth-bound at every vector/matrix length large enough to exceed L1 cache, so GB/s is this track's primary metric, same as the gemv track.

level-1: r = sum_i(x_i*y_i) [dot], y = a*x+y [axpy], r = ||x||_2 [nrm2], x = a*x [scal]. level-2: y = alpha*A*x + beta*y [gemv, A general MxK]; y = alpha*A*x + beta*y [symv, A symmetric MxM, only the canonical upper- or lower-triangle stored/read — half the memory traffic of a general gemv at the same M, a genuine byte-accounting difference this spec's metric formulas must reflect, not just a different access pattern]; x = A^-1*x [trsv, A triangular — NOT evidenced in any of this track's 4 surveyed papers, kept as an explicitly out-of-evidence optional op, see open_questions].

blas-l1-vector-kernelsteady-state bandwidth for level-1 vector ops (dot, axpy, nrm2, scal) across a vector-length sweep spanning L1 through DRAM- resident working sets, with an explicit reduction-accuracy axis for the two reduction ops (dot, nrm2) — the common-denominator variant, grounded directly in fBLAS's own `sdot`/`ddot` evaluation harness (`evaluation/individual_modules/`, `evaluation/cpu_comparison/host_dot.cpp`), the only paper in this track whose level-1 benchmark code was read in full.
inputs
suitesynthetic vectors, no external dataset (matches fBLAS's own on-the-fly-generated inputs for its memory-bound DOT/GEMV experiments)
selectionvector length n swept across the working-set sizes that cross each cache level's capacity on a representative x86 target (32KB L1, 1MB L2, 30MB L3 — the same rough figures this spec's other tracks assume where a specific target isn't pinned); no surveyed paper states which cache levels its own sweep was designed to cross (fBLAS's `n` is a free CLI parameter with no stated design rationale beyond "must be a multiple of width"), so this selection is this spec's own construction, not literature-derived.
recommended_subsetn (elements, fp32) in {2048 (~8KB/vector, fits L1 alongside the other operand), 8192 (~32KB/vector, at the L1 boundary), 65536 (~256KB/vector, fits L2), 1048576 (~4MB/vector, exceeds typical L2, fits L3), 8388608 (~32MB/vector, at/beyond typical L3, DRAM-bound), 67108864 (~256MB/vector, unambiguously DRAM-bound)}; each n must additionally be a multiple of the target's SIMD/streaming width (fBLAS's own constraint, `width=64` for its `sdot`/`sgemv` FPGA config — generalize to whatever width the CPU/FPGA/GPU target actually uses).
dense_operandprecision in {fp32, fp64} (fBLAS's own `sdot`/`ddot` split; neither fp16 nor int8/uint8 reduction is evidenced for a "plain" level-1 dot/axpy/nrm2/scal in this track's 4 papers — the one mixed-int8/int32-accumulator reduction found, VeGen's, is a distinct enough case (ISA-targeting, not numerical-accuracy-targeting) to get its own variant below rather than being folded in here)
protocol
reduction_accuracyfor dot and nrm2 specifically (NOT axpy/scal, which have no reduction step): report results at BOTH the target's natural/ default accumulation order (whatever a straightforward sequential or SIMD-width-wide-streaming accumulation produces — fBLAS's own dot kernel, inferred from its `width`-parameterized streaming JSON config, is presumably this) AND a compensated (Kahan or pairwise-tree) summation variant, at the LARGEST swept n (67108864) where floating-point reduction-order error actually accumulates to a measurable level — none of this track's 4 papers discusses summation order or compensated summation at all (see survey.md Divergences), so this axis is this spec's own addition to close a real gap the instructions call out ("reduction-accuracy considerations for dot/norm"), not a reproduction of any paper's own practice.
preprocessingone-shot buffer allocation/H2D (or on-fabric generation, matching fBLAS's own choice for these specific memory-bound experiments) of x, y; excluded from the timed region, reported once
warmup10
reps100 (fBLAS's own harness takes `-r <runs>` with no fixed default — this spec fixes 100 as an explicit default; higher than the gemm-track's 50 default because level-1 vector ops at small-to-mid n are even shorter-duration than GEMV, hence noisier per call)
statisticmean AND sample standard deviation, both reported (fBLAS's own choice, `host_dot.cpp`: `stddev=sqrt(stddev/runs)`) — this is a deliberate departure from this benchmark suite's usual median-preferred convention (see benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml, benchspecs/gemv/spec.yaml), kept here because fBLAS is the one paper in either track surveyed so far to report a formal dispersion statistic rather than just min/max or a single number, and that dispersion information (not just a de-noised central-tendency number) is itself useful for a vector-length sweep this short-duration; ALSO report min and max alongside, so a reader who wants this suite's usual median-based comparison can still approximate it.
timerper platform class: FPGA (OpenCL) - host-side wall clock (`current_time_usecs()`) wrapping `enqueueTask`+`finish()` for every kernel/helper queue, i.e. an explicit full-pipeline drain before stopping the clock (fBLAS's own convention, read directly from `host_dot.cpp`); GPU - device-side kernel time (CUDA/HIP events), matching this suite's convention elsewhere; CPU - monotonic wall clock.
timing_scopekernel only; data-transfer time (H2D/D2H, or the FPGA equivalent `enqueueWriteBuffer`/`enqueueReadBuffer`) is measured SEPARATELY in its own accumulator and reported alongside, never folded into the compute-time metric — this directly follows fBLAS's own code-level separation of `transfer_times` from `fblas_times` in `host_dot.cpp`, the most literal match to this benchmark suite's own "preprocessing never silently mixed into per-iteration time" principle found in either track surveyed so far.
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once, before the steady- state loop; per-run transfer time (see timing_scope) is reported per-run, not amortized as a one-shot preprocessing cost, since fBLAS's own harness measures it fresh every iteration rather than once
metric
primaryGB/s = data_bytes/time, where data_bytes = op-dependent: dot = 2*n*sizeof(dtype) (two input vectors, scalar output not counted — fBLAS's own formula); axpy = 3*n*sizeof(dtype) (x read, y read, y written); nrm2 = n*sizeof(dtype) (one input vector, scalar output not counted); scal = 2*n*sizeof(dtype) (x read, x written)
secondaryGOps/s (fBLAS's own term; = 2*n/time for dot [multiply- add pair per element], = 2*n/time for axpy, = 2*n/time for nrm2 [multiply + add per element, sqrt not counted], = n/time for scal); for the reduction_accuracy comparison specifically, also report the two variants' relative slowdown (compensated vs. natural-order) as a distinct number, since paying for accuracy at zero measured cost would itself be a finding worth surfacing
correctness|result - reference| < flteps, where reference is OpenBLAS/MKL's `Xdot`/`Xaxpy`/`Xnrm2`/`Xscal` (fBLAS's own reference library choice) and flteps = 1e-4 for fp32, 1e-6 for fp64 — fBLAS's own hardcoded values, read directly from `host_gemv.cpp` (lines ~194-198; the same constants are reused for dot in `host_dot.cpp`, which references `flteps` without re-declaring it). This is a deliberate departure from this suite's usual max-RELATIVE-error convention (benchspecs/gemm/ spec.yaml, benchspecs/gemv/spec.yaml): dot and nrm2 return a single scalar that can legitimately be near zero (e.g. two near-orthogonal vectors), where a relative-error gate becomes unstable/meaningless — an ABSOLUTE tolerance is the more defensible choice for these two specific ops, and fBLAS's own choice is kept as-is rather than overridden, unlike this spec's treatment of TLR-MVM/MARLIN's tolerances in the gemv track.
blas-l2-gemv-symv-kernelsteady-state bandwidth for level-2 matrix-vector ops, covering both general GEMV (fBLAS's `sgemv`/`dgemv`) and symmetry-exploiting SYMV (SySTeC's `ssymv`, which reads only the canonical triangle) at matched M — the pairing exists specifically to make the symmetric-storage bandwidth *reduction* (not just a different access pattern) a first-class, measured comparison rather than two unrelated numbers, since that reduction is exactly what SySTeC's own compiler is built to automatically exploit.
inputs
suitesynthetic dense (for gemv) and dense-symmetric (for symv, only the canonical triangle populated/read) matrices
selectionM=K square (gemv) and M=M square-symmetric (symv) sweep, sized around fBLAS's own tile configuration (2048x2048 tiles, `sgemv.json`) since that is this track's only concrete GEMV tile-size evidence; SySTeC gives no concrete SYMV problem size in the sources read in this pass (open question)
recommended_subsetM=K in {512, 1024, 2048, 4096} for both gemv and symv (symv's matrix is square by construction; gemv's is also square here for a matched, apples-to-apples comparison at each M — a rectangular gemv sweep is out of scope for this variant since SYMV has no rectangular analogue to compare against; use gemv-dense-kernel in benchspecs/gemv/spec.yaml for a rectangular-shape sweep instead)
dense_operandprecision in {fp32, fp64} (matches fBLAS's own `sgemv`/`dgemv` split; SySTeC/Finch's own precision choice for `ssymv.jl` not confirmed from the ~15-line kernel snippet read in this pass — assume fp64, Finch/Julia's default numeric type, flagged as an assumption in open_questions)
protocol
preprocessingone-shot allocation/residency; for symv specifically, the one-shot cost of packing A into its canonical-triangle storage layout (if the harness's input representation is a full dense matrix that must first be repacked) is also preprocessing, reported separately, once — NOT charged per-call, since a real symmetric-matrix application would populate the triangle directly rather than repack from a dense representation on every call
warmup20
reps200 (matches gemv-dense-kernel's reasoning in benchspecs/gemv/spec.yaml — memory-latency-bound, short-duration calls need more reps for a stable statistic)
statisticmean and stddev, matching blas-l1-vector-kernel's choice within this track for consistency (fBLAS's own convention); report min/max alongside as well
timersame per-platform rule as blas-l1-vector-kernel
timing_scopekernel only; H2D/D2H and any triangle-repacking (see preprocessing above) excluded
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once, before the steady- state loop
metric
primaryGB/s = data_bytes/time, where data_bytes(gemv) = M*K* sizeof(dtype) + K*sizeof(dtype) + M*sizeof(dtype) (matches gemv-dense-kernel's formula in benchspecs/gemv/spec.yaml exactly, for cross-track consistency), and data_bytes(symv) = (M*(M+1)/2)*sizeof(dtype) + M*sizeof(dtype) [x] + M*sizeof(dtype) [y] — HALF the matrix-read term relative to gemv at the same M, reflecting that only the canonical triangle is stored/read; a harness that reports symv's bandwidth using the GENERAL gemv formula (i.e. as if the full M*M matrix were read) would silently overstate its measured GB/s relative to what was actually moved — this is exactly the kind of byte-accounting error this spec's explicit per-op formula is meant to foreclose.
secondaryGFLOP/s (2*M*K for gemv, 2*M*M for symv — note FLOP count is NOT halved for symv the way byte count is, since the compiler still performs 2 useful multiply-adds per matrix element read, one for each of y[i] and y[j] per the symmetrization identity in survey.md — so symv's FLOP/byte ratio is genuinely 2x gemv's at the same M, which is the entire point of exploiting symmetry); bandwidth_reduction_factor = gemv_GB/s / symv_GB/s at matched M, reported as this variant's headline comparison number
correctnessmax relative error vs. OpenBLAS/MKL `Xgemv`/`Xsymv` < 1e-6 (fp64) / < 1e-3 (fp32) — matches gemv-dense-kernel's convention in benchspecs/gemv/spec.yaml (vector-output ops keep the max-relative-error convention; only the scalar-output level-1 reduction ops in blas-l1-vector-kernel use fBLAS's own absolute- tolerance convention, per that variant's correctness field).
blas-l1-mixed-precision-reductionmeasured (not merely instruction-count-estimated) runtime throughput of a mixed-precision, integer-accumulated dot-product reduction targeting fused dot-product ISA extensions (AVX512-VNNI and equivalents) — grounded in VeGen's own `dot_16x1x16_uint8_int8_int32` benchmark kernel, but this spec REQUIRES an actual wall-clock/cycle-accurate measurement rather than the static instruction-count comparison VeGen's own recovered evaluation figure appears to use (see survey.md, "Timing protocol... not recoverable" and the inference that VeGen's evaluation may be closer to a static-cost-model comparison for at least some reported numbers) — a fairness fix this spec makes explicitly, not a reproduction of an unconfirmed practice, since instruction count does not account for issue-width, port contention, or memory-system effects that a real dot-product kernel's throughput depends on.
inputs
suitesynthetic uint8 x int8 vector pairs (VeGen's own kernel signature; sourced conceptually from TVM's 2D-convolution inner loop per the paper's own description, though the exact convolution shape that produced this specific dot-product length was not recovered in this pass)
selectionvector length n a multiple of the target ISA's dot-product instruction width (16 for AVX512-VNNI's `vpdpbusd`, matching the kernel name's own "16x1x16" shape notation)
recommended_subsetn in {16, 64, 256, 1024, 4096, 16384} (the native instruction width and small multiples thereof, plus a DRAM-scale point at 16384 for a bandwidth-bound comparison point analogous to blas-l1-vector-kernel's sweep)
dense_operanduint8 x (input 1), int8 (input 2), int32 accumulator (VeGen's own precision combination; exact rationale for the uint8/int8 asymmetry, rather than int8/int8, not recovered — matches the real VNNI instruction's own signature, which is itself asymmetric for hardware-design reasons unrelated to this specific kernel)
protocol
preprocessingone-shot allocation; excluded, reported once
warmup10
reps200 (short-duration integer kernel, same reasoning as blas-l1-vector-kernel)
statisticmedian (report min and max) — this spec's own default choice (VeGen's own statistic, if any beyond the static instruction-count comparison, was not recovered)
timerCPU cycle counter (RDTSC or equivalent) or monotonic wall clock; report which
timing_scopekernel only
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once
also_reportstatic instruction count for the generated code (VeGen's own metric, per the one recovered figure) ALONGSIDE the measured runtime — not as a replacement for it, so this variant's numbers remain comparable to VeGen's own published figure while also closing the gap this spec's claim identifies
metric
primaryGOps/s (2*n/time, multiply-add pair per element, matching this track's other level-1 formula)
secondaryinstruction count (VeGen's own metric, see also_report); speedup vs. the reference auto-vectorizing compilers VeGen itself compares against (ICC, GCC, LLVM) on the same measured-runtime basis, not the static-instruction- count basis alone
correctnessexact match (bit-exact int32 accumulator output vs. a reference scalar-loop implementation) — integer accumulation has no floating-point rounding-order ambiguity, so an exact-match gate is both achievable and the correct (not merely convenient) choice here, unlike the floating-point reduction ops in blas-l1-vector-kernel.
blas-l1l2-generated-kernel-suiteaggregate throughput and correctness across a BROAD suite of compiler/DSL-generated level-1/2 (and adjacent) kernels compared against the same vendor-BLAS reference set — the variant this track most needs given that 3 of its 4 papers (Exo 2, SySTeC, and to a lesser extent VeGen) are fundamentally "benchmark a generator across many kernels" rather than "benchmark one named routine", unlike fBLAS and unlike the gemv track's papers. Exo 2's own claim ("comparable to or better than MKL, OpenBLAS, BLIS... on AVX2, AVX512, and Gemmini") is exactly this shape of claim; this variant's protocol exists to make that claim independently checkable per-kernel rather than only as an aggregate statement, since no per-kernel breakdown for the BLAS L1/2 subset specifically was recoverable from the sources read in this pass (see survey.md open_questions).
inputs
suitethe union of every level-1/2 kernel each generator in this track actually claims to produce/optimize: from Exo 2 (BLAS level 1, 2 — exact op list not recovered, see open_questions, so use the canonical BLAS L1/L2 op list: axpy, dot, nrm2, scal, gemv, symv, trsv), from SySTeC (ssymv specifically, its one confirmed level-1/2-adjacent op), from VeGen (the dot-product-reduction kernel class, per blas-l1-mixed-precision-reduction above)
selectionevery op named above, at the vector/matrix-length sweep defined in blas-l1-vector-kernel (level-1 ops) and blas-l2-gemv-symv-kernel (level-2 ops) respectively — this variant does not define a new size sweep, it defines a new AGGREGATION protocol over the other variants' own sweeps, run through whichever generator produced the kernel
recommended_subsetsame recommended_subset lists as blas-l1-vector-kernel and blas-l2-gemv-symv-kernel, run once per generator under test
dense_operandprecision as each generator's own paper claims support for (report which); no single precision is assumed across generators
protocol
preprocessingone-shot code generation/compilation for each kernel (Exo 2's scheduling-library-driven codegen, SySTeC's Finch-program compilation, VeGen's vectorizer output) — this is genuinely one-shot per (generator, kernel, size) triple in realistic use (compile once, run many times), so it is excluded from the timed region and reported separately, once per kernel, NOT amortized into the per-call throughput number
per_kernel_protocoleach individual kernel in the suite is measured under whichever of blas-l1-vector-kernel / blas-l2-gemv-symv-kernel's protocol fields (warmup, reps, statistic, timer, timing_scope) matches its BLAS level — no separate protocol is defined here beyond the aggregation rule below
correctness_gate_before_aggregationa kernel that fails its own variant's correctness gate (blas-l1-vector-kernel's or blas-l2-gemv-symv-kernel's, matched by op) is EXCLUDED from the aggregate and reported as a named failure, not silently dropped or averaged in at a 0/failing value — this directly follows the "N/A (unsupported)" principle benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml already established for cross-platform baseline gaps, applied here to cross-kernel correctness gaps within a single generator's own claimed suite
metric
primaryper-kernel GB/s or GFLOP/s (whichever the matched single-kernel variant defines as primary), reported individually for every kernel in the suite — never pre-aggregated before being reported
secondarygeometric mean speedup vs. the vendor-BLAS reference (MKL, OpenBLAS, BLIS — Exo 2's own named reference set, and the same set fBLAS's `cpu_comparison` and, by strong implication, SySTeC/Finch's typical baselines also use) across every kernel that PASSED its correctness gate; geometric mean (not arithmetic mean) because speedup ratios across a heterogeneous kernel suite should not be dominated by whichever kernel happens to have the largest absolute speedup, matching standard practice for cross-benchmark speedup aggregation
correctnessper-kernel, matching blas-l1-vector-kernel's or blas-l2-gemv-symv-kernel's tolerance by op (see correctness_gate_before_aggregation above for how failures are handled at the suite level, rather than a single suite-wide tolerance).
Fairness notes
  • fBLAS's own harness already separates transfer time from compute time in code (`transfer_times` vs. `fblas_times` in `host_dot.cpp`) — the most literal, code-level match to this benchmark suite's stated "preprocessing never silently mixed into per-iteration time" principle found across either track surveyed today (gemv or blas-level1-2). This spec's blas-l1-vector-kernel and blas-l2-gemv-symv-kernel variants keep that same per-run separation rather than collapsing it into a one-shot amortized preprocessing number, since fBLAS's own design measures transfer fresh every iteration (unlike, e.g., CA3DMM's one-shot process-grid setup in benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml's gemm-distributed-e2e variant).
  • Reduction-accuracy (compensated vs. natural-order summation) for dot/nrm2 is an axis the task instructions explicitly call out as key to this track, but NONE of the 4 surveyed papers discusses it — fBLAS's dot kernel almost certainly uses a fixed, simple streaming-order accumulation (inferred from its width-parameterized JSON config, not confirmed from a reduction-order statement in any source read), and VeGen's kernel sidesteps the question entirely via exact integer accumulation. This spec introduces the reduction_accuracy field in blas-l1-vector-kernel as its own addition to close this gap, not as a generalization of any paper's stated practice — flagged explicitly rather than presented as literature-derived.
  • Symmetric storage (SYMV) genuinely halves memory traffic relative to general GEMV at the same M, but does NOT halve FLOP count (each matrix element read still produces two useful multiply-adds, per the symmetrization identity in survey.md's SySTeC section) — a harness that naively reuses the GEMV byte-counting formula for SYMV would silently overstate SYMV's measured GB/s. This spec's blas-l2-gemv-symv-kernel variant defines SYMV's byte formula explicitly and separately from GEMV's for exactly this reason, and makes the resulting bandwidth_reduction_factor a required, explicit, headline comparison number rather than leaving it implicit in two separately-reported numbers a reader would have to divide themselves.
  • fBLAS is the only paper in this track (and one of only 2 papers across both tracks surveyed today, alongside MARLIN in the gemv track) to hardcode a concrete numeric correctness tolerance anywhere in its own artifact. This spec's blas-l1-vector-kernel variant keeps fBLAS's own absolute-tolerance convention (1e-4 float / 1e-6 double) rather than overriding it with this suite's usual max-relative-error convention, specifically because scalar reduction outputs (dot, nrm2) can legitimately be near zero, where a relative-error gate is the wrong tool — this is a deliberate, operation-specific exception, not an inconsistency: blas-l2-gemv-symv-kernel's vector-output ops keep the max-relative-error convention used throughout the rest of this benchmark suite.
  • VeGen's own recovered evaluation figure (Figure 2, per the search-summary source) reports instruction count and a derived speedup ratio, with no runtime/cycle measurement confirmed from any source read in this pass — this spec's blas-l1-mixed-precision-reduction variant requires an actual measured runtime alongside (not instead of) that instruction-count metric, since instruction count alone cannot account for issue-width, port contention, or memory-system effects that determine a real dot-product kernel's achieved throughput. This is this spec's explicit fix to what looks, from the one figure recovered, like a potential gap in VeGen's own evaluation methodology — stated as an inference from limited evidence, not a confirmed reading of the paper's full evaluation section (which could not be fetched in this pass).
  • 3 of this track's 4 papers (Exo 2, SySTeC, VeGen) evaluate a generator/compiler across a broad, heterogeneous kernel set rather than a single named BLAS routine — unlike this benchmark suite's other tracks (gemm, gemv), where every surveyed paper benchmarks the kernel itself. blas-l1l2-generated-kernel-suite exists specifically to make suite-level claims like Exo 2's own ("comparable to or better than MKL/OpenBLAS/BLIS") independently checkable per-kernel, with an explicit rule (exclude and name failures, geometric-mean the rest) for how a partial-pass suite is aggregated, since no paper in this track states its own aggregation rule for a case where some generated kernels underperform or fail correctness.
Open questions
  • SySTeC's own CGO'25 paper body (not just its README) was not read in this pass; a SYMV-specific speedup number, hardware target, timing protocol, precision, and correctness-validation method are all unconfirmed — the repo's `tests/` directory (listed but not opened) is the most likely place to find this. blas-l2-gemv-symv- kernel's symv precision assumption (fp64) is a guess pending this.
  • VeGen's and Exo 2's full evaluation-section methodology could not be recovered from any source reachable in this pass (every PDF fetch attempt returned undecodable binary content or an HTTP 403/404 error, and no local PDF-to-text utility was available). In particular: Exo 2's exact BLAS L1/L2 op list and per-op problem-size sweep, and whether VeGen's own evaluation used a measured runtime anywhere alongside the one instruction-count figure recovered, are both unconfirmed.
  • Exo 2's BLAS L1/L2 benchmark kernels were not found in the repo's `apps/x86` directory (which shows `conv`, `halide`, `resnet`, `sgemm`, `ssyrk` only) at the depth explored in this pass — they may be defined via the scheduling-library mechanism itself (generated, not statically present as example files), live in an unexplored path (`tests/`, or a separate companion benchmark repo not linked from this track's `artifact_url`), or may not be present in the public repo at all if they were evaluated only in a private/artifact-evaluation branch. This blocks fully populating blas-l1l2-generated-kernel-suite's Exo-2-sourced op list beyond "the canonical BLAS L1/L2 op list" placeholder used above.
  • fBLAS's own paper-stated repetition count (as opposed to its README's illustrative `-r 1` smoke-test example) was not independently reconfirmed in this pass; the earlier benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml survey cites arXiv 1907.07929 for fBLAS's GEMM-side numbers but this survey did not re-fetch that source specifically to pin down the DOT/GEMV repetition count used to produce fBLAS's own published numbers.
  • No surveyed paper in this track evidences a `trsv` (triangular solve) benchmark of any kind — it is listed in this spec's `operation` field per the task instructions' own example op list but has no evidence basis in this track's 4 papers and is not given a dedicated variant; a future revision should either find evidence for it or drop it from scope explicitly.
qr4 papers4 variants

QR factorization spanning four claims this track's own literature treats as genuinely different: dense single-node/GPU Householder QR with pivoting strategy (none / column-pivoted-RRQR / PAQR's pivoting-avoiding variant) as a required, disclosed parameter alongside shape and rank-deficiency location; distributed ScaLAPACK PDGEQRF at scale with tile size and process grid as required parameters (inheriting ScaLAPACK's own internal residual-check convention); sparse multifrontal QR with symbolic-analysis reordering strategy as a required, disclosed parameter; and batched transform-domain (tensor, "t-QR") QR of many small-to-medium frontal slices. No paper in this 4-paper track targets TSQR/Communication- Avoiding-QR specifically or an explicitly tall-skinny (M >> N) benchmark shape — this is a genuine gap in the track's own literature, not a disagreement to reconcile (see survey.md); this spec's dense variant still sweeps shape (square and tall-skinny) using the Householder/RRQR/PAQR algorithms this track's own papers DO implement, and flags TSQR/CAQR's absence explicitly rather than fabricating evidence for an algorithm none of the surveyed papers run.

A[M,N] = Q[M,M] * R[M,N] (or the economy form Q[M,N]*R[N,N] for M>=N), Q orthogonal (Q^T*Q = I), R upper triangular. Column-pivoted variants additionally produce a permutation Pi such that A*Pi = Q*R with |R_ii| non-increasing (rank-revealing); PAQR produces the same asymptotic cost as unpivoted QR while approaching QRCP's forward-error accuracy on rank-deficient A, WITHOUT physically pivoting columns. Sparse multifrontal QR additionally performs a symbolic fill-reducing reordering pass before numerical factorization. Batched/tensor QR (t-QR) treats a 3rd-order tensor's tube dimension as a batch axis: an M x N x K tensor's t-QR is K independent 2D QR factorizations of the frontal slices in transform (FFT) domain.

qr-dense-single-node-pivot-kernelsteady-state single-node (CPU or single-GPU) dense Householder QR factorization time, with PIVOTING STRATEGY (none / column-pivoted-RRQR / PAQR) and matrix SHAPE (square vs. tall-skinny) both required, disclosed, swept parameters, plus RANK-DEFICIENCY LOCATION as a third swept axis for the rank-deficient cases — this is the axis SidLakhdarCBALGTJWDDA23 (PAQR, this track's central paper) is built around: unpivoted QR (dgeqrf), column-pivoted QRCP (dgeqp3), and PAQR (dgepoqrf) are compared on the SAME matrix at the SAME shape, with deficient-column location (beginning/middle/end/random) itself swept as a first-class parameter, since a pivoting-avoidance algorithm's behavior is sensitive to where in the elimination order the deficiency falls.
inputs
suitesynthetic dense matrices with a controlled numerical-rank construction, matching SidLakhdarCBALGTJWDDA23's own test_dgepoqrf.c generator: full-rank columns drawn U(-1,1), deficient columns set to exactly zero, with deficiency LOCATION as a swept parameter (see protocol below) rather than a single fixed pattern.
selectiontwo shape classes, since no paper in this track implements TSQR/CAQR and this spec will not fabricate a communication-avoiding baseline none of the surveyed papers run: (a) SQUARE, M=N, matching SidLakhdarCBALGTJWDDA23's own LAPACK Table 2 point (10000x10000); (b) TALL-SKINNY, M >> N (M/N in {10, 100}), exercising the same three algorithms (dgeqrf/dgeqp3/dgepoqrf) at the shape regime where Householder QR's per-column cost dominates and where a future TSQR/CAQR baseline would be the natural comparison point once this track's paper coverage expands (flagged in open_questions).
recommended_subsetsquare: N in {1000, 5000, 10000} (matches SidLakhdarCBALGTJWDDA23's own Table 1/Table 2 points). tall-skinny: (M,N) in {(10000,1000), (100000,1000), (100000,100)}.
dense_operandfp64, matches SidLakhdarCBALGTJWDDA23's LAPACK/ ScaLAPACK arm exactly (its MAGMA batched arm additionally uses fp32, reported as a separate precision point if run).
protocol
pivoting_strategyrequired, disclosed per run: one of {none (dgeqrf), column-pivoted (dgeqp3/QRCP), paqr (dgepoqrf)}. All three MUST be run on the exact same generated matrix instance per (shape, deficiency-location) point, matching SidLakhdarCBALGTJWDDA23's own test-driver structure exactly (create_matrix() is called once per algorithm with the same srand(0) seed, giving all three algorithms an identical input).
rank_deficiency_locationrequired, disclosed, swept over {full-rank, deficient-at-beginning, deficient-at-middle, deficient-at-end, random-50-50} (matches SidLakhdarCBALGTJWDDA23's own type-0/2/4/5/6 sweep in test_dgepoqrf.c exactly), at a fixed deficiency FRACTION of 50% of columns (matches the paper's own default construction).
tile_sizerequired, disclosed per run (LAPACK block size, ILAENV-selected by default); report the library default alongside one off-default comparison point, matching this project's cholesky/lu-spec tile-size-disclosure convention — no surveyed paper in this arm discusses block size explicitly, so this is a spec addition to keep this track internally consistent with its sibling dense- factorization tracks.

warmup1 full factorization (a spec addition: SidLakhdarCBALGTJWDDA23's own LAPACK arm has NO warmup in its performance-measurement path at all; its separate ScaLAPACK arm DOES warm up, with two full factorizations before the measured run — this spec adopts the ScaLAPACK arm's practice uniformly since it is the more conservative choice found anywhere in this track).
reps5 (a spec addition: SidLakhdarCBALGTJWDDA23's own LAPACK/ScaLAPACK arms are BOTH single-shot with zero measured repetitions — the least repetition-disciplined evidence found across this project's three dense-factorization tracks so far, see survey.md's Divergences section).
statisticmedian (report min and max alongside) — a spec addition, since no repeated-timing-loop exists in this arm's own literature to state a divergent statistic from.
timerhost wall-clock (std::chrono or equivalent monotonic clock) for CPU runs — NOT C `clock()` (CPU time), which SidLakhdarCBALGTJWDDA23's own driver uses and which silently excludes time spent blocked/descheduled, a measurement choice this spec deliberately does not inherit; device-side event timer (synchronized) for GPU/MAGMA runs.
timing_scopekernel-only factorization time; matrix generation and Q-formation (if Q is explicitly formed for the orthogonality check below) are excluded and reported separately.
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once.
metric
primaryGFLOP/s (square: (4/3)*N^3; tall-skinny M>N: 2*M*N^2 - (2/3)*N^3 — standard Householder-QR FLOP counts, LAPACK convention)
secondaryms (median, min, max); for the rank-deficient cases, forward error vs. QRCP on a manufactured-solution least-squares problem (see correctness below) as a secondary, non-gating accuracy comparison — this is this variant's actual research question per SidLakhdarCBALGTJWDDA23's own paper, kept as secondary rather than primary since it is an accuracy claim, not a performance claim
correctnessTWO required, gating measurements — a deliberate spec addition, since SidLakhdarCBALGTJWDDA23's own LAPACK/ScaLAPACK performance-measurement path computes NEITHER (its accuracy claims live in a separate, non-overlapping MATLAB harness per survey.md): (1) **orthogonality**, the QR-track's mandatory correctness check per this project's design brief: max|I - Q^T*Q| / (N*eps) < 30 (same LAPACK-testsuite-style normalization and threshold as this track's sibling cholesky/spec.yaml residual gate, applied here to Q instead of the factorization residual, since no surveyed paper in this arm states a numeric orthogonality threshold); (2) backward-error residual ||A - Q*R||_F / (||A||_F * max(M,N) * eps) < 30 for the unpivoted and PAQR arms, or ||A*Pi - Q*R||_F / (||A||_F * max(M,N) * eps) < 30 for the column-pivoted arm. A run failing either gate does not count toward reported throughput. SECONDARY (reported, non-gating): forward error on a manufactured-solution least-squares problem (x_true = [0..N-1], b = A*x_true, solve via the computed factors, report ||x_computed - x_true||_2 / N) — this is LinYWT021's own accuracy- check methodology (see variant qr-sparse-multifrontal-kernel below), adopted here as a cross-variant convention this spec introduces for consistency, since it is the only concrete forward-error methodology recovered anywhere in this track's own artifacts.
