Note: the source paper's own 'TACO-Separate' baseline uses a mild best-of-N practice ('when multiple decomposition options existed, we evaluate all combinations and report best execution time') -- this spec instead requires reporting the #1 TACO-recommended decomposition's time, per the same anti-best-of-N principle applied to WACO in the sibling mttkrp track
Fairness notes
  • parTC's own reference generator only ever contracts a FROSTT tensor against a shuffled/copied version of itself (same nonzero count by construction, sparsification_factor=1) -- this understates the general sparse-sparse contraction problem, where the two operands' sparsity patterns need not overlap at all in a way that makes the contraction trivially self-similar. The sparse-sparse variant above requires an independent-tensor-pair case in addition to the self-contraction case for exactly this reason.
  • None of the 3 papers in this track state an explicit warmup/repetition/ statistic protocol in their accessible text; parTC's own shipped code goes further and silently ignores its own repetition-count CLI argument, making the reference artifact a bare single-shot timer. This is the weakest timing-protocol rigor found across every track surveyed so far in this project; the spec fixes warmup=10/reps=50/median+min/max uniformly rather than inheriting any paper's (non-existent) practice.
  • SparseLNR's own baseline ('TACO-Separate') uses a best-of-N practice across manually-tried decomposition combinations -- the composite-kernel variant above resolves this the same way the mttkrp track resolves WACO's top-10-schedule best-of-N: report the #1-ranked/first-tried decomposition, not the best of many tries.
  • parTC ships a correctness-check block disabled by default (#if 0); this spec requires correctness validation enabled and passing before any timing counts, per the project's standing fairness principle.
  • Insum's fixed-length sparse formats (GroupCOO/BlockGroupCOO) compute over padded zero slots by design -- the sparse-dense variant above requires reporting both nominal (padded-element-count) and effective (true-nnz) GFLOP/s so that the format's own padding overhead is visible rather than hidden inside a single favorable-looking throughput number.
Open questions
  • Insum's accessible text (a 6-page workshop-length paper, likely a precursor of the full ASPLOS 2026 paper) states no warmup/repetition/ statistic protocol and no amortization count k for its 14.8s compile+ autotune overhead; the full ASPLOS 2026 paper (paywalled at the given DOI, not independently accessible) may resolve both.
  • parTC's own paper text (both HAL deposit IDs tried, hal-04659658 and hal-05047235, including a direct-file PDF URL) was blocked by Anubis anti-bot protection for every fetch attempt; the exact FROSTT tensor list used in the paper's own results table, its stated baselines' specific system names, and its output-array allocation strategy (two-pass vs. dynamic growth) could not be verified beyond what the repo code and abstract snippet reveal.
  • SparseLNR's accessible fulltext does not state a numeric precision (fp32/fp64) anywhere; the spec's fp64 default for the composite-kernel variant's dense_operand is this spec's own choice (matching the sibling mttkrp track's fp64 default), not verified against the source paper.
  • None of the 3 papers' accessible material describes exactly how sparse- sparse contraction output storage is sized (two-pass symbolic-count-then- fill, as in classic SpGEMM, vs. dynamic/incremental growth) -- this affects both the fairness of the timing scope (is output-sizing cost counted?) and peak memory reporting; unresolved from accessible sources.
tensor-train-decomposition2 papers2 variants

Tensor-Train (TT) decomposition of an N-mode tensor into a chain of small 3D TT-cores G^(1)..G^(N) such that X[i1..iN] ~= G^(1)[:,i1,:] G^(2)[:,i2,:] ... G^(N)[:,iN,:] (matrix-chain product of the cores' slices). This track's two papers exercise opposite halves of a TT system's lifecycle: STTID DECOMPOSES a given sparse tensor into TT-cores under an accuracy target; EL-Rec never decomposes anything but instead RECONSTRUCTS (TT-core-products) a learned, fixed-TT-rank embedding table on every training step. The spec keeps these as separate variants (see survey.md's Divergences on "decomposition vs. reconstruction timing").

Decomposition (STTID): given sparse X[I1..IN] and accuracy target epsilon, compute TT-cores G^(i)[R_{i-1}, I_i, R_i] (R_0=R_N=1) via interpolative/skeleton decomposition such that the relative reconstruction error < epsilon, subject to a rank ceiling R_i <= rmax. Reconstruction (EL-Rec): given trained TT-cores G^(i)[R_{i-1}, q_i, R_i] of fixed rank R_i (a training hyperparameter, not accuracy-derived) and a TT-SHAPE factorization of an embedding index, compute the matrix-chain product on-the-fly for each of many (batch-size) lookups per training step.

tt-sparse-decomposition-kernelsteady-state, one-shot sparse-tensor-to-TT-cores decomposition time for a GIVEN accuracy target epsilon, with epsilon and the rank ceiling rmax as required, disclosed parameters (the actual compression-vs-error tradeoff axis this track's papers expose) -- the variant STTID is purpose-built for. TT-rank is reported as an OUTPUT of the run (the per-mode ranks the rank-revealing decomposition actually realized under epsilon), never as a pre-fixed input, matching STTID's own artifact practice.
inputs
suiteFROSTT (real, primary) + knowledge-graph hyperedge tensors (real, supplementary) + synthetic random sparse tensors (scalability supplementary), matching the 3-category split STTID's own run.sh actually exercises rather than FROSTT alone

TT-rank and TT-shape (the factorization of the embedding index/dimension into per-core sizes) are both required, disclosed input parameters here, the reverse of the decomposition variant's rank-as-output convention.

metric
primarytraining throughput: wall-clock time (s) per k=1000 iterations at batch size 4096 (equivalently, samples/s = 1000 * 4096 / time)
secondaryspeedup vs. DLRM (dense embedding table, same batch size/hardware), vs. FAE, and vs. TT-Rec (prior TT-compressed system); memory footprint of the TT-compressed table vs. the dense-embedding-table baseline
correctnessPRIMARY (required) gate: none in the numerical-reconstruction sense used by the decomposition variant -- EL-Rec's TT-cores are learned from scratch, so there is no uncompressed ground-truth embedding table to numerically check against (see survey.md Divergences). Instead, the REQUIRED gate is downstream-task validity: the trained model must reach a test-set loss/accuracy within a disclosed tolerance of the dense-embedding-table (uncompressed) baseline trained under the same protocol -- EL-Rec's own artifact validates this via a separate script (`Table4/*_train_and_test.py`) producing a loss curve (`loss.png`), which this spec treats as the REQUIRED evidence a reported training-throughput number is not from a degenerate/non-learning run, not merely optional secondary color. Exact metric (test BCE loss vs. AUC) and tolerance were not recovered from the sources reached (see open_questions) -- "within 1% relative test loss of the dense baseline" is this spec's own placeholder default pending that confirmation.
Fairness notes
  • TT-rank plays an OUTPUT role in the decomposition variant (derived from an accuracy target epsilon) and an INPUT role in the reconstruction/training variant (a pre-chosen hyperparameter with no accuracy-target derivation). The spec never reports "TT-rank" as one comparable cross-variant axis without this distinction spelled out, per survey.md's Divergences -- doing so would misrepresent EL-Rec's fixed-rank practice as if it searched for a target-accuracy rank the way STTID does.
  • STTID's own `run.sh` fixes epsilon at a single value (1e-10) across every dataset category. This spec sweeps epsilon over 3 values instead of adopting the single fixed value, per this spec's general principle that a compression-vs-error tradeoff axis the papers themselves treat as fixed should still be exposed as a sweep in the benchmark, since the whole point of a spec parameter (per this track's key axes) is to make that tradeoff visible, not to reproduce one paper's single operating point.
  • Neither paper's own artifact excludes a warmup region (STTID: no shell-level warmup step; EL-Rec: iteration 1 counted identically to iteration 1000). This spec preserves both practices explicitly (rather than silently imposing this project's usual single-warmup-run default) because each paper's own headline numbers are presumably computed the same way, and a warmup exclusion here would make a reproduction attempt diverge from the number being reproduced without a clear reason to.
  • EL-Rec's own artifact does not appear to state a repetition count for its Figure-11 timing numbers (a single elapsed-time measurement per configuration, from the fetched script). This spec's reps=3/median default is a spec addition, per this project's general anti-single- sample fairness principle, not evidence of the paper's own practice.
  • EL-Rec's correctness gate is fundamentally a downstream-task-quality check, not a numerical-reconstruction check (see Divergences) -- unlike every other variant in this project's tensor-track specs so far, which gate on a numerical tolerance. This spec keeps that task-quality gate as REQUIRED (not merely a reported secondary), because for a learned-from-scratch compressed representation, task quality is the only correctness notion that exists; dropping it would let a training-throughput number come from a run that never actually learned anything useful.
Open questions
  • STTID's "up to 550x GPU speedup" headline figure's exact baseline and per-dataset breakdown were not recovered (the paper's own fulltext was not reachable; only the Zenodo metadata record and the artifact repo were available).
  • Whether STTID's internal labeled-region timer (`timer.cpp`) is invoked multiple times per `run.sh` line (i.e., repetition happens inside the binary, not visible at the shell level) was not confirmed by reading the `main()` driver source directly.
  • STTID's GPU model/hardware for its headline claim was not recovered.
  • EL-Rec's precision (fp32 assumed, PyTorch default) was not explicitly confirmed in the fetched training script.
  • EL-Rec's exact Table-4 accuracy metric (test BCE loss vs. AUC vs. something else) and the tolerance implicitly used for its own "comparable accuracy" claims were not recovered -- this spec's "within 1% relative test loss" default is a placeholder, not evidence-derived, and should be revisited once `Table4/ELRec_train_and_test.py` is read in full.
  • EL-Rec's GPU model/hardware and exact per-baseline Figure-11 numbers were not recovered; only that a specific Docker image (`happy233/zheng_dlrm:latest`) is referenced by the README.
tucker2 papers2 variants

Tucker decomposition of an N-mode sparse tensor: X ~= G x1 A^(1) x2 A^(2) ... xN A^(N), where G is a small dense core tensor and A^(i) are dense factor matrices, computed iteratively (HOSVD/HOOI/HOQRI). This track's two papers exercise opposite ends of that iteration: SymProp optimizes the per-iteration TTMc/TTMc-chain KERNEL for symmetric sparse tensors, while SGD_Tucker optimizes the whole SGD-driven DECOMPOSITION LOOP (mini-batch ALS-style updates) for general sparse tensors. The spec keeps these as separate variants rather than forcing one iteration semantics across both (see survey.md Divergences).

G[R1..RN], A^(i)[I_i,R_i] (i=1..N) such that X[I1..IN] ~= sum_{r1..rN} G[r1..rN] * A^(1)[:,r1] o A^(2)[:,r2] o ... o A^(N)[:,rN] (outer product), computed via alternating per-mode TTMc contractions (S3TTMc / S3TTMcTC when the input is symmetric, so only one canonical mode's contraction needs computing per sweep) followed by a small core/factor update (HOOI power-iteration or HOQRI QR-based step, or a stochastic-gradient mini-batch update as in SGD_Tucker).

tucker-symmetric-ttmc-kernel-fp64steady-state per-sweep S3TTMc/S3TTMcTC kernel throughput exploiting full input symmetry (single canonical-mode contraction suffices per HOOI/HOQRI sweep, not N), preprocessing (CSS format construction) excluded and reported separately once. This is the variant SymProp is purpose-built for; it directly reuses this project's mttkrp track's mttkrp-symmetric-kernel-fp64 input suite and rank sweep, since S3TTMc/S3TTMcTC are the same symmetric-contraction kernel family surveyed there for the Tucker/HOOI/HOQRI use case specifically (as opposed to that track's CP-ALS use case).
inputs
suiteSymProp's own real hypergraph-derived symmetric tensors as primary, synthetic Erdos-Renyi-generated symmetric tensors (SySTeC-style generator, the shared-convention generator this project's sibling mttkrp/cholesky tracks also use) as a scalability supplement
selectionreal: all 5 named datasets from the paper's own evaluation (contact-school, trivago-clicks, walmart-trips, stackoverflow, amazon-reviews) -- see survey.md's open question about a second, unreconciled dataset-name extraction from the same PDF, which this spec does NOT use pending direct table verification; synthetic: order N in {3,4,5}, density swept to hit target UNNZ in {1e4, 1e5, 1e6}
recommended_subsetcontact-school (order 5, dim 245, unnz 12704), trivago-clicks (order 6, dim 154987, unnz 208076), walmart-trips (order 8, dim 62240, unnz 47560), synthetic-3d-nnz1e5, synthetic-4d-nnz1e5, synthetic-5d-nnz1e4
dense_operandtarget Tucker rank R in {2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20} per mode (uniform rank across modes, matching SymProp's own sweep), fp64
protocol
formatCSS (compressed sparse symmetric); construction excluded from kernel timing, reported separately once
warmup10 (spec default; SymProp's own two extraction passes both confirm a warmup phase exists but neither states a count)
reps50 (spec default matching this project's general convention; SymProp's own fulltext reports a min-of-(10000-runs-or-5s) alternative statistic, kept as a REPORTED secondary statistic below rather than the primary, per this spec's anti-best-of-N fairness principle)
statisticmedian (report min/max); ALSO report min-of-(10000 runs or 5s) alongside, to remain directly comparable to SymProp's own headline numbers
timerdevice-side events (GPU) / std::chrono steady clock (CPU); SymProp is a CPU/OpenMP artifact per its repo (no GPU code found), so CPU timing is the primary path for this variant
timing_scopeone canonical-mode TTMc/TTMc-chain kernel call only (mathematically sufficient under full symmetry -- NOT the mode-0-only simplification flagged as unsound for GENERAL/asymmetric tensors elsewhere in this project's mttkrp track); data rearrangement/output replication to non-canonical positions excluded, reported separately
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once (CSS construction time)
metric
primaryGFLOP/s using the SYMMETRY-REDUCED flop count actually performed (report the theoretical dense-equivalent/general-tensor GFLOP/s alongside it, so the speedup attributable to symmetry alone is visible, not hidden inside one number)
secondaryms; speedup vs. TTMc-SPLATT (general, symmetry-unaware) and vs. S3TTMc-CSS (symmetric but without SymProp's symmetry propagation); flag cases where a baseline cannot run at all (out-of-memory) as a distinct outcome, not silently excluded from the reported average (see survey.md: this is SymProp's actual headline pattern for its largest cases)
correctnessmax relative error of the TTMc/TTMc-chain kernel OUTPUT vs. a symmetrized dense/COO reference computed in fp64 < 1e-6 (tolerance value is a spec addition -- neither extraction pass of SymProp's own text states a numeric tolerance; 1e-6 matches this project's mttkrp-track convention for the same kernel family). This is a kernel-output correctness gate, distinct from a decomposition-level reconstruction-error gate (that belongs to the end-to-end variant below, since a single TTMc call has no notion of "how well the Tucker decomposition reconstructs X").
tucker-general-decomposition-e2eend-to-end sparse Tucker decomposition wall-clock time to reach a target relative reconstruction error (or, if the reconstruction-error target is not reached, wall-clock time for a fixed, disclosed iteration budget k), on general (asymmetric) real sparse tensors -- the variant SGD_Tucker's own evaluation style maps onto. Unlike the kernel variant above, "iteration" here means one full decomposition sweep (one HOOI power-iteration OR one SGD mini-batch update, whichever the system under test implements), NOT a single TTMc kernel call -- the two are not interchangeable (see survey.md Divergences).
inputs
suiteFROSTT (Formidable Repository of Open Sparse Tensors and Tools), the general-purpose real-sparse-tensor suite this project's mttkrp track already standardizes on for the general/asymmetric case; used here INSTEAD OF SGD_Tucker's own MovieLens-only artifact dataset, per this spec's fairness principle that the input suite must not be cherry-picked from a single paper's shipped demo data -- SGD_Tucker's own practice of evaluating on one dataset is flagged as a divergence below, not adopted as the track suite
selectionsame union/inclusion criterion as this project's mttkrp-general-kernel-fp64 variant (order 3-4, nnz 3.1M-143.6M, excludes the 3 explicitly out-of-memory FROSTT tensors); reused verbatim here rather than re-derived, since both tracks need the same general-sparse-tensor suite and re-deriving it would risk an inconsistent selection criterion across this project's tracks
recommended_subsetnips (2.5K x 2.9K x 14K x 17, 3.1M nnz), uber (183 x 24 x 1.1K x 1.7K, 3.3M nnz), chicago-crime (6.2K x 24 x 77 x 32, 5.3M nnz), enron (6K x 5.7K x 244.3K x 1.2K, 54.2M nnz), nell-2 (12.1K x 9.2K x 28.8K, 76.9M nnz)
dense_operandtarget Tucker rank R in {10, 25, 50} per mode (uniform), fp64; batch/mini-batch width, if the system under test is SGD-based, is a required, disclosed secondary parameter (this is SGD_Tucker's own artifact CLI practice: core rank AND mini-batch width are both required, not silently fixed)
protocol
formatraw COO on input; one-shot format conversion (if the system under test needs one, e.g. CSF) excluded from the iteration loop, timed and reported separately once
iteration_budgetk=100 decomposition sweeps as the default fixed budget (matches SGD_Tucker's own artifact, which hardcodes exactly 100 SGD iterations with no early-stopping criterion); systems that converge to the target reconstruction error in fewer iterations report the break-even iteration count k* in addition to the fixed-budget number, so slow-per-iteration/few-iteration systems are not penalized relative to fast-per-iteration/many-iteration ones by the fixed-budget number alone
warmupnone (matches SGD_Tucker's own artifact, which times iteration 0 identically to every other iteration -- flagged as a DEVIATION from this project's general warmup convention in notes_on_fairness, not silently adopted)
reps3 full k=100 runs (spec default; neither paper in this track states a repetition count for the end-to-end/convergence-curve case)
statisticmedian (report min/max) of the per-run wall-clock time to reach the reconstruction-error target, or of the fixed-k=100 total wall-clock time if the target is not reached
timerhost wall-clock (matches SGD_Tucker's own `gettimeofday`-based timer; SymProp's timer, per survey.md, is not confirmed to differ)
timing_scopefull decomposition loop (all N per-mode updates each sweep, plus any core-tensor update), INCLUDING the per-iteration reconstruction-error check itself if the system under test computes one on every iteration (as SGD_Tucker's artifact does, printing RMSE/MAE every iteration) -- this differs from the kernel variant's convention of excluding correctness-check overhead from timed kernel calls, because for THIS variant the per-iteration quality check is part of what makes the claim ("time to reach target accuracy") meaningful, not incidental overhead
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once (format conversion + parameter/factor-matrix random initialization)
metric
primarywall-clock time (s) to reach the reconstruction-error target (see correctness below); if not reached within k=100, report the k=100 wall-clock time AND the reconstruction error actually achieved, rather than treating a non-converged run as an undefined/dropped data point
secondaryper-iteration mean wall-clock time (ms); break-even iteration count k* if convergence occurs before k=100; NO GFLOP/s number is required for this variant (SGD_Tucker's own paper never reports one -- see survey.md; a system MAY additionally report GFLOP/s if it is meaningful for that system's algorithm, but the spec does not mandate deriving one for SGD-style mini-batch updates where the flop count per iteration is data-dependent and not fixed in advance)
correctnessPRIMARY reconstruction-error gate: relative Frobenius reconstruction error ||X - [[G; A^(1),...,A^(N)]]||_F / ||X||_F (train-set) < 1e-2 as the default target (a spec addition -- neither paper states a numeric target; 1e-2 is a deliberately loose default appropriate for real, noisy sparse recommender-style tensors like SGD_Tucker's MovieLens case, NOT the tight 1e-6/1e-8 numerical-kernel tolerances used elsewhere in this project's specs, because Tucker decomposition of a real noisy tensor is a statistical-fit problem, not an exact numerical-linear-algebra identity). SECONDARY (reported, not gating): held-out test-set RMSE/MAE convergence curve across all k iterations run, matching SGD_Tucker's own per-iteration train+test reporting practice -- dropping this would hide the actual quantity SGD_Tucker's paper's "2x faster... with equivalent accuracy" claim is built on.
Fairness notes
  • The two papers' "iteration" units (one symmetric-mode TTMc kernel call vs. one full SGD mini-batch decomposition sweep) are NOT interchangeable and this spec never reports a single cross-paper "time per iteration" number that would conflate them -- see survey.md Divergences. The kernel variant's GFLOP/s and the e2e variant's wall-clock-to-accuracy are deliberately different metric families for this reason, not an oversight.
  • SGD_Tucker's own artifact evaluates on exactly one real dataset (MovieLens, the only one shipped in its repo). This spec's e2e variant substitutes the FROSTT suite already standardized elsewhere in this project rather than adopting SGD_Tucker's single-dataset practice, per this spec's general anti-cherry-picking principle -- a system that only reports MovieLens numbers is not given a passing benchmark result on that basis alone.
  • SGD_Tucker's own artifact excludes NO warmup iteration (iteration 0 is timed identically to iterations 1-99, including any first-touch/ cache-cold effects). This spec's e2e variant preserves that convention explicitly (rather than silently imposing this project's usual single-warmup-run default) because SGD_Tucker's own headline "2x faster" claim is presumably computed the same way, and imposing a warmup exclusion here would make a reproduction attempt diverge from the number being reproduced without a clear reason to do so.
  • SymProp's real-tensor list could not be reconciled across two independent extraction passes of the same source PDF (see survey.md). This spec uses the extraction believed more reliable (a prior, separate, full-fulltext pass already validated for this project's mttkrp track) rather than either splitting the difference or silently picking the more recent, lower-fidelity pass.
  • Neither paper states a numeric correctness tolerance for its respective variant. Both tolerances in this spec (1e-6 kernel-output relative error; 1e-2 reconstruction-error target) are spec additions, chosen for consistency with this project's other kernel-correctness conventions (1e-6) and with the real-noisy-data character of SGD_Tucker's own evaluation (1e-2), respectively -- flagged here as NOT evidence-derived, consistent with this project's general practice of adding a gate rather than leaving correctness unchecked.
Open questions
  • SymProp's real-dataset list disagreement between two extraction passes of the same OSTI PDF is unresolved; a direct read of the PDF's actual dataset table (not a markdown-summarized extraction) is needed before the recommended_subset above can be considered fully verified.
  • SymProp's numeric correctness tolerance was not recovered from any source reached.
  • SGD_Tucker's Section 5 (dataset table, hardware, named baselines) was not recovered from arXiv HTML, DeepAI, ar5iv, or two TU Delft open-access PDF links that both 404'd; only the abstract and the artifact's C++ source were usable. Whether the paper evaluates on tensors beyond the MovieLens data shipped in its artifact is unknown -- this spec's substitution of the FROSTT suite for SGD_Tucker's own evaluation should be revisited if the paper's own dataset table surfaces and shows a materially different (e.g. much larger or much higher-order) real-tensor practice than FROSTT covers.
  • SGD_Tucker's `core_kernel` CLI parameter's precise mathematical definition (read from source: it sizes the `core_dimen[i] x core_kernel` shape of an internal per-mode auxiliary matrix `parameter_g[i]`) was inferred from the artifact's source code, not confirmed against the paper's own terminology -- needed before exposing it as a named, stable harness parameter.
  • Whether SGD_Tucker's baselines (unnamed in the abstract; "state of the art") are P-Tucker, Vest, or a sparse CP-ALS-style system is an unverified guess, not confirmed from any source reached.

graph-pattern-mining10 papers3 variants

Counting (not full enumeration) the number of occurrences of a fixed, unlabeled subgraph pattern — triangles, k-cliques, 4-node motifs, and a handful of named 5-7 vertex shapes — in a large simple undirected graph, measured as steady-state search kernel time with one-shot graph preprocessing (CSR build, orientation, any auxiliary index) reported separately, never folded silently into per-pattern time.

count(G, P) = number of distinct (up to automorphism) vertex subsets of simple undirected graph G = (V,E) that are isomorphic to pattern P; G given as CSR/edge-list, P given as a small fixed adjacency list (3-7 vertices). Full match enumeration/listing is explicitly OUT of scope for the core variants (see notes_on_fairness).

gpm-kernel-small-f32steady-state counting-kernel time for small patterns (3-4 vertices: the clique ladder K3-K4 plus the full 4-motif census), preprocessing excluded and reported separately — the scope every one of the 8 in-scope papers already uses for its smallest patterns (GraphFold TC, GLumin P4, cuTS/STMatch triangle-in-query-set, GraphSet motif_counting).

A cell that exceeds the 1800s timeout, or exceeds a declared memory budget (80GB single-GPU / 256GB host), is recorded DNF (did-not- finish), never as 0 or omitted silently; DNF cells are excluded from aggregate statistics (report coverage %, e.g. "38/45 cells completed").

For com-friendster: cross-validate between >=2 independently-implemented systems in the suite (GraphSet's own brute-force triangle counter, or two of the harness's own tested artifacts) since no single-machine brute-force reference is feasible at 1.8B edges — a run is only "correct" if all cross-checked systems agree exactly.

Fairness notes
  • GraphSet's own GPU timer includes CUDA managed-memory allocation and the H2D copy inside the same clock as the search kernel (`context->init` is inside the timed region in `gpu/gpu_graph.cu`), while STMatch, cuTS, GraphFold, and GLumin all explicitly start their clock after H2D transfer completes. This spec's kernel-only variants follow the 4-artifact majority (transfer excluded) — GraphSet's own reported numbers measure a superset of what this spec calls "kernel-only" and should not be compared directly against the other three without re-timing under this spec's scope.
  • Every one of the 8 in-scope artifacts times exactly one run per (graph, pattern) cell with no warmup and no repetition (see survey.md Divergences) — the single biggest methodological gap found across this project's tracks so far, worse than e.g. spmm where at least batched-mean timing is universal. This spec fixes it with an explicit warmup+repeat protocol, but adds a timeout-aware single-sample exception (protocol.timeout in each variant) because a naive "always run 5+ reps" rule is not practical when a single cell can already approach the 1800s timeout at billion-edge/7-clique scale — the fix has to be honest about where repetition is actually affordable.
  • Correctness checking is essentially absent across the track: only GraphSet (gtest hardcoded references + brute-force triangle counter), cuTS (GSI cross-diff), and INFINEL (opt-in verification mode, not used in this spec's core variants) have any automated correctness path; the other 5 in-scope artifacts (STMatch, GraphFold, GLumin, VSGM, Fringe-SGC) rely on eyeballing printed counts. This spec makes a correctness gate mandatory before any timing counts, using exact-match (not a floating-point tolerance, since match counts are exact integers) against either a brute-force/NetworkX oracle (small graphs/patterns) or cross-validation between >=2 independently implemented systems (large graphs/patterns where no single-machine oracle is feasible).
  • INFINEL's full-match-LISTING workload (not counting) is architecturally different — its own numbers show 2TB of output for RMAT27 triangle listing — and is deliberately excluded from the core counting variants above rather than forced into a shared "time" metric that would compare incommensurable things (counting kernels never materialize output; listing kernels are IO-bound on the output itself). See open_questions.
  • DTMiner (temporal motif mining) and VertexSurge (variable-length path queries) are excluded entirely from this spec's variants: neither counts occurrences of a FIXED pattern shape in a static graph, which is the operation this spec measures. Forcing them into the same variants as the other 8 would misrepresent what's being compared. See open_questions for a possible future track split.
  • com-friendster (1.81B edges) is used by only 4 of 8 in-scope artifacts, and one of those (STMatch) ships it commented out by default with a documented buildability caveat (needs a 64-bit edge-index type change). It is kept in recommended_subset anyway, not because a majority of papers exercise it by default, but because it is the single graph that actually stresses the "billion-edge" claim several of these papers' titles/abstracts make (VSGM's entire evaluation is built around it) — dropping it would let the suite quietly avoid testing the scale regime the track's own papers are named for.
Open questions
  • Whether a future `graph-pattern-mining-listing` variant/track should cover INFINEL's full-match-enumeration workload (distinct metric: output GB/s or output-write-bandwidth-bound time, not a counting-kernel GEPS number) — deferred here since it needs a fundamentally different memory/output-buffer protocol than the counting variants, and only 1 of 10 surveyed papers targets it.
  • Whether DTMiner (temporal motif mining) and VertexSurge (variable- length path matching) warrant their own track(s) rather than being folded into graph-pattern-mining at all — both were in the track's input file but measure a different operation (see notes_on_fairness). Their survey facts are recorded in survey.md for completeness but no variant above exercises them.
  • Exact vertex/edge counts for several graphs (mico, and everything in GraphFold/GLumin/Fringe-SGC's own suites) are not restated inside the respective repos — the counts used in recommended_subset are the standard SNAP-published sizes for the same-named public datasets, not independently re-verified against each artifact's own preprocessed copy (self-loop/multi-edge removal could shift edge counts slightly from the raw SNAP download).
  • Whether the four_motif_census and named_5v_plus pattern definitions given in pattern_set above exactly match what any given surveyed artifact's own unlabeled `Pn.g`/bit-string pattern files encode was NOT independently verified topology-by-topology (only the clique ladder, which is explicitly named in code/CLI flags across 3 artifacts, is fully cross-verified) — see survey.md's "Pattern-set naming is inconsistent" divergence. Implementers should treat pattern_set's adjacency-list definitions as this spec's own canonical definitions, not as a guaranteed reproduction of any single paper's exact P7.g.
  • No warmup/repeat/timeout numbers from any surveyed artifact could anchor this spec's protocol defaults (warmup=1, reps=5, 1800s timeout, 300s single-sample cutoff), since none of the 8 in-scope artifacts do more than a single run — these are the harness designer's own practical choices, not inherited from the literature, and should be revisited once Phase 2 has real wall-clock data for how long typical cells actually take on the target measurement machine.
bfs7 papers4 variants

Breadth-first search from a set of source vertices over a directed or undirected graph in CSR/CSC form, measured as traversed-edges-per-second with preprocessing (format conversion, reordering, bitmap construction) strictly separated from per-search kernel time.

parent[V] = BFS(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, CSR), source in V); A is unweighted (or weight-agnostic — only connectivity matters); output is a parent/predecessor array (or level array) over all V vertices, undefined (INT64_MAX-sentinel) for unreached vertices.

Fairness notes
  • Root-vertex selection is the single biggest source of incomparability in this track: Graph500-BFS and BLEST use 64 random roots (good), efg uses 100 random roots (fine on its own, but not directly comparable to a 64-root number without re-running), and Corder uses ONE fixed maximum-degree root for every graph and every algorithm — the single most favorable and least representative choice possible, since a max-degree root in a skewed real-world graph typically reaches the giant component almost immediately and minimizes the frontier-imbalance effects that make BFS hard to parallelize in the first place. The spec fixes this at 64 fixed-seed random roots from the giant component for every variant, and bfs-reordering-cost explicitly re-derives Corder's own experiment with matched roots rather than inheriting its single-root convention.
  • BLEST reports zero GTEPS numbers (ms only); Graph500-BFS reports harmonic-mean GTEPS; efg reports an edge-weighted-aggregate GTEPS. None of these three statistics are numerically interchangeable (harmonic mean is pulled down by slow outlier searches, arithmetic/weighted mean is pulled up by fast ones). The spec picks median-of-per-search-GTEPS with min/max reported, which is neither of the two literature conventions but is the only choice that (a) is robust to outliers in either direction and (b) always allows recovering min/max for readers who want the harmonic- or arithmetic-mean framing themselves from raw per-search numbers, which median discards but min/max partially recovers.
  • Direction-optimization (push/pull hybrid) status is undisclosed or ambiguous for 2 of 7 papers (BLEST's pull-based description doesn't confirm whether it also pushes; efg and Corder don't discuss it at all), yet direction optimization alone typically accounts for a 5-15x speedup over naive top-down BFS on skewed real-world graphs — larger than most of the algorithmic contributions in this track. A benchmark that doesn't require disclosure risks comparing a hybrid number against a naive-baseline number and attributing the entire gap to the paper's actual contribution. All variants above make disclosure mandatory.
  • Corder itself flags a cherry-pick (excluding 'urand' from its own reported averages because it is "not skewed") — this is transparent in the paper's own text, which is good practice, but the spec's recommended_subset includes both skewed (real-world, kron) and non-skewed (urand-style uniform-random) graphs in EVERY variant so that "the technique doesn't help on unskewed graphs" is a visible, reportable result rather than an excluded one.
  • efg's compression-ratio and BLEST's preprocessing-time numbers are exactly the kind of one-shot, separately-reported preprocessing the fairness principles ask for — adopted as the model for preprocessing_reported across all four variants above, in contrast to RCM (survey paper 7), whose BFS-as-subroutine time is never separated from total reordering time at all in the available sources, a pattern this spec's preprocessing_reported field is designed to prevent.
Open questions
  • Bit-GraphBLAS's BFS-specific protocol (root selection, warmup/reps, whether the 433x speedup figure is kernel-only or includes B2SR format construction) could not be confirmed from available sources (IEEE paywall, no arXiv, artifact ships only the underlying BMV microbenchmark). If/when fulltext becomes available, its ~700-matrix SuiteSparse sweep methodology should be cross-checked against the bfs-reordering-cost variant's SuiteSparse selection criterion for possible alignment.
  • FuseIM's exact evaluation graphs/sizes and whether its probabilistic-BFS timing includes host-device transfer could not be confirmed (ACM DL 403, no arXiv). Probabilistic (weighted, randomized-edge-activation) BFS is a related but distinct kernel from the deterministic-reachability BFS this spec targets; if the track later wants to cover probabilistic traversal explicitly, it likely needs its own variant (different correctness notion — expected-value comparison across many samples, not a single exact parent-array match) rather than being folded into the variants above.
  • The official Graph500 R-MAT parameters (A=0.57, B=0.19, C=0.19, D=0.05) were assumed for bfs-kernel-rmat-graph500 based on well-known Graph500 defaults, not directly confirmed by reading RIKEN-RCCS/Graph500-BFS/generator/graph_generator.hpp line-by-line (only user_settings.h and mpi/parameters.h were inspected). Should be verified before treating the synthetic-suite variant as bit-for-bit official-Graph500-compliant.
  • Whether GAP-twitter (BLEST) and the "twitter" graph used by efg/Corder are related snapshots (same crawl, different post-processing) or genuinely independent datasets that happen to share a name was not resolved — the recommended_subset above treats them as distinct instances (different vertex counts: ~61.6M vs ~41.6-41.7M) pending confirmation.
kcore-kclique5 papers5 variants

Five variants covering the k-core/k-clique graph-kernel family on large simple undirected graphs: static full k-core decomposition via parallel peeling, batch-dynamic k-core maintenance under a stream of edge updates, exact k-clique counting via GPU-specialized search/orientation, approximate probabilistic clique/triangle counting via Bloom-filter/MinHash sketches, and maximal clique enumeration via GPU search-tree exploration. These are 4 distinct kernel PROBLEMS sharing only the k-core/k-clique graph-theory family, not 1 problem with 4 knobs — see notes_on_fairness for why this spec has 5 variants instead of the usual 1-4.

Multi-kernel track; each variant below has its own operation definition. Common thread: given a static (or dynamically updated) simple undirected graph G=(V,E) in CSR/adjacency-list form, either (a) compute coreness(v) for every v in V (k-core decomposition, static or maintained under updates), (b) count or enumerate cliques of size k (or all maximal cliques) in G.

kcore-static-peelsteady-state full k-core decomposition (per-vertex coreness for ALL cores simultaneously) on a static simple undirected graph via parallel peeling, one-shot preprocessing (CSR build / degree-degeneracy orientation) excluded from the kernel timer and reported separately — the common denominator across LiuSZ24's static EKCore/AKCore baselines and KCGPU's degeneracy-only peeling.

Excludes Shun20's hypergraph inputs (structurally different data model — bipartite vertex-hyperedge incidence, not a plain adjacency list; see open_questions).

Fairness notes
  • This spec has 5 variants, above the "1-4" guidance in the design instructions, because the kcore-kclique track's 5 papers genuinely target 4 distinct kernel problems (static k-core, dynamic k-core, exact k-clique counting, approximate clique/triangle counting) plus a 5th architecturally-distinct problem (maximal clique enumeration, unbounded output vs. bounded count). Forcing these into fewer variants would blur correctness definitions that are genuinely incompatible (exact integer match vs. bounded relative error vs. exact-match-on-an- unbounded-output-set) — see survey.md's Divergences section for the full reasoning.
  • KCGPU's own paper times DAG-orientation preprocessing together with k-clique counting and uses a 5h wall-clock cutoff as its DNF boundary; kclique-count-exact's kernel-only default splits these out and reports preprocessing once, following this project's general preprocessing convention (see other tracks, e.g. graph-pattern-mining). KCGPU's own reported numbers should be read as measuring a superset of what this spec calls "kernel" and are not directly comparable to this spec's kernel-only column without re-timing under this spec's scope.
  • 4 of the 5 surveyed papers effectively run each timed configuration ONCE: RDMCE (single run + 3600s timeout), KCGPU (literally `for(i=0;i<1;i++)` in main.cu, 5h DNF cutoff), and Shun20 (no stated repetition count in the extracted evaluation text) all report what appears to be a single measured sample per cell; LiuSZ24 is the partial exception with an explicit `-rounds 3`. This spec adds explicit warmup + repetition + median/min/max reporting to every variant except kclique-count-approx, which already inherits a more rigorous protocol directly from ProbGraph (see next note).
  • ProbGraph's own timing protocol (omit first 1% as warmup, derive enough samples for mean + 95% non-parametric CI) is the most rigorous of the 5 papers and is adopted VERBATIM for kclique-count-approx rather than replaced with this project's usual median-of-N convention, since ProbGraph already cites and follows a named formal parallel-benchmarking methodology reference — no reason to weaken it.
  • Algorithm-class axis ("peeling vs. local/search algorithms", per the design brief): kcore-static-peel and kcore-dynamic-batch use PEELING (iteratively strip minimum-degree/minimum-core vertices in rounds or buckets — this is true of LiuSZ24's PLDS/LDS/EKCore/AKCore, KCGPU's kcore.cuh, and Shun20's WE/WI hypergraph k-core alike). kclique-count-exact and kclique-count-approx instead SEARCH/COUNT over an oriented DAG (no peeling, no iterative vertex removal). mce-enum uses SEARCH-TREE ENUMERATION with dynamic work-stealing (RDMCE's "root-down exposure"). KCGPU additionally exposes a distinct per-vertex "local" k-clique-count mode (KCLIQUE_LOCAL, in kclique_local.cuh) alongside its global-aggregate KCLIQUE mode — out of scope for kclique-count-exact (which measures the global count) but noted here as a candidate `kclique-count-local` variant if this track is revisited with more local-algorithm papers.
  • Static vs. dynamic/streaming is a hard problem split in the source literature, not a protocol knob: LiuSZ24's PLDS/CLDS cannot be meaningfully compared to KCGPU's or Shun20's one-shot static peeling on the same axis (different cost model — amortized per-batch latency vs. one-shot wall time on a fixed graph). Kept as two fully separate variants (kcore-static-peel, kcore-dynamic-batch) per the design brief's explicit instruction, rather than a "streaming: true/false" field on one variant.
  • KCGPU reports only the graph's DEGENERACY (one scalar, the largest non-empty core number) via its count() API, not a full per-vertex coreness array the way LiuSZ24's EKCore and Shun20's WE-kcore do. kcore-static-peel's correctness gate accounts for this with a scalar-vs-max comparison rather than requiring a full array match, but this means KCGPU's own numbers are informative about degeneracy-only computation cost, not full per-vertex coreness computation cost — a real implementation-capability gap between the 3 papers in this variant, not just a reporting-format difference.
Open questions
  • Artifact mismatch for Shun20 (conf/ppopp/Shun20): `artifact_url` on file is a third-party CS-course-project repo (github.com/DevSheth/prallel-hypergraph-algorithms) that reimplements only 4 of the paper's ~9 algorithms and does NOT include k-core decomposition at all. The real artifact is github.com/jshun/ligra (apps/hyper/HyperKCore.C, HyperKCore-Efficient.C). This survey used jshun/ligra directly for source-code facts; recommend correcting `artifact_url` in Phase 1's output/included.json and papers.json for this paper — out of scope for this survey task itself.
  • Hypergraph k-core (Shun20) is a structurally different operation (bipartite VertexProp/HyperedgeProp frontier propagation over vertex-hyperedge incidence, not neighbor-degree peeling on a plain adjacency list) using a disjoint graph suite (SNAP-community-as- hyperedge, KONECT bipartite, synthetic uniform-random hypergraphs) that doesn't overlap kcore-static-peel's simple-graph suite. It is intentionally NOT folded into kcore-static-peel (incommensurable) and not given its own numbered variant either, since only 1 of 5 papers in this track operates on hypergraphs. Recorded here as a candidate `kcore-hypergraph` extension variant if this track gains more hypergraph papers.
  • RDMCE's scripts/ and exp/ directories (as surveyed) show no automated correctness checker comparing RDMCE/G2-AIMD/MCE-GPU maximal-clique counts on the same graph; mce-enum's correctness gate (exact count match) is this spec's requirement, not something the surveyed artifact currently does. The exp/*.py plotting scripts were not read in full and might do an implicit cross-check — worth re-verifying before assuming it's completely absent.
  • Whether the DNF/completion-rate outcomes reported in mce-enum should be taken from RDMCE's own paper claims ("completes on every test dataset where baselines DNF") or independently re-derived was not resolved here — RDMCE's claims are the paper's own contribution narrative and should be re-verified empirically, not assumed, when this variant is actually run.
  • Shun20's T1/T72h timing-scope boundary (whether hypergraph loading is excluded) could not be confirmed from the extracted PDF text alone, unlike LiuSZ24/KCGPU where the scope is explicit; would need reading `ligra/ligra.h`'s `parallel_main` wrapper directly if a `kcore-hypergraph` variant is ever implemented.
  • k=4 appears in both kclique-count-exact (KCGPU, GPU) and kclique-count-approx (ProbGraph, CPU)'s exact-baseline reference by design (allows a future cross-check), but the two papers' "exact" k=4-counting implementations are independent (KCGPU's from-scratch GPU orientation code vs. ProbGraph's GMS-suite CPU baseline) — their exact reference numbers on the same graph should be independently verified to agree before being treated as interchangeable ground truth.
  • This track's kclique-count-exact variant (KCGPU) targets the same mathematical count (k-clique counting, k=4..7 overlap) as the `graph-pattern-mining` track's `clique_ladder` pattern set (benchspecs/graph-pattern-mining/spec.yaml), evaluated there by general-purpose subgraph-isomorphism engines (GraphFold's CF4-CF7, GLumin's CliqueSolver). KCGPU is a k-clique-SPECIALIZED kernel (graph orientation + degeneracy + warp-level binary encoding, no general pattern DAG) — a different implementation family, kept as a separate variant in this track rather than merged into graph-pattern-mining. A future harness could usefully cross-report KCGPU against GraphFold/GLumin on the same graphs to compare specialized-vs-general clique counting, but that comparison is out of scope for either spec as currently written.
triangle-counting5 papers4 variants

Exact global triangle count of a static, undirected, simple graph via edge-orientation + neighbor-intersection; measured as steady-state counting throughput with orientation/format-conversion preprocessing reported separately, across single-GPU and MPI-distributed-CPU variants that the surveyed literature treats as genuinely different regimes (no paper in this track straddles both platforms).

T = |{(u,v,w) : uv,vw,wu in E}| for undirected simple graph G=(V,E); computed via a directed orientation of each edge (typically low-degree -> high-degree, i.e. degree ordering / DODGR construction) followed by local set-intersection of directed out-neighborhoods, summed and, depending on the orientation convention, divided by a small constant (1, 3, or 6) to yield the unique undirected triangle count.

tc-gpu-kernel-exactsteady-state single-GPU counting-kernel throughput, graph already resident in device memory in the algorithm's native format (CSR / DCSR / bitmap / tensor-core layout); orientation and any format-specific reordering conversion EXCLUDED from the timed region but reported separately. The common denominator TC-Compare/GroupTC's own 9-algorithm harness and ToT's per-phase CUDATimer split both actually measure.

selectionreal (non-synthetic) undirected/undirectable graphs used by >=1 code-verified surveyed GPU artifact, 1e5 <= |E| <= 2e9 (excludes toy instances below 1e5 edges and instances too large for a single GPU's device memory in CSR+working-set form); union of TC-Compare's 19-dataset SNAP list, capped at the memory-fitting subset.

correctnessEXACT integer match (zero tolerance — triangle counts are integers, not floating-point sums) vs. a trusted single-threaded CPU reference (merge-based sorted-neighbor triangle counting, computed once per graph and cached), cross-checked against SNAP's own published "Number of triangles" statistic (snap.stanford.edu/data per-dataset page) wherever the graph originates from SNAP. Implementations using reduced-precision accumulation (e.g. ToT's fp16 Tensor Core MMA) MUST still produce the exact integer count to qualify for this variant's leaderboard on a given graph; if precision loss causes a mismatch on some instance, that (implementation, graph) pair is marked NOT-VERIFIED and excluded, rather than silently reported — this closes the gap ToT's own README documents ("-e 1 ... may mitigate precision problems in some cases") but never resolves.
tc-gpu-e2e-preprocend-to-end single-GPU throughput including one-shot CSR build + orientation + algorithm-native format conversion, amortized over k=100 repeated counts on the same resident graph — TC-Compare's own 100-iteration convention read as an amortization count rather than a pure-kernel repetition count, and the realistic "load graph once, count many times" usage pattern implied by streaming/dynamic-graph follow-on work in this space.

Fairness notes
  • TC-Compare's own 9-algorithm harness times a 100-iteration loop with a single accumulator and reports only the mean; ToT's driver runs n=1 with no repetition at all. tc-gpu-kernel-exact requires per-iteration timestamps and mandates median+min/max, matching this track's own SpMM-benchspec fix for the identical anti-pattern.
  • katric is the only one of the 3 distributed papers to explicitly document folding edge orientation/neighborhood-sorting into the counted 'algorithm time' rather than separating it like TriPoll does; tc-dist-strong-scaling-real and tc-dist-weak-scaling-synthetic both require the TriPoll-style separation instead, so orientation cost isn't silently hidden inside the counting number for algorithms that happen to interleave the two.
  • None of the 5 papers compares against an independently published ground-truth triangle count; TC-Compare and TriPoll rely only on multiple-algorithm-must-agree cross-checks, which cannot catch a bug shared by all algorithms under test. All 4 variants above mandate an EXACT match against either a trusted independent reference implementation or SNAP's own published per-dataset triangle count.
  • ToT's README documents a real, unresolved precision hazard (fp16 Tensor Core summation drifting on large graphs) and offers only a partial, non-guaranteed mitigation. This spec does not accept 'approximately correct' as passing for an EXACT-counting track: any implementation that can't guarantee the exact integer count on a given graph is excluded from that graph's leaderboard entry rather than silently scored.
  • No paper in this track reports a fixed RNG seed for its RMAT/KaGen synthetic instances, making none of the 3 distributed papers' synthetic-graph numbers independently reproducible. tc-dist-weak-scaling-synthetic fixes a seed explicitly.
Open questions
  • Whether ToT's paper-level dataset table (names/sizes actually benchmarked in the TPDS'25 article) exists anywhere accessible — ACM DL (403) and IEEE Xplore (418) both blocked WebFetch, and no arXiv preprint could be located via web search. The recommended_subset for the GPU variants is therefore built from TC-Compare's dataset list, not ToT's own, and ToT's real reported speedup/dataset numbers remain unverified beyond the abstract's headline figures.
  • TC-Compare's data_getter/g500/run.sh checked-in invocation (-R -s 17 -e 2) is explicitly labeled as an example in the repo, not necessarily the paper's actual evaluated scale(s); the true Graph500-scale sweep used in the IPDPS'24 paper itself was not independently confirmed (IEEE Xplore blocked).
  • Whether lcc (StrauszVGBH22) separates edge orientation from the counted LCC/TC time the way TriPoll does, or bundles it like katric, was not resolved from the ar5iv-fetched text (the paper states only that I/O + distribution is excluded, not where orientation falls) — the spec conservatively assumes it may be bundled and requires explicit separation regardless.
  • Whether a genuinely shared single benchmark instance (byte-identical graph, not just same-name-different-crawl) exists across katric/lcc/TriPoll for e.g. LiveJournal or uk-2007-05 was not verified; the recommended_subset names the graph family, but exact source URLs/preprocessing (symmetrization, self-loop removal) may need to be pinned per-download to guarantee identical edge counts across re-implementations.
community-detection4 papers4 variants

Discover a partition of a graph's vertices into communities that (for the Louvain-family variants) maximizes modularity, measured as wall-clock time to convergence with the resulting partition's quality reported jointly and gated — a faster run that converges to a materially worse partition does not count as an improvement. A separate variant covers the track's two non-modularity algorithm families (structural-entropy optimization, single-pass threshold clustering) so their real contributions remain benchmarkable without conflating them with modularity-comparable numbers.

C[V] = CommunityDetection(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, CSR/edge-list), weighted or unweighted); output is a vertex-to-community-ID labeling over all V vertices; for Louvain-family variants the labeling is produced by iterating (local-move phase to a modularity-gain threshold) then (community aggregation into a coarser graph) until no further gain; number of communities is DISCOVERED, not a caller-supplied parameter (this is the key structural difference from the graph-partitioning track).

cd-kernel-modularitysteady-state Louvain-family (modularity-maximizing) community detection kernel time on a fixed real-graph suite, with final modularity reported jointly and gated: a run whose modularity falls below the quality floor is disqualified from the throughput ranking regardless of how fast it completed
inputs
suiteunion of SNAP ground-truth-community graphs used or referenced by the track's Louvain-family papers (GALA, NiuOSC26), plus canonical SNAP staples for size coverage
selectionnamed SNAP graphs with disambiguated vertex/edge counts, undirected (symmetrize directed inputs before running; report whether the implementation under test does this itself or requires pre-symmetrized input)
recommended_subsetfacebook_combined (SNAP ego-Facebook, 4,039 v / 88,234 e) — small control instance, matches HSSInfo's worked example, com-DBLP (SNAP, ~317K v / 1.05M e, has ground-truth communities), com-Amazon (SNAP, ~334K v / 925K e, has ground-truth communities), com-Youtube (SNAP, ~1.13M v / 2.99M e, has ground-truth communities), com-Amazon-full / roadNet-CA-scale control not required; com-LiveJournal aka com-lj (SNAP, ~4.0M v / 34.7M e) — matches GALA's own README worked example exactly, com-Orkut (SNAP, ~3.07M v / 117.2M e, has ground-truth communities), soc-LiveJournal1 (SNAP, ~4.85M v / 68.99M e, directed — symmetrize), com-Friendster (SNAP, ~65.6M v / 1.81B e) — large-scale control, matches this track's other large-graph BFS-track precedent (see benchspecs/bfs/spec.yaml)
dense_operandN/A (no dense operand; edge weights default to 1.0 if the input graph is unweighted)
size_classessmall: <100K vertices (facebook_combined); medium: 100K-5M vertices (com-DBLP, com-Amazon, com-Youtube, com-lj, soc-LiveJournal1); large: >5M vertices (com-Orkut, com-Friendster)
protocol
formatCSR or adjacency edge-list, built once from the SNAP download; graph load/format-build NOT counted in per-run community-detection time (see cd-e2e-preprocessing for the amortized/included version)
warmup1 discarded full run (community detection is inherently one-shot per input, unlike BFS's repeated-root-search model, so 'warmup' here means one throwaway full convergence run to prime caches/GPU context, not a partial-iteration warmup)
reps10 independent full runs on the SAME graph and SAME thread/GPU count, each with a FRESH random seed/tie-break state (do NOT fix a single seed across reps — the point of this variant is to characterize the nondeterminism that NiuOSC26 identifies as an open problem in existing parallel Louvain)
statisticmedian time; report min/max/stddev of BOTH time AND final modularity across the 10 reps — a tight time distribution paired with a wide modularity distribution is itself a reportable, meaningful result (see cd-determinism-repeatability for a dedicated deep-dive variant)
timerwall-clock (host-side, e.g. omp_get_wtime()/std::chrono/gettimeofday) or device-side events for GPU implementations, wrapping the community-detection call only
timing_scopelocal-move + aggregation phases only; graph load/parse/CSR-build excluded and reported separately, once per graph instance
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once per graph instance: graph load + format-build time (this is exactly what GALA's own artifact currently fails to separate — see notes_on_fairness)
thread_gpu_disclosureREQUIRED: thread count (CPU) or GPU model + count (GPU) used for each reported number, since parallel schedule affects both time and the specific local optimum reached
algorithm_family_disclosureREQUIRED: exact Louvain variant (vanilla Louvain / Leiden-style refinement / community-versioning / distance-2-coloring / other) and modularity-gain threshold used, since GALA's own -t default (1e-6) is not necessarily what a submitter should assume
metric
primarymedian wall-clock time to convergence (ms), across the 10 reps
secondarymedian final modularity Q (report min/max across reps); iteration count (local-move + aggregation rounds)
correctnessQUALITY GATE (operationalizes "faster but lower-modularity is not a win"): compute a reference modularity Q_ref on the same graph using an established, single-threaded, to-convergence Louvain reference implementation (e.g. python-louvain / igraph community_multilevel, resolution=1.0, default parameters). A submitted run's median modularity Q_impl must satisfy Q_impl >= 0.98 * Q_ref (2% relative tolerance, matching the track's few disclosed accuracy tolerances elsewhere in this benchmark suite). Runs below this bar are DISQUALIFIED from the throughput ranking regardless of speed and must be reported as failing, not silently omitted.
cd-e2e-preprocessingend-to-end throughput including one-shot graph loading and CSR/adjacency-list construction; community detection is inherently single-shot per input (no repeated-query amortization argument the way BFS or SpMV have), so this variant reports ONE full run's total time rather than an amortized-over-k number

Fairness notes
  • The task's framing note — "a faster but lower-modularity result is not a win" — is the central fairness risk in this track and is why cd-kernel-modularity's correctness field is a hard GATE (disqualifying, not merely a caveat) rather than a passive metric, unlike most of this benchmark suite's correctness fields which check exactness/tolerance but don't disqualify a legitimately-different-but-valid algorithmic tradeoff. Modularity maximization is itself NP-hard and heuristic, so "correct" doesn't mean "exact" here — it means "not meaningfully worse than a trusted reference," which is why the gate uses a reference implementation + tolerance rather than a closed-form check.
  • GALA's own artifact times graph loading INSIDE its reported "elapsed time" (`start = get_time()` called before `load_bin_graph`), while HSSInfo's own artifact already separates `init time` from `community detection time`. cd-e2e-preprocessing and cd-kernel-modularity together fix this by making both numbers mandatory and separately visible for every submission, adopting HSSInfo's own (better) convention as the spec-wide default rather than GALA's.
  • NiuOSC26 is the only one of the 4 papers whose entire contribution is a convergence GUARANTEE for parallel Louvain under concurrency — existing parallel implementations (including, plausibly, GALA's and the Grappolo baseline NiuOSC26 itself builds on and improves) can converge to different local optima across runs due to threads reading stale modularity/community-weight data. cd-determinism-repeatability operationalizes this as a first-class, measurable variant (a reproducible run-to-run modularity spread) instead of leaving "convergence" as an unverified claim in a paper's text — this is the same "operationalize the paper's own claimed contribution as a reportable variant" pattern used for bfs-reordering-cost in benchspecs/bfs/spec.yaml.
  • ProbGraph explicitly uses a time-based (non-reproducible) hash seed ("We use the current time in milliseconds as a random seed", §VI-C) and is transparent about this rather than hiding it — this is adopted as the model for the objective_disclosure requirement in cd-alt-objective-report: submitters must disclose seed handling rather than the spec assuming determinism by default.
  • ProbGraph itself makes the "faster-but-worse-quality is not a win" argument against its OWN heuristic baselines (Reduced Execution, Partial Graph Processing, AutoApproximate — all shown in the paper's own Fig. 6 to be both slower AND less accurate than ProbGraph's Bloom-filter/MinHash schemes) — i.e. the fairness principle this spec enforces across algorithm families is one the track's own most rigorous paper already applies internally to its own comparison set.
  • HSSInfo's and ProbGraph's memory-centric framing (19x memory shrink; storage budget s capped at 33% additional) is adopted as the model for making memory a first-class primary metric in cd-alt-objective-report, rather than relegating it to a footnote as cd-kernel-modularity does (where time and modularity are primary and memory is not currently tracked — a scope gap flagged in open_questions below).
Open questions
  • No arXiv or open-access fulltext exists for NiuOSC26 (IPDPS 2026, unpublished/paywalled at survey time) or HSSInfo (TPDS 2023, IEEE Xplore paywalled, no arXiv mirror). Their evaluation methodology facts above are reconstructed entirely from artifact code and README; actual published dataset lists, thread-count sweeps, hardware, and repetition/statistic conventions used IN THE PAPERS could not be confirmed and may differ from what the code alone suggests. Revisit if either becomes openly accessible.
  • GALA's README and its own `data/prepare_graph.sh` script disagree on the single documented worked-example graph (com-lj vs. com-amazon) — unresolved which one is actually used in the PPoPP'25 paper's reported numbers (paywalled, ACM DL DOI page returns only metadata via WebFetch).
  • Whether GALA's or NiuOSC26's Louvain implementations produce bit-reproducible partitions under a FIXED seed (as opposed to merely "eventually converging" under NiuOSC26's proof) was not confirmed from either artifact — cd-determinism-repeatability is designed to measure this empirically since it cannot currently be confirmed by reading the code alone.
  • This spec does not yet define a memory metric for cd-kernel-modularity/ cd-e2e-preprocessing (only cd-alt-objective-report tracks memory as primary) even though HSSInfo's whole contribution is memory reduction on the SAME Louvain-adjacent territory. If a future Louvain-family paper with a memory-efficiency claim joins this track, memory should likely be promoted to a tracked secondary metric in cd-kernel-modularity too, rather than being confined to the alt-objective variant.
  • No Leiden or pure label-propagation paper appears among the 4 surveyed papers (Vite, referenced only as GALA's "-p 2" pruning-strategy name, is a Grappolo-lineage tool but not itself one of the 4 papers). The variants above are written to be extensible to a future Leiden submission (Leiden's well-connectedness guarantee is a stronger property than plain modularity-gain convergence and would need its own disclosure field alongside algorithm_family_disclosure) but this has not been exercised against a real Leiden paper's artifact.
connected-components4 papers4 variants

Connectivity-decomposition kernels on graphs (or, for one sub-problem, regular pixel/voxel grids), covering the three genuinely distinct sub-problems this track's own papers actually evaluate: biconnected components (BCC, undirected), strongly connected components (SCC, directed), and binary-image 2D/3D connected-component labeling (CCL, regular grid, not a general sparse graph). Each sub-problem gets its own variant family rather than being forced into a single shared shape, since their operations, correctness definitions, and even connectivity semantics ("8-connectivity" vs. "strongly reachable" vs. "removal of one vertex disconnects") are not interchangeable.

BCC: label[V], componentHead[label] = BCC(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, symmetric/undirected CSR)); label[v] identifies which biconnected component each non-root vertex's incident tree edge belongs to, and the set of cut vertices/cut edges is derivable from label[] and componentHead[] in O(1) per query. SCC: scc_id[V] = SCC(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, DIRECTED CSR)); scc_id[v] identifies the strongly-connected component containing v, such that contracting each scc_id-class to a single vertex yields a DAG. Image-CCL: label[H,W] (2D) or label[D,H,W] (3D) = CCL(image[H,W] or [D,H,W] (binary, foreground/background)); label assigns a unique positive integer to every maximal foreground blob under a fixed connectivity rule (8-connectivity for 2D, 26-connectivity for 3D), 0 for background.

cc-bcc-kernel-inmemorysteady-state biconnected-components kernel time on named undirected real-world graphs that fit in device/node memory, with the internal connected-components subroutine's algorithm family (Shiloach-Vishkin pointer-jumping vs. Afforest/k-out-sampling vs. other) mandatorily disclosed, since both surveyed BCC papers show this subroutine choice is consequential to reported performance

algorithm_family_disclosureREQUIRED: report the SCC algorithm's family as one of {max-ID/signature-propagation with edge removal (ECL-SCC's own family), Forward-Backward BFS-pivot with trim (Fleischer/ McLendon-descended, the family every OTHER surveyed SCC paper including both baselines uses), spanning-tree + relaxed- synchronization (iSpan's family), other (name it)} — since the surveyed paper's central finding is that the RIGHT choice is graph-regime-dependent (max-ID-propagation wins decisively on low-degree/deep-DAG mesh graphs, is merely competitive to sometimes-slower on power-law graphs where FB-family algorithms are specifically optimized), a benchmark that doesn't disclose which family is under test cannot separate "this implementation is fast" from "this algorithm family suits this graph regime."
graph_regime_disclosureREQUIRED: classify each tested graph as {power-law (few high-degree vertices, typically one dominant giant SCC)} or {structured/low-degree (near-constant vertex degree, typically many small SCCs forming a deep DAG)} or {other, describe} — the two regimes surveyed papers show behave qualitatively differently under every SCC algorithm family tested.
