formatdirected CSR, built once; construction NOT counted in per-search time
warmup1
reps9 for individually-distinguishable graph instances (matches ECL-SCC's own convention); for a mesh FAMILY with multiple ordinates, report the per-ordinate median-of-9 individually AND the across-ordinate mean/min/max — do NOT collapse straight to a single family-level number without disclosing both aggregation levels, since ECL-SCC's own two-level aggregation (median-of-9- per-ordinate, then mean-across-ordinates) is easy to misread as a simple repetition median if not made explicit
statisticmedian of 9 runs per graph instance; mean across ordinates for a mesh family, both reported
timerdevice-side events or std::chrono, wrapping the SCC computation only
timing_scopeSCC computation only, explicitly excluding graph reading, output, verification, AND host-device transfer of the input graph (the input is assumed already resident on the accelerator, following ECL-SCC's own explicit, stated rationale — this must be disclosed as an assumption, not a free default, since it differs from the bfs/sssp specs' own convention of excluding only OUTPUT transfer)
preprocessing_reportedN/A for host-device input transfer per timing_scope above (assumed pre-resident); CSR construction time reported separately if measured on the host before transfer
metric
primarythroughput = vertices / scc_time_seconds, in millions of vertices/second (ECL-SCC's own metric, adopted here specifically because it is size-normalized across the very wide graph-size range this sub-problem's suite spans, from 262K-vertex meshes to multi-million-vertex power-law graphs)
secondaryscc_time_ms (median of 9, raw, for readers who want unnormalized numbers); number_of_SCCs, largest_SCC_size, DAG_depth as reported diagnostic outputs
correctnessREQUIRED gate before timing counts: full SCC MEMBERSHIP (not just component count) must exactly match a single-threaded sequential Tarjan's-algorithm reference run once per graph instance — ECL-SCC's own practice, the strongest correctness check found across either track's connected-components-adjacent papers. A matching SCC count alone is NOT sufficient (two different, both-wrong labelings can coincidentally produce the same count).
cc-image-ccl-2d3dsteady-state binary-image connected-component-labeling kernel time on named real image datasets, under a fixed connectivity rule (8-connectivity 2D / 26-connectivity 3D), with the underlying algorithm family and the specific test axis (plain average runtime vs. density/granularity/blocksize sensitivity) both disclosed — this variant is explicitly scoped to a REGULAR-GRID sub-problem, not the general sparse-graph connectivity this spec's other 3 variants cover, and inherits the surveyed paper's own richer, multi-axis test taxonomy rather than collapsing it to a single number
inputs
suitethe YACCLAB project's own named 2D image dataset collection, since it is the only workload source surveyed for this sub-problem and is itself a maintained, versioned, community benchmark rather than a one-off paper artifact
selectionall 7 datasets used across YACCLAB's own correctness AND average-runtime test categories, for direct comparability with the project's own published numbers
recommended_subset3dpes (surveillance video frames, binary foreground/background masks), fingerprints (biometric fingerprint scans), hamlet (historical document scan, binarized text page images), medical (medical imaging, binarized), mirflickr (general photography, binarized), tobacco800 (historical document scan corpus), xdocs (document image corpus)
dense_operandN/A (binary image, not a dense operand in the linear-algebra sense; the pixel grid itself is the input structure)
connectivity_rule8-connectivity for 2D (project-wide invariant, per YACCLAB's own stated convention: 'Notice that 8-connectivity is always used in the project'); 26-connectivity for the 3D extension where applicable — this is a FIXED protocol parameter, not a per-submission choice, unlike the sparse-graph variants' directed/undirected axis
algorithm_family_disclosureREQUIRED: report the labeling algorithm's family as one of {block-based Union-Find (BUF, the surveyed paper's own contribution), block-based Komura-Equivalence (BKE, the surveyed paper's other contribution), classic (non-block) Union-Find, raster-scan two-pass, decision-tree-based (e.g. the project's own C_SAUF/C_BBDT/C_DRAG baselines), other (name it, from YACCLAB's own 18-algorithm baseline list if applicable)}
protocol
formatbinary image loaded via a standard image-decoding library (e.g. OpenCV imread), decode time NOT counted in per-image labeling time but reported separately
warmup1
reps10 (YACCLAB's own disclosed default, tests_number.average = 10 in its config files)
statisticREQUIRED to be explicitly named (mean or median) per submission — this spec could not confirm from YACCLAB's own reachable configuration files which statistic its `average` test category computes internally, so unlike this spec's other variants it does NOT default to median; a submission under this variant MUST state which statistic it used and, if reproducing YACCLAB's own published numbers, must match YACCLAB's own (unconfirmed, flagged in open_questions) convention or explicitly note the discrepancy
timerhost-side high-resolution timer (std::chrono) or CUDA events for GPU algorithms, wrapping the labeling call only
timing_scopelabeling computation only; image decode/load and any output-writing excluded
preprocessing_reportedN/A (no separate preprocessing phase in this sub-problem beyond image decode, which is excluded from timing scope entirely rather than being a reportable one-shot cost, since it is dominated by an unrelated image-codec's performance, not the CCL algorithm's)
test_axis_disclosure_requiredREQUIRED: report which of YACCLAB's own test categories the submitted numbers come from — at minimum `average` (plain runtime) is required; `density`, `granularity`, and `blocksize` sensitivity results are OPTIONAL but strongly encouraged given this sub-problem's own benchmark framework already supports them natively, and a bare `average` number without any sensitivity context is easy to cherry-pick a favorable blocksize for
metric
primarylabeling_time_ms (per image, aggregated per dataset per the statistic named above)
secondarymemory_access_count (YACCLAB's own `memory` test category output, a hardware-portable secondary metric this sub-problem's benchmark framework treats as first-class, unlike any other variant in either track's specs); number_of_components as a reported diagnostic output
correctnessREQUIRED gate before timing counts: full label-EQUIVALENCE match against a reference labeling for every image in the dataset (not merely a matching component count) — YACCLAB's own dedicated, separately-runnable `correctness` test category, run against the SAME 7 named datasets plus a synthetic `check` dataset — must pass before any `average`/`density`/`granularity`/`blocksize` timing numbers from the same implementation are considered valid.
Fairness notes
  • This track's own 4 papers span 3 different sub-problems (BCC, SCC, image-CCL) that a naive reading of the track name ("connected components") would not predict, and none is a plain weakly-connected-components paper in the Shiloach-Vishkin/Afforest sense the track brief anticipated. Rather than force a shared variant shape none of the 4 papers would actually populate meaningfully, this spec defines 4 variants across the 3 real sub-problems (2 for BCC, 1 for SCC, 1 for image-CCL), each grounded in what its source paper(s) actually measure — the same "survey what's real, don't force a template" discipline the sibling bfs/sssp specs apply when a surveyed paper's role is tangential to the track's nominal topic.
  • Both surveyed BCC papers REQUIRE undirected, single-component input and actively modify their source graphs to satisfy this (symmetrizing directed graphs, and in one case adding edges purely to force single-connectivity). This is a disclosed but real representativeness concern: a graph's natural directedness and component structure are edited away before biconnectivity is ever measured on it, meaning "BCC performance on graph X" in this literature always means "BCC performance on a MODIFIED version of graph X," not the graph as distributed. The spec's symmetrization_disclosure and single-connectivity-forcing disclosure fields make this modification visible rather than implicit, but do not eliminate it — a genuinely fair BCC benchmark would need either graphs that are natively undirected/connected, or a standardized (not per-paper-invented) modification protocol, neither of which the current 2-paper evidence base is enough to establish; flagged as an open question.
  • The internal connectivity-subroutine choice inside BCC algorithms (Shiloach-Vishkin vs. Afforest/k-out-sampling vs. other) is exactly the "algorithm family" axis the track brief asked this survey to check, but it shows up one layer beneath each paper's own headline contribution (the spanning-tree/skeleton construction), not at the top level. FAST-BCC-Filter's own text flags this choice as graph-type-dependent without running the ablation that would show how much it matters. The spec's internal_cc_subroutine_disclosure field surfaces this rather than leaving it as an unexamined implementation detail, since a benchmark that doesn't ask "which CC family did you actually call" cannot separate a BCC-specific algorithmic contribution from a CC-subroutine choice that happened to be favorable.
  • SCC's headline finding (ECL-SCC vs. SCC-GPU/iSpan) is REGIME- DEPENDENT: a 6-8x win on mesh graphs, roughly parity (sometimes a slight loss) on power-law graphs. This is the most honestly-disclosed regime-dependence found across either track's survey — the paper does not claim a single blanket speedup number. The spec's graph_regime_disclosure field is designed specifically to prevent a future submission from citing only the mesh-graph speedup (or only the power-law comparison) without stating which regime the number applies to, since the two regimes are evaluated on structurally different graph families with no overlap in this survey's evidence base.
  • Image-CCL (YACCLAB/BUF/BKE) is included in this track's variant set despite being a genuinely different domain (regular pixel grid, not sparse graph) because it IS one of the 4 papers the track's classification pipeline assigned to "connected-components," and the project's own working discipline (per this repo's CLAUDE.md) is to survey and spec what papers actually measure rather than silently dropping an inconvenient one. Readers assembling a benchmark suite across kernel categories should treat cc-image-ccl-2d3d as measuring a related-but-distinct primitive from cc-bcc-* and cc-scc-kernel, not as a fourth data point on the same underlying "connectivity kernel" performance curve — the three variant families are not meant to be aggregated into one blended connected-components score.
  • Timing-statistic naming (mean vs. median) is inconsistently disclosed across all 4 papers, including one paper (FAST-BCC-Filter/PEA-BCC) using DIFFERENT statistics for its own GPU vs. CPU-baseline numbers within a single evaluation section. The spec fixes median as the required default for the 3 sparse-graph variants (matching this track's own majority practice and the sibling bfs/sssp specs) but deliberately does NOT default the image-CCL variant's statistic, since this survey could not confirm YACCLAB's own convention from reachable sources — silently assuming median there risks misrepresenting the very benchmark framework this variant is modeled on.
Open questions
  • FAST-BCC-Filter/PEA-BCC (IPDPS26)'s reachable evaluation section does not describe an explicit per-run BCC-correctness check (its artifact-evaluation appendix substitutes a reproduce-the-paper's-own- figures check for a correctness-against-a-reference check); whether an undisclosed correctness gate exists in the actual build/run scripts was not resolved without executing the artifact, which was out of scope for this survey. cc-bcc-kernel-inmemory's correctness requirements are therefore modeled on FAST-BCC (PPoPP23)'s stronger, explicit practice rather than on this paper's own (apparently weaker or at least undisclosed) one.
  • YACCLAB's exact timing statistic (mean vs. median across its disclosed 10-repetition default) and its exact correctness-reference implementation were not identified from the reachable `config_*.yaml` files; resolving this would require reading `performance_evaluator.h` / `yacclab_test.h` / `check_labeling.h` in the C++ source, not reached given this survey's time budget. The cc-image-ccl-2d3d variant's statistic field is left unresolved (REQUIRED to be disclosed per-submission) rather than guessed, specifically because of this gap.
  • Whether the two BCC papers' input-graph modification (symmetrization and, in one case, forced single-connectivity) measurably changes reported BCC structure/speedup in a way that would differ from benchmarking on natively-undirected, natively-connected graphs was not investigated quantitatively — flagged as a fairness concern in notes_on_fairness but not resolved.
  • Whether FAST-BCC (PPoPP23)'s reported per-test time includes graph loading/format-parsing was not confirmed from the reachable README/script text (the benchmark script's CSV output format is consistent with either interpretation); cc-bcc-kernel-inmemory's timing_scope field states the spec's OWN required convention (loading excluded) rather than assuming it matches this paper's unconfirmed practice.
  • Whether a genuinely unified "connectivity kernel" benchmark spanning WCC, BCC, and SCC (the three problems that ARE comparable, unlike image-CCL) would be more useful than three separate variant families was considered but not attempted here, since no paper in this 4-paper sample evaluates more than one of these three problems in a way that would let this survey ground a unified spec in actual literature practice rather than inventing one from scratch.
pagerank4 papers3 variants

Global PageRank via power iteration over a directed graph in CSR/CSC form, measured both as steady-state per-iteration throughput at a fixed iteration budget and as time-to-convergence under an explicit epsilon, with preprocessing (format conversion, any reordering) strictly separated from iteration time and correctness gated against an independent fp64 reference rank vector.

r_{t+1}[v] = (1-alpha)/N + alpha * sum_{u: (u,v) in E} r_t[u] / outdeg(u), for all v in V, iterated from r_0[v] = 1/N until either a fixed iteration budget k is exhausted or ||r_t - r_{t-1}||_1 < epsilon; A[V,V] is the (unweighted, direction-preserving) sparse adjacency, dangling nodes (outdeg(u)=0) redistribute their mass uniformly over all V; damping alpha = 0.85, personalization vector uniform (global PageRank, not personalized/single-source).

pagerank-fixed-iter-kernel-f32steady-state per-iteration kernel throughput at a fixed iteration budget k=20, preprocessing excluded but reported separately — reconciles the track's two competing fixed-count conventions (Corder/Shun20's 1-iteration microbenchmark and GeraK23's 50-iteration cap) at a middle value the track itself already uses for profiling (Corder's own 20-iteration L2-cache-miss figure)
inputs
suiteunion of SNAP and LAW/WebGraph real directed/undirected graphs used by the 2 surveyed papers that measure global PageRank (GeraK23, ChenC22/Corder), disambiguated by exact vertex/edge counts, plus GAP-Benchmark-Suite-style synthetic fill-ins for size-class coverage — same disambiguation convention as the sibling `bfs` benchspec, which surveys the same two papers for BFS
selectionnamed real graphs appearing in >=1 of the 2 global-PageRank papers' own suites (union, not intersection, since overlap is only partial), |E| spanning ~1e6 to ~4e9 to cover both papers' size ranges; synthetic Graph500 kron/uniform-random generators included since both papers use them as a "non-power-law control" graph
recommended_subsetsoc-LiveJournal1 (SNAP, ~4.85M v / 68.9M e, directed) — GeraK23's 'soc-lj'; matches ChenC22's 'live' (4.8M v / 68.5M e) closely enough to plausibly be the same underlying graph (unconfirmed, see open_questions), com-Orkut (SNAP, ~3.07M v / 234.3M e, undirected) — GeraK23's 'orkut', twitter-2010-efg (Kwak et al. crawl as packaged by GeraK23's efg repo, 41.6M v / 1.47B e, directed) — NOT confirmed identical to ChenC22's 'twitter' (41.7M v / 1.5B e); kept as a separate disambiguated instance pending verification, com-Friendster (SNAP, ~65.61M v / 3.61B e, undirected) — GeraK23's 'frndster', uk-2007-05 (LAW webgraph, 105.22M v / 3.74B e, directed) — GeraK23's 'uk-07-05', sk-2005 (LAW webgraph, 65.61M v / 1.95B e, directed) — GeraK23's 'sk-05', gsh-2015-host (LAW webgraph, 68.66M v / 1.8B e, directed) — GeraK23's 'gsh-15-h', kron_g500-logn23 (Graph500 Kronecker generator, scale 23, ~63-67M v / ~2.1-2.12B e) — GeraK23's 'kron27' and ChenC22's 'kron' target the same generator family at the same scale; pin the exact seed/parameterization used, do not assume identical output files, urand-scale26 (Graph500 uniform-random generator, scale 26, ~67.1M v / 1.07-2.14B e) — GeraK23's 'urnd26' and ChenC22's 'urand'; the non-skewed control graph BOTH papers use, and ChenC22 explicitly excludes it from its own averages as 'not skewed' — this spec's suite keeps it IN every variant (see notes_on_fairness), pld (ChenC22, pay-level-domain web hyperlink graph, 42.9M v / 0.6B e, directed) — exact public source not confirmed from the accessible text, flagged in open_questions, wiki-links-corder (ChenC22's 'wiki', hyperlink graph, 18.3M v / 0.2B e, directed) — small/medium control instance; NOT the same instance as the `bfs` benchspec's 'wiki-topcats', disambiguated by name, mpi (ChenC22, highly-skewed social/influence graph, 52.6M v / 2.0B e) — ChenC22's own extreme-skew stress test, kept as-is since no public canonical source name was confirmed, com-dblp (SNAP, 317,080 v / 1,049,866 e) — small-size control instance; also one of MeLoPPR's 6 graphs, bridging the two papers' size ranges, com-amazon (SNAP, 334,863 v / 925,872 e) — small-size control instance, also one of MeLoPPR's graphs, com-youtube (SNAP, 1,134,890 v / 2,987,624 e) — small/medium control instance, also one of MeLoPPR's graphs
correctness_reference_subsetciteseer (3,327 v / 4,676 e), cora (2,708 v / 5,278 e), pubmed (19,717 v / 44,327 e) — MeLoPPR's 3 smallest graphs, cheap enough to brute-force an independent fp64 reference rank vector on a laptop; RECOMMENDED as the first correctness check for any new implementation before trusting it on the multi-billion-edge instances above, since a wrong kernel is far cheaper to catch here
dense_operandN/A — no dense operand; rank vector length N, fp32 for the timed kernel, fp64 for the correctness reference (see correctness below)
size_classessmall: <2M vertices (com-dblp, com-amazon, com-youtube); medium: 2-70M vertices (com-Orkut, soc-LiveJournal1, wiki-links-corder, pld, twitter-2010-efg, kron_g500-logn23, urand-scale26, mpi); large: >70M vertices (com-Friendster, uk-2007-05, sk-2005, gsh-2015-host)
protocol
formatCSR (push/CSC pull, per direction disclosure below) given/converted once; conversion NOT timed here (see pagerank-e2e-reorder for the amortized version)
warmup1 full k=20-iteration run, discarded
reps5
iterationsfixed k=20 (see claim rationale above); every rep runs exactly k=20 iterations regardless of when/whether the rank vector would have converged
dampingalpha = 0.85 — the Page & Brin original constant and the de facto library default (cuGraph, Ligra, NetworkX); NONE of the 2 surveyed global-PageRank papers state a numeric alpha, so this value is asserted by the spec, not drawn from either paper (see survey.md Divergences #5)
dangling_node_handlingredistribute dangling mass uniformly over all V each iteration (standard treatment); an implementation that instead drops dangling mass (a common shortcut) must disclose this, since it changes the converged fixed point
statisticmedian of 5 reps; report min/max
timerdevice-side events (CUDA/HIP events) for GPU implementations, std::chrono for CPU, wrapping only the k-iteration loop
timing_scopekernel only (the k=20-iteration loop); graph load, CSR/CSC build, and any reordering are one-shot and excluded, reported separately
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once per graph instance: CSR/CSC build time, and — if a reordering method is applied — its wall time (following ChenC22/Corder's own amortization-argument convention, made explicit rather than folded silently into iteration time)
direction_disclosureREQUIRED: report whether the implementation is push (CSR, source scatters to destinations, typically atomic destination updates — GeraK23's and ChenC22's Ligra-backend convention), pull (CSC, destination gathers from in-neighbors, no atomics needed since PageRank has no frontier — every vertex is active every iteration unlike BFS), or hybrid/direction-optimized (state the switch threshold or criterion, following Shun20's disclosed default of 1/20 fraction of in-degree sum — the only one of the 4 surveyed papers to disclose this)
metric
primaryms per iteration = total_time_for_k_iterations / k
secondarytotal_time_ms for the k=20-iteration run; GTEPS = (nnz * k) / total_time_seconds / 1e9 (same throughput unit GeraK23 uses for BFS/SSSP/PageRank, for cross-kernel comparability within this project's benchmark suite)
correctnesscompute an independent fp64 reference rank vector once per graph via a trusted power-iteration implementation (e.g. scipy.sparse or networkx.pagerank) run to a tight epsilon=1e-12, same alpha=0.85, same dangling-node handling, for the SAME k=20 iterations (not to full convergence — this isolates numerical-precision/implementation correctness from "how close a 20-iteration snapshot is to the true fixed point," which is a separate, expected, non-zero gap for a fixed-iteration variant). Required gate: L1 distance between the timed fp32 rank vector and this fp64/k=20 reference must be < 1e-4 (relative to the rank vector summing to 1.0). Additionally report, as an informational (non-gating) number, the L1 distance between the k=20 rank vector and a FULLY CONVERGED (epsilon=1e-10) fp64 reference, to make explicit how far from the true fixed point a fixed-iteration snapshot actually is on each graph.
pagerank-converge-kernel-f32steady-state kernel time-to-convergence under an explicit epsilon, preprocessing excluded — a spec-level FIX to a real gap in the surveyed literature: none of the 4 papers in this track runs PageRank to a disclosed convergence tolerance (see survey.md Divergences #1); this variant exists so the track has at least one apples-to-apples "how long until I actually have a usable rank vector" number, not just fixed/arbitrary iteration-count snapshots

Fairness notes
  • ChenC22/Corder explicitly excludes its own 'urand' graph from its reported averages, stating it is "not skewed" and therefore unrepresentative of the paper's target workload. This is transparent self-disclosure (good practice) but still a cherry-pick of the reported AVERAGE, not of the underlying data. This spec's recommended_subset keeps urand-scale26 in EVERY variant precisely so that "the reordering/compression technique doesn't help on unskewed graphs" remains a visible, reportable result across the whole suite rather than a number quietly dropped from an average — matching the same fix already applied in the sibling `bfs` benchspec for the same underlying dataset.
  • Both surveyed global-PageRank papers (GeraK23, ChenC22) report a fixed-iteration number as their headline PageRank result (50-iteration cap and 1-iteration-per-Table-5-cell respectively) with NO stated convergence tolerance anywhere. Reporting a fixed-iteration time alone, without ever showing how far that snapshot is from the converged fixed point, lets an implementation look fast simply by doing less total work (fewer effective iterations to reach a comparable quality) without that tradeoff being visible. The spec's pagerank-fixed-iter-kernel-f32 variant requires reporting the L1 distance to a fully-converged reference as an informational number specifically to make this tradeoff visible rather than hidden, and pagerank-converge-kernel-f32 exists so a true apples-to-apples "time to a real answer" number is always obtainable.
  • Direction-optimization (push/pull/hybrid) status is undisclosed for 3 of the 4 surveyed papers (GeraK23 is push-only by design and does disclose this; ChenC22's Ligra backend is atomics/push-like but doesn't confirm direction-optimization status, and its GPOP backend's direction is entirely undisclosed; MeLoPPR doesn't apply). Only Shun20 discloses and quantifies it. Since PageRank (unlike BFS) has every vertex active every iteration in the naive formulation, a pull-based CSC gather can avoid atomics entirely and is often substantially faster than a push-based CSR scatter with atomic contention on high-degree destinations — exactly the kind of implementation-choice gap that inflates apparent "algorithmic" speedups if left undisclosed. All three variants above make direction disclosure mandatory, mirroring the sibling `bfs` benchspec's identical requirement.
  • MeLoPPR is the only one of the 4 papers to state a concrete damping factor (alpha=0.95), but for a different problem (Personalized, not global, PageRank). Rather than let this one disclosed number silently become "the" damping factor for the whole track, the spec fixes alpha=0.85 for its own global-PageRank variants (the standard value, used by every major library referenced across the 4 papers) and explicitly notes in survey.md that this value is asserted by the spec, not evidenced by either of the 2 relevant papers.
  • None of the 4 papers validates PageRank's numeric output against an independent reference with a stated tolerance — MeLoPPR's "precision" metric is a top-k set-overlap ratio against its own approximate, depth-truncated reference, which is a fundamentally different (weaker) notion than a rank-vector distance, and is self-referential in a way that can't catch a systematically-biased-but-consistent implementation. The correctness gates in all three variants above (L1 distance vs. an independently computed fp64 reference) are a genuine fix to this gap in the surveyed practice, per the task's own "correctness gate before timing counts" fairness principle, not a codification of anything any of the 4 papers actually did.
Open questions
  • GeraK23's PageRank figure (Fig. 11) never names which specific graphs from its BFS Table II are actually used for PageRank — unlike BFS, there is no PageRank-specific table. The exact graph list for GeraK23's own reported PageRank numbers is therefore unconfirmed; this spec's recommended_subset is built from the union of both papers' NAMED graphs generally, not a guarantee that GeraK23's own PageRank figure used all of them.
  • Whether GeraK23's 'soc-lj'/twitter and ChenC22's 'live'/twitter are the same underlying graph snapshots (same crawl, different preprocessing/dedup) or independently collected graphs that happen to be close in size was not resolved from the accessible text — same open question already flagged in the sibling `bfs` benchspec for these exact two papers. Until resolved, treat cross-paper PageRank numbers on same-named graphs as suggestive, not proven bit-identical.
  • ChenC22/Corder's 'pld' graph (pay-level-domain web hyperlink graph, 42.9M v / 0.6B e) has no confirmed public source/download link in the accessible text (citation [20] in the paper was not resolved); a submitter targeting this instance would need to track down the exact reference before it can be pinned as a byte-identical file.
  • ChenC22/Corder's "Pagerank Delta" numeric threshold `d` and GeraK23's implicit damping/tolerance for its cuGraph-based PageRank calls are both unstated in the accessible fulltext; neither could be pinned without access to the actual source (GPOP/Ligra config for Corder, the specific cuGraph API call parameters for GeraK23).
  • Whether it is worth adding a 4th, explicitly-separate "personalized-pagerank" track/spec to properly cover MeLoPPR (rather than only discussing it in this survey) was not resolved — it is a different-enough problem (single-source, depth-truncated, top-k-set correctness notion) that folding it into a "variant" of this spec would blur the comparison this spec is trying to make fair; flagged for whoever owns track-scoping decisions rather than decided here.
sssp3 papers4 variants

Single-source shortest paths on a weighted directed or undirected graph (CSR), measured as steady-state kernel time with preprocessing (format conversion, initial delta-parameter selection) strictly separated from per-search kernel time; source-vertex selection and edge-weight distribution are made explicit, disclosed axes rather than silent defaults, since this track's own papers disagree sharply on both.

dist[V] = SSSP(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, CSR), weight w: E -> R+, source in V); dist[v] = shortest-path weight sum from source to v (INF-sentinel for unreachable v); output additionally includes a parent/predecessor array so correctness can be checked as a valid shortest-path tree, not merely a distance vector.

sssp-kernel-weighted-staticsteady-state search-phase kernel time on named real-world weighted graphs, with the edge-weight distribution and delta-stepping (or equivalent priority-coarsening) parameter selection method both mandatorily disclosed; preprocessing (CSR construction, initial delta computation) excluded but reported separately
inputs
suiteunion of the real-graph families used across the track's papers (Lonestar/SuiteSparse per ADDS, GAP/SNAP-social/OSM-road per GraphIt) plus the bfs track's real-graph suite for cross-track instance reuse where a shared undirected instance exists
selectionnamed graphs with disambiguated vertex/edge counts; a candidate instance qualifies if it appears in >=1 surveyed paper's own evaluation OR is drawn from the bfs spec's recommended_subset (for cross-track comparability of the same underlying graph under both an unweighted-BFS and a weighted-SSSP lens)
recommended_subsetcom-LiveJournal (SNAP, ~4.8M v / 69M e, undirected) — shared with bfs spec, com-Orkut (SNAP, ~3.1M v / 117M e, undirected) — shared with bfs spec; NOT the same as GraphIt's 234M-e symmetrized Orkut, disambiguated by edge count, GAP-twitter (GAP Benchmark Suite, 61.6M v / 1.47B e symmetrized, directed) — shared with bfs spec, GAP-road (GAP Benchmark Suite, ~23.9M v / 58M e, directed, USA road network) — matches GraphIt's RoadUSA size class, GAP-web (GAP Benchmark Suite, ~50.6M v / 1.93B e, directed), com-Friendster (SNAP, ~65.6M v / 3.61B e, undirected) — shared with bfs spec, soc-Pokec (SNAP, 1,632,803 v / 30,622,564 e, directed) — exact size per Srinivasan et al., com-Youtube (SNAP, 1,134,890 v / 2,987,624 e, undirected) — exact size per Srinivasan et al. and per ECL-SCC's power-law suite in the connected-components track, small/control instance, com-DBLP (SNAP, ~317K v / 1M e) — small-size control instance, shared with bfs spec, germany_osm (OpenStreetMap-derived, ~12M v / 32M e, undirected road network) — exact size per GraphIt, massachusetts_osm (OpenStreetMap-derived, ~0.45M v / 1.2M e, undirected road network) — exact size per GraphIt, small/control instance, RMAT24-scale-free (a=.45,b=.15,c=.15,d=.25 Kronecker generator, ~16M v / 268M e) — per Srinivasan et al., paired with RMAT24-uniform-random below to make skewed-vs-unskewed a visible axis, same discipline as bfs spec's Corder-urand handling, RMAT24-uniform-random (a=b=c=d=.25 Kronecker generator, ~16M v / 268M e)
dense_operandN/A (weighted scalar per edge, not a dense operand)
edge_weight_distributionREQUIRED, explicit per-instance choice (this is the track's sharpest divergence — see notes_on_fairness): for road networks, use REAL travel-distance/time weights where available (matches GraphIt's `origweights` and is the only physically meaningful choice for that graph family); for all other graphs, run BOTH of two disclosed synthetic regimes rather than picking one silently: (a) uniform-random integer weights in [1, 1000] (matches GraphIt's `_rand1000` and is the most common convention across the wider SSSP literature), and (b) uniform-random integer weights in [1, log2(|V|)] (matches GraphIt's `_logn`, relevant because it changes which delta-stepping granularity is optimal and is the regime under which wBFS-style delta=1 special-casing becomes competitive) — reporting only one regime without naming it (as Srinivasan et al.'s SSSP-update precursor does) is exactly the gap this field is designed to close
size_classessmall: <5M vertices (com-DBLP, com-Youtube, massachusetts_osm); medium: 5-70M vertices (com-LiveJournal, com-Orkut, soc-Pokec, GAP-road, RMAT24 pair, germany_osm); large: >70M vertices (GAP-twitter, GAP-web, com-Friendster)

reps64 (aligned with the bfs spec's REAL_BFS_ROOTS convention for cross-track consistency, superseding every surveyed SSSP paper's own smaller/fixed-source practice — see notes_on_fairness)
root_selectionuniform-random from the giant (weakly-)connected component, fixed RNG seed = 0, same 64 roots reused across all implementations under test on a given graph+weight-regime instance — directly reuses the bfs spec's root-selection discipline rather than any of this track's own papers' single-vertex or hand-picked-source-set conventions
statisticmedian of per-search wall-clock time, report min/max alongside; ADDS's own convention (8-run arithmetic mean per graph) is a valid alternative statistic to ALSO report for direct ADDS-comparability, but median-with-min/max is the spec's primary statistic for outlier robustness, matching the bfs spec's reasoning
timerdevice-side events (CUDA/HIP events) for GPU implementations or std::chrono for CPU implementations, wrapping only the search call; must exclude host-device transfer of the OUTPUT distance/parent arrays

Hand-tuning without disclosing the search budget is NOT an acceptable submission under this spec — see notes_on_fairness for why GraphIt's own per-framework hand-tuning, while transparent, still creates a tuning-effort asymmetry risk this field is designed to surface, not eliminate.
metric
primarysearch_time_ms (median, min, max across 64 reps)
secondaryedge_relaxations_per_second = total edge-relaxation operations (including re-relaxations of the same edge under bucket-based coarsening) / search_time_seconds — a first-principles construction since no surveyed paper reports a standardized weighted-SSSP throughput metric (see open_questions); ALSO report work_efficiency = 1 / vertices_processed, following ADDS's own instrumentation convention, since it is the only metric in this track's literature that directly isolates algorithmic quality from raw hardware throughput
correctnessexact per-vertex distance match against an independent single- threaded reference SSSP (Dijkstra for the [1,1000]/[1,log|V|] integer-weight regimes; a tolerance of relative error < 1e-9 for real-valued road-network weights, to allow for floating-point summation-order differences under parallel relaxation) — modeled on ADDS's own `verify.py` exact-diff discipline rather than Srinivasan et al.'s proof-only or GraphIt's compiler-test-suite-only approaches, since a per-run empirical check catches implementation bugs a one-time proof or compile-time test cannot. The output parent array must additionally form a valid tree (no cycles, every non-source parent pointer reduces distance), the same tree-validity requirement the connected-components track's BCC variants use for their own spanning-structure outputs.
sssp-e2e-preprocessingend-to-end throughput including one-shot preprocessing (CSR conversion, weight-array construction, and initial delta selection if static), amortized over k=64 searches — same k as the kernel-only variant's repetition count and the bfs spec's e2e variant, so the amortization argument stays apples-to-apples across both tracks

Fairness notes
  • Source-vertex selection is, as in the bfs track, the largest single source of incomparability: ADDS uses one unspecified vertex per graph, Srinivasan et al. use a single FIXED vertex 0 for every graph (with a disclosed but limited 2-vertex sensitivity check), and GraphIt uses 10 hand-picked vertices explicitly filtered to avoid hangs — none of the four papers uses a random-sampling convention. The spec fixes this at 64 fixed-seed random roots from the giant component, directly reusing the bfs spec's convention per this track's explicit design brief, which is a real strengthening relative to every surveyed paper's own practice: a hand-picked or single fixed source cannot be assumed representative of a graph's full behavior, and "filtered to avoid hangs" (GraphIt's own stated criterion) risks silently excluding exactly the hard cases a benchmark should surface.
  • Delta-stepping parameter disclosure is this track's sharpest and most consequential divergence. ADDS's own ablation study proves the point quantitatively: disabling its dynamic-delta mechanism alone cuts its reported speedup over Near-Far from 3.5x to 2.4x on an RTX 3090 — a third of the paper's headline number comes from delta selection, not from the underlying data structure. GraphIt goes further in a different direction: it hand-tunes delta PER GRAPH AND PER COMPETING FRAMEWORK (its own artifact's README lists distinct tuned deltas for GraphIt, GAPBS, Julienne, and Galois on the same graph), which is more even-handed than tuning only the authors' own method, but still opens a tuning-BUDGET asymmetry risk: if the authors spent materially more tuning effort on their own tool's delta than on the baselines', the reported speedup partially reflects tuning effort, not algorithmic quality, and the paper's text does not disclose the tuning search budget/method used for either its own tool or the baselines. The spec resolves this by (a) requiring every submission to disclose its delta-selection METHOD from a closed set of options, (b) explicitly disallowing undisclosed hand-tuning without a stated search budget, and (c) adding a dedicated sssp-delta-sensitivity variant that reports the full delta-vs-performance curve rather than a single cherry-pickable number, so a reader can independently judge how sensitive a reported speedup is to the delta choice.
  • Edge-weight distribution disclosure ranges from GraphIt's exemplary three-named-regimes-tied-to-every-table-entry practice down to Srinivasan et al.'s undisclosed weight-generation method for its SSSP experiments. Since delta-stepping's optimal granularity and even which algorithmic family wins (e.g. wBFS-as-delta=1-special-case only makes sense for small-integer weights) depend directly on the weight distribution, an SSSP benchmark that doesn't fix and disclose this axis risks comparing numbers that are not measuring the same problem at all. The spec adopts GraphIt's three-regime practice (real weights where physically meaningful, [1,1000] uniform-random, [1,log|V|] uniform-random) as a REQUIRED field for every variant.
  • Metric choice diverges sharply from the bfs track: none of this track's four papers use GTEPS. Srinivasan et al. give the most explicit reasoning against it ("TEPS is not a suitable metric for dynamic networks since our goal is to process as few edges as possible"), which is specific to the dynamic-update problem shape but points at a more general concern — a throughput metric implicitly rewards doing MORE work per second, which is exactly backwards for delta-stepping's own accuracy/parallelism tradeoff (a coarser delta processes more edges, often with more redundant relaxations, to finish sooner; a finer delta processes fewer, more "necessary" edges but with less parallelism — ADDS's Figure 10 shows both regimes exist across its 226 graphs). The spec adopts wall-clock time as the primary metric for all four variants (never GTEPS as primary), with work-efficiency (ADDS's own vertex-processing-count convention) as a mandatory secondary metric specifically to keep the accuracy/parallelism tradeoff visible rather than collapsed into a single throughput number.
  • efg's inclusion in this track's input list despite implementing only BFS is the same "topic-adjacency over-inclusion" pattern this project's CLAUDE.md already warns about for artifact-search false positives, here occurring one level up at paper-classification time instead of artifact-matching time. The spec does not define a variant for it and treats its absence from every variant's evidence as the correct outcome, not a gap to be filled.
Open questions
  • No standardized weighted-SSSP throughput metric (an edges-relaxed-per- second-style GTEPS analogue) could be identified across this 4-paper sample; the spec's `edge_relaxations_per_second` secondary metric is a first-principles construction, not one inherited from the literature, and should be cross-checked against a broader SSSP benchmark corpus (e.g. the DIMACS shortest-path challenge's own conventions, which none of the 4 surveyed papers reference) before being treated as settled.
  • The TPDS22 journal version of Khanda et al. (the paper actually named in this track's input list) claims a GPU implementation in its abstract that this survey's CPU-only precursor-paper proxy does not cover; whether the sssp-dynamic-update variant's protocol needs GPU-specific adjustments (e.g. a different synchronization_granularity_disclosure convention, since "asynchrony level" as defined for CPU threads may not map cleanly to GPU warps/blocks) is unresolved pending access to the actual TPDS22 fulltext.
  • Whether Srinivasan et al.'s "asynchrony level" parameter and this spec's delta-selection-method disclosure should eventually be unified into one cross-cutting "coarsening/synchronization-granularity disclosure" field spanning both static and dynamic-update SSSP variants was considered but left as two separate fields, since the two parameter families currently apply to disjoint variants (sssp-delta-sensitivity vs. sssp-dynamic-update) and no paper in this 4-paper sample combines them in a single implementation to test whether a unified field would even be meaningful.
  • efg's Elias-Fano compressed-graph representation is evaluated for BFS only in every reachable source; whether it composes with a Δ-stepping SSSP kernel (weight storage under compression, decompression cost inside the relaxation inner loop) is an open algorithmic question this survey could not resolve and that would need to be answered before any future "sssp-on-compressed-graphs" variant could be specified.
graph-partitioning2 papers4 variants

Divide a graph's vertices into k balanced blocks while minimizing the cut (sum of edge weights crossing block boundaries), measured as wall-clock partitioning time with cut quality and achieved imbalance reported jointly — a faster partitioner that produces a worse cut, or that silently violates its own balance constraint, is not a win. The track's two papers occupy almost disjoint (k, graph-scale, hardware) regimes, so the spec keeps them as separate scale-regime variants rather than forcing a single combined leaderboard, while anchoring both to the one convention they already agree on (imbalance epsilon = 3%).

P[V] = Partition(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, weighted or unweighted, undirected), k, epsilon); output is a vertex-to-block-ID assignment P: V -> {0, ..., k-1} such that (a) BALANCE: for every block p_i, weight(p_i) <= (1+epsilon) * sum(weight(V)) / k, and (b) the CUT = sum of weights of edges (u,v) with P(u) != P(v) is minimized subject to (a). k and epsilon are caller-supplied parameters (unlike the community-detection track, where the number of communities is discovered rather than specified).

gp-kernel-small-ksteady-state partitioning kernel time at G-kway's operating point — small power-of-2 k, graphs in the low-tens-of-millions-of-edges range — runnable on either a single GPU or a single CPU node, so GPU- and CPU-based partitioners can be compared on shared public instances instead of on disjoint hardware as the two surveyed papers currently are
inputs
suitepublic DIMACS10 Graph Partitioning Challenge instances, the only graphs in this track confirmed both public and used by a surveyed paper (G-kway); excludes G-kway's 6 industrial circuit-timing graphs, which are not confirmed publicly downloadable or regeneratable (see notes_on_fairness)

primarymedian partitioning time (ms), across 10 reps
secondarymedian cut size (both raw edge-weight-sum count and as % of total edge weight); achieved max block imbalance (%, must be <= epsilon, see correctness)
correctnessBALANCE is a hard constraint, not a tolerance: any run whose maximum block weight exceeds (1+epsilon)*sum(weight(V))/k is INVALID and its cut/time numbers do not count, matching both papers' own definition of the partitioning problem (this is a stricter, closed-form analogue of the community-detection track's modularity quality gate, since imbalance has an unambiguous pass/fail threshold where modularity does not). CUT QUALITY is gated via performance profile, not a fixed reference implementation (TeraPart's own convention, adopted here rather than inventing a new one): for each (graph, k), compute best_cut = min cut achieved by any implementation under test on that instance; a submission's median cut must satisfy cut_impl <= 1.10 * best_cut (10% of the best-known cut on that instance) to count as a valid quality-competitive result; submissions exceeding this must still report their number but are flagged as quality-noncompetitive rather than silently ranked on speed alone.
gp-kernel-large-ksteady-state partitioning kernel time at TeraPart's operating point — wide/irregular k up to tens of thousands, graphs from hundreds of millions to trillions of edges — CPU/distributed-only, since no GPU partitioner in this track (or known to the surveyed literature) currently operates at this scale
inputs
suiteSuiteSparse Matrix Collection + Network Repository + LAW (Laboratory for Web Algorithmics) web graphs + KaGen-generated synthetic graphs, matching TeraPart's own two-tier Benchmark Set A/B split
selectionmedium tier: SuiteSparse/NetworkRepo graphs with 5e6 <= |E| <= 2e9 (TeraPart's own Benchmark-Set-A range; exact 72-graph list is TeraPart's own and not fully enumerable from the fulltext excerpt obtained — submitters MUST disclose their exact medium-tier list, following this benchmark suite's general pattern for submitter-disclosed subsets, e.g. benchspecs/bfs/spec.yaml's bfs-reordering-cost RCM-matrix selection); huge tier: the 5 named LAW web graphs below, fixed and non-substitutable since they are individually named in TeraPart's own paper
recommended_subsetgsh-2015 (LAW webgraph, 25.7B edges) — matches TeraPart's own instance exactly, clueweb12 (LAW webgraph, 37.4B edges) — matches TeraPart's own instance exactly, uk-2014 (LAW webgraph, 42.5B edges) — matches TeraPart's own instance exactly, eu-2015 (LAW webgraph, 80.5B edges) — matches TeraPart's own instance exactly, hyperlink (LAW webgraph, 112.2B edges) — matches TeraPart's own instance exactly, KaGen rgg2D (random geometric, 8.59B v / 1.10T e, generated with avg degree 256) — matches TeraPart's own generator+parameters exactly, KaGen rhg (random hyperbolic, 8.59B v / 1.01T e, generated with avg degree 256, power-law exponent 3.0) — matches TeraPart's own generator+parameters exactly
dense_operandN/A

protocol
formatcompressed graph representation with on-the-fly decoding (TeraPart's own approach to keeping huge-tier graphs in memory) OR plain CSR for the medium tier; graph load/decompression excluded from per-run partitioning time, reported separately
warmup1 discarded full partitioning run per (graph, k) pair actually completed (huge-tier + k=30000 combinations may be infeasible to warm up separately from the timed run given multi-minute runtimes — disclose if warmup is skipped for cost reasons)
reps5 independent runs with different seeds for single-machine/shared-memory results, 3 for distributed-memory results — matches TeraPart's own repetition counts exactly
statisticarithmetic mean of running time, peak memory, and cut size across seeds (TeraPart's own convention, kept as-is here rather than substituting median, since averaging across only 3-5 seeded reps at this scale is TeraPart's own deliberate choice and changing it would break direct comparability with the one paper that actually operates in this regime); harmonic mean for relative speedups; geometric mean for any aggregate cross-instance metric
timerwall-clock (host-side), single-node and distributed
timing_scopecoarsening (parallel label-propagation clustering + graph contraction) + initial partitioning + uncoarsening/local-search refinement; graph load/decompression excluded and reported separately
preprocessing_reportedseparately: graph load/decompression time; report the compression ratio achieved if a compressed representation is used (TeraPart's own practice, since decompression-on-the-fly speed at scale is itself a claim worth verifying independently of partitioning time)
platform_disclosureREQUIRED: node count, cores/node, interconnect (if distributed); single-machine core count and RAM (if shared-memory)

secondarymean cut size (% of total edge weight); mean peak memory (GiB); performance-profile curve (fraction of instances with cut_impl <= tau * best_cut, swept over tau) across the full recommended_subset, TeraPart's own preferred cross-instance summary
correctnesssame hard balance constraint as gp-kernel-small-k; same performance-profile cut-quality gate (cut_impl <= 1.10 * best_cut per instance), computed within this variant's own recommended_subset separately from gp-kernel-small-k's (the two regimes are not pooled into one performance-profile curve, since no instance or k value is shared between them)
gp-memory-scalingdedicated memory-efficiency measurement at the largest (graph, k) each submitted implementation can complete within a fixed memory budget — operationalizes TeraPart's own headline contribution (16x peak-memory reduction at comparable quality/speed) as a first-class, reportable variant instead of a claim buried in a single "under 8 minutes, 900 GiB" narrative, and gives any future memory-efficiency- focused submission (in the spirit of HSSInfo in the community-detection track, though no such paper currently exists in THIS track) a variant that measures what it actually contributes
inputs
suitegp-kernel-large-k's huge tier (5 LAW web graphs + 2 KaGen synthetic generators), since memory pressure is the entire point of testing at this scale; gp-kernel-small-k's suite may optionally be included for completeness but is not expected to be memory-bound

imbalance_epsilon0.03 (3%)

reps3 (matching TeraPart's own distributed-experiment repetition count, since this variant targets the huge tier); report all 3 peak-memory numbers, not only the mean, since a single OOM-adjacent run is itself informative

timing_scopeN/A

metric

secondarycross-reference to gp-kernel-large-k's time and cut-size numbers on the same (graph, k) — a memory-efficient implementation that is dramatically slower or produces a much worse cut is not an unqualified win, same fairness principle as elsewhere in this benchmark suite
correctnesssame hard balance constraint and cut-quality gate as gp-kernel-large-k, computed only over runs that completed without OOM; runs that OOM at a given (graph, k) are reported as a data point (infeasible at this memory budget) rather than silently excluded
gp-e2e-preprocessingend-to-end throughput including one-shot graph loading and format/CSR construction; like community detection (and unlike BFS), graph partitioning is inherently single-shot per (graph, k) input — there is no repeated-query amortization argument — so this variant reports ONE full run's total time rather than an amortized-over-k number

Fairness notes
  • TeraPart and G-kway share almost no operating point: TeraPart never tests k<=32, G-kway never tests k>32 or graphs within two orders of magnitude of TeraPart's smallest "huge"-tier instance. Rather than force a single combined ranking that would compare a single-GPU circuit-timing-graph partitioner against a 128-node trillion-edge partitioner (a comparison neither paper's own authors would consider meaningful), the spec keeps gp-kernel-small-k and gp-kernel-large-k as separate regimes, each internally coherent, and unifies them only through the ONE shared convention both papers already use identically: epsilon=3% imbalance.
  • G-kway's own repeatability disclosure ("average of ten runs," no seed, no variance anywhere in the paper) is the weakest of the two papers in this track — contrast TeraPart's explicit 5-or-3 seeded reps with three different, deliberately-chosen mean conventions. gp-kernel-small-k's mandatory per-rep seed disclosure and min/max/stddev reporting directly fixes this gap for future submissions rather than perpetuating G-kway's own thinner protocol as the small-k default.
  • Roughly half of G-kway's own benchmark suite (the 6 industrial circuit-timing graphs) is not confirmed publicly downloadable or regeneratable — no dataset release or generation script accompanies the paper or artifact, only citations to the internal tools (Taskflow, OpenTimer) that produced them. gp-kernel-small-k therefore uses ONLY G-kway's other 4 graphs (all standard public DIMACS10 instances) plus 2 additional public DIMACS10 controls, rather than including graphs a third party cannot actually obtain to reproduce a submission.
  • GKSG, one of G-kway's two baselines, is not open-source; G-kway's own reported GKSG numbers are from the DAC'24 authors' own reimplementation of GKSG's published algorithm, not a run of GKSG's original authors' code. Any submission claiming to reproduce or beat "GKSG's" numbers specifically (as opposed to G-kway's own numbers) should disclose whether it is comparing against the original GKSG paper's claims, G-kway's reimplementation, or its own reimplementation — three potentially different baselines sharing one name.
  • TeraPart's performance-profile convention (fraction of instances with cut within tau of the best across ALL tested algorithms on that instance) is adopted as this spec's cut-quality gate mechanism in preference to inventing a fixed-reference-implementation gate (the approach used in the community-detection track's spec, where a single trusted reference implementation's modularity is the anchor). Graph partitioning's literature already has this convention as its established fairness mechanism precisely because "best known cut for this NP-hard instance" is itself a moving target across the field, so re-deriving a fixed reference would be less faithful to the track's own practice than adopting what TeraPart already does.
Open questions
  • TeraPart's exact 72-graph medium-tier ("Benchmark Set A") list was not enumerable from the arXiv HTML extraction obtained (the fulltext described the tier's composition, size range, and sources but not every graph name) — gp-kernel-large-k's medium-tier selection criterion is stated but the exact list is left to the submitter to disclose, following this benchmark suite's general pattern (see benchspecs/bfs/spec.yaml's bfs-reordering-cost variant for precedent). Revisit if the full PDF (rather than the HTML conversion) becomes available and enumerates the list.
  • Whether TeraPart's 72-graph medium tier or G-kway's 4 DIMACS10 graphs overlap BY NAME was not confirmed (TeraPart's fulltext extraction tagged its sources generically as "(D)" for DIMACS among others, without a full name list) — if a specific overlap (e.g. both papers happening to use the same DIMACS10 europe_osm or road_usa instance) is later confirmed, that instance should be promoted to a required control point tested identically by both scale-regime variants for a direct, paper-to-paper apples-to-apples data point.
  • No GPU partitioner in this track (or cited by either surveyed paper) currently operates at TeraPart's scale (>1B edges, k>=1000), and no CPU/distributed partitioner in this track was evaluated by its authors at G-kway's fine-grained small-k circuit-graph scale. Whether this reflects a genuine algorithmic/hardware limit (e.g. GPU memory ceiling for graphs with 100B+ edges) or simply that neither paper's authors tried the other regime could not be determined from the sources surveyed, and would need a third data point (a paper or submission that actually crosses regimes) to resolve.
  • This track has only 2 papers, both agreeing on epsilon=3% and both using a Metis-family baseline, but disagreeing on nearly everything else (k range, hardware, dataset scale, quality-reporting units, repeatability rigor). Whether a 3rd paper would land closer to TeraPart's regime, G-kway's regime, or a genuinely new middle ground (e.g. multi-GPU at TeraPart-adjacent scale) is unknown; the variant structure above is designed to be extensible to a third regime without forcing it into either existing variant, but this has not been exercised against a real 3rd paper.
mst2 papers3 variants

Computing a minimum spanning tree/forest (MST/MSF) of a weighted undirected graph, measured as steady-state throughput on a fixed real graph suite (aligned with benchspecs/bfs/spec.yaml's suite where overlap exists) at the single-node/single-GPU scale, as a distributed weak/strong-scaling curve at cluster scale, and — because this track's two papers between them demonstrate that weight distribution and tie-density materially change which algorithm family wins — as a dedicated weight-distribution sweep. Total-weight verification is a mandatory correctness gate in every variant, not an opt-in flag.

MST(or MSF)[|V|-1 edges] = argmin_{T subseteq E, T spans G} sum(w(e) for e in T); G = (V, E, w) undirected, w: E -> weight domain (see weight_distribution below); MSF generalizes to graphs with multiple connected components (one tree per component).

mst-kernel-real-graphssteady-state kernel throughput on named real-world graphs at the single-node/single-GPU scale (0.4M-180M edges), format given/loaded once, preprocessing excluded from the per-call number but measured and reported separately — the common-denominator claim ECL-MST's own evaluation makes directly, extended with a handful of graphs from benchspecs/bfs/spec.yaml's suite that neither MST paper used, so the two tracks' graph-suite overlap is explicit rather than coincidental.
inputs
suiteunion of DIMACS, Galois, SNAP, and SuiteSparse Matrix Collection (SSMC) graphs, same four sources ECL-MST itself draws from
selectionreal+synthetic graphs already used by >=1 of this track's papers, PLUS 3 graphs already standardized in benchspecs/bfs/spec.yaml's real-graph suite that neither MST paper covers (added for explicit cross-track alignment per this track's brief), with an explicit criterion: edges in [1e5, 2e8] (fits comfortably on one GPU or one multi-core node, matching ECL-MST's own ~2-billion-edge GPU-memory ceiling with headroom).
recommended_subset2d-2e20.sym, amazon0601, as-skitter, citationCiteseer, cit-Patents, coPapersDBLP, delaunay_n24, europe_osm, in-2004, internet, kron_g500-logn21, r4-2e23.sym, rmat16.sym, rmat22.sym, soc-LiveJournal1, USA-road-d.NY, USA-road-d.USA, com-LiveJournal, com-Orkut, wiki-topcats
graph_typeundirected (self-loops and multi-edges removed; missing back-edges added if the source is directed, matching ECL-MST's own graph-cleaning discipline); connected-component count disclosed per graph (needed for the MSF-vs-MST-only geomean split below, since 3 of ECL-MST's own comparison codes — Jucele, Gunrock — cannot produce a general MSF).
weight_distributionuniform-random integer in [1, 254], fixed seed=42, assigned once per graph and reused across all repetitions — see mst-weight-distribution-sensitivity for the dedicated sweep of this choice; graphs with native edge weights use them as-is and this field is 'native' instead.
protocol
formatCSR/CSR-equivalent binary format (matching both papers' actual artifacts — KaMSTa's binary 9-byte-edge-record format and ECL-MST's ECLgraph binary CSR), given/converted once; conversion from a raw edge list (if starting there) timed once and reported separately, never inside the per-call number.
warmup1 run (discarded)
reps9
statisticmedian (report min/max/stdev alongside) — matches ECL-MST's own protocol exactly, adopted over KaMSTa's weaker mean-of->=3 practice per notes_on_fairness
timerdevice-side events (CUDA/HIP) for GPU implementations, std::chrono/omp_get_wtime for CPU, one timestamp pair per repetition
timing_scopeMST computation kernel only. Graph-file-read time excluded (both papers exclude this). For GPU implementations: host-device transfer of the input graph and the output MST is EXCLUDED from the primary number but a SEPARATE "including memcpy" number is ALSO required (matching ECL-MST's own dual-reporting practice exactly — this is the one place this spec adopts a surveyed paper's protocol unchanged rather than tightening it, since it already satisfies this repo's fairness principles).
preprocessing_reportedformat conversion (raw edge list -> native CSR/binary) timed once, reported separately, same discipline as benchspecs/spmv/spec.yaml
algorithm_family_disclosureREQUIRED: report which classic-algorithm lineage the technique under test derives from — Boruvka, Kruskal, Prim, or "converged" (ECL-MST's own finding that a fully-parallelized Kruskal and a parallelized Boruvka become the same code) — as a descriptive label, NOT a filter criterion (a technique is not excluded for being Prim-based; see notes_on_fairness on why Prim-family codes are structurally disadvantaged by a pure-throughput metric and that disadvantage should be visible, not hidden by exclusion).
precisioninteger edge weights (see weight_distribution); MST total weight accumulated in a width sufficient to avoid overflow for the largest graph in the suite (>=64-bit)
metric
primaryMega-edges/s = |E| / computation_time_seconds / 1e6, matching ECL-MST's own throughput definition exactly (so this spec's numbers are directly comparable to Table/Figure values already published for ECL-MST's own baselines)
secondarycomputation_time_seconds (median, min/max); TWO geomeans over the recommended_subset — "MSF GeoMean" (all graphs, MSF-capable implementations only) and "MST GeoMean" (single-connected-component graphs only, so MST-only-capable baselines can be included fairly) — matching ECL-MST's own split exactly, since it is a genuine fairness mechanism worth preserving rather than reinventing.
correctnessMANDATORY (not opt-in, unlike KaMSTa's own `do_check` CLI default) total-MST-weight verification against an independently computed reference (sequential Kruskal or Boruvka on the same input, exact-integer-arithmetic sum) — exact equality required (integer weights admit no tolerance ambiguity). Per-edge-set identity matching (ECL-MST's own stricter `verify()` check) is OPTIONAL and, if reported, any mismatch must be investigated for whether it is a genuine bug or a valid alternate MST under a tied-weight instance before being counted as a failure — total-weight equality alone is the pass/fail gate, per notes_on_fairness.
mst-distributed-scalingweak- and strong-scaling throughput at distributed-cluster scale (up to tens of thousands of cores) on parameterized synthetic generator families, matching KaMSTa's own evaluation shape exactly since it is the only paper in this track's evaluation at this scale — kept as a fully separate variant from mst-kernel-real-graphs rather than trying to force one Mega-edges/s number to span both a single GPU and a 65,536-core cluster.
inputs
suiteKaGen-generated synthetic graph families: 2D-GRID, 2D-RGG, 3D-RGG, RHG (random hyperbolic), GNM, RMAT — same six families KaMSTa's own repo evaluation_suites config uses
selectionweak scaling: log_n=17, log_m=20 PER CORE as the base unit (2^17 vertices, 2^21 edges per core, scaled up with core count) — KaMSTa's own repo-confirmed default; strong scaling: 6 named real-world instances at fixed total size — friendster, twitter, uk-2007, it-2004, wdc-14, US-road (24M-1.7B vertices, 57M-123B edges), same instances KaMSTa's own paper reports.
recommended_subset
weak_scaling_familiesRMAT, GNM, RGG_2D, RGG_3D, RHG, GRID_2D
strong_scaling_graphsfriendster, twitter, uk-2007, it-2004, wdc-14, US-road
graph_typeundirected; generated via KaGen with a fixed RNG seed per (family, core-count) cell for reproducibility (not disclosed as fixed in the paper itself — this spec's own addition, since an unseeded generator makes weak-scaling curves non-reproducible run-to-run)
weight_distributionuniform-random integer in [1, 254], matching KaMSTa's own confirmed default (max_edge_weight=254 in its repo config) exactly — this is the ONE variant in this track that intentionally does NOT sweep weight distribution, since isolating the scaling axis requires holding weight distribution fixed; see mst-weight-distribution-sensitivity for the dedicated sweep
protocol
formatgraph generated directly in-memory by KaGen (no file I/O in the timed region); local kernelization/contraction preprocessing IS considered part of the algorithm under test for hybridBoruvka/filter_hybridBoruvka specifically (per KaMSTa's own framing) but must still be reported as its own line item, not silently merged into total time
core_count_sweepREQUIRED sweep, reported as a curve: 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 16384, and (where available) up to 65536 cores — matching KaMSTa's own repo-confirmed default sweep plus the paper's stated maximum
threads_per_process_sweep1 and 8 threads per MPI process, matching KaMSTa's own repo config default; report which combination each core-count point uses
warmup1 run (discarded)
reps4, matching KaMSTa's own repo-confirmed default (evaluation/graphs.yaml: iterations: 4) — weaker than this spec's 9-rep default elsewhere, but adopted as-is here since a single strong-scaling point on the largest real graph (123B edges, up to 65536 cores) is itself an expensive, multi-machine-hour measurement where 9 reps is not a proportionate ask
statisticmedian (report min/max/stdev alongside) — strengthens KaMSTa's own mean-only reporting per notes_on_fairness, at no extra measurement cost since the reps are already being collected
timerwall-clock (MPI_Wtime or equivalent) around the MST computation call on rank 0, synchronized via a barrier immediately before the timed region starts
timing_scopeMST computation only; graph GENERATION time is excluded and reported separately (KaMSTa's own confirmed practice); the paper's own specific disclosed exclusion — "encoding time not included, decoding [of the compressed edge list] counted twice" — is adopted verbatim as this variant's edge-list-compression timing convention, since it is unusually precise and no reason was found to deviate from it.
preprocessing_reportedgraph generation time and any compressed-edge-list decoding time, both reported separately, once per (family/graph, core-count) cell
algorithm_family_disclosurehybridBoruvka or filter_hybridBoruvka (KaMSTa's own two named options), reported per data point since the paper itself treats this as a first-class comparison axis, not a fixed choice
precisioninteger edge weights in [1,254] (see weight_distribution above); MST total weight accumulated with a distributed all-reduce sum in >=64-bit
metric
primaryedges/second = |E| / computation_time_seconds, matching KaMSTa's own throughput unit
secondarycomputation_time_seconds (median, min/max); speedup vs. the two named prior distributed baselines (sparseMatrix [Baer et al.], MND-MST [Panja et al.]) where available; weak-scaling efficiency = time_at_1_core_equivalent / time_at_N_cores (ideal=1.0)
correctnessMANDATORY (default-enabled, unlike KaMSTa's own opt-in `--checks` CLI flag) distributed total-MST-weight verification: local per-rank partial sums combined via `MPI_Allreduce`-equivalent, compared exactly against a reference MST weight gathered from a sequential computation on the same input (matching KaMSTa's own `check()`/`gather_mst` implementation, just made mandatory rather than opt-in).
mst-weight-distribution-sensitivitythe dedicated, explicit weight-distribution sweep this track's brief asks for as a first-class axis — motivated directly by ECL-MST's own 99-random-seed study (Section 5.4), which shows up to ~4x throughput variance on high-average-degree scale-free graphs depending purely on which 20 sample edges happen to be picked for its filter threshold, i.e. this track's own literature already demonstrates weight/threshold randomness is NOT a negligible axis, yet neither paper reports it as a swept, first-class benchmark dimension in its own headline numbers.
inputs
suitesame as mst-kernel-real-graphs, restricted to the subset with average degree >= 4 (coPapersDBLP, as-skitter, cit-Patents, kron_g500-logn21, soc-LiveJournal1, rmat22.sym) since this is exactly the regime ECL-MST's own study identifies as sensitive, plus 2 low-average-degree controls (USA-road-d.USA, delaunay_n24) to confirm the expected near-zero sensitivity there
selectionsame criterion as mst-kernel-real-graphs, filtered to avg_degree buckets as above
recommended_subsetcoPapersDBLP, as-skitter, cit-Patents, kron_g500-logn21, soc-LiveJournal1, rmat22.sym, USA-road-d.USA, delaunay_n24
weight_distribution_sweepREQUIRED sweep, reported as a curve/box-plot per graph (matching ECL-MST's own box-and-whisker presentation in Figure 6, which is adopted as the required reporting FORMAT for this variant, not just a suggestion): (a) uniform-random integer in [1,254] with 20 different fixed seeds (matching ECL-MST's own seed-count order of magnitude, reduced from its 99 for proportionate cost; report median/min/max/quartiles across the 20 seeds), (b) uniform-random integer in [1, 254*100] (a 100x wider range, sharply reducing tie probability), (c) uniform-random integer in [1, 16] (a DELIBERATELY narrow, high-tie-density range — stress-tests the "total weight is the invariant, not edge-set identity" fairness point directly, since high tie density is exactly where MST non-uniqueness becomes common), (d) native/real edge weights where the graph provides them (n/a for all recommended_subset entries here, since none carry native weights — noted as a gap: this track's suite has no real-weighted MST benchmark instance, see open_questions).
protocol
formatsame as mst-kernel-real-graphs
warmup1 run per (graph, weight_setting, seed) cell, discarded
reps9 per (graph, weight_setting, seed) cell, matching mst-kernel-real-graphs's statistical rigor
statisticmedian per cell; then median/min/max/quartiles ACROSS the 20 seeds for setting (a), matching ECL-MST's Figure 6 box-plot convention
timersame as mst-kernel-real-graphs
timing_scopesame as mst-kernel-real-graphs (kernel only, memcpy reported separately if GPU)
preprocessing_reportedsame as mst-kernel-real-graphs, PLUS: if the technique samples edges to pick a filtering/pivot threshold (ECL-MST's own mechanism), report how many edges are sampled and by what method, since this is the specific mechanism whose sensitivity this variant is designed to expose
precisioninteger weights per the weight_distribution_sweep settings above
metric
primaryMega-edges/s per (graph, weight_setting) cell; for setting (a), report as a distribution (median/min/max/quartiles across 20 seeds) not a single number
secondarycoefficient of variation (stdev/mean) of throughput across the 20 seeds in setting (a), a single-number sensitivity summary; tie-count (number of MST edges whose weight equals another edge incident to the same cut) per weight_setting, since this is the mechanistic driver of any observed sensitivity
correctnessMANDATORY total-weight verification (same as mst-kernel-real-graphs), PLUS an explicit tie-awareness requirement: under weight_setting (c) (narrow [1,16] range, high tie density), an edge-set-identity diagnostic check (if run at all) MUST be evaluated against "produces SOME valid MST of the correct total weight," not against one specific reference implementation's tie-breaking order — this is the concrete fix for the fairness concern raised by ECL-MST's own stricter verify() function (which checks per-edge agreement against one specific serial Kruskal tie-breaking order and could therefore flag a legitimately different, equally-valid MST as wrong under exactly this high-tie-density setting).
Fairness notes
  • KaMSTa's own CLI ships its total-weight correctness check (`--checks`) OFF by default, and the paper's own reported numbers do not state whether `--checks` was enabled for the headline performance runs. This spec makes the check mandatory (default-on, not opt-in) for every variant, so no reported throughput number can exist without having passed the correctness gate on that same run.
  • ECL-MST's own `verify()` function checks per-edge-set identity against ONE specific serial reference implementation's tie-breaking order, which is stricter than necessary — MST is not unique when edge weights tie, so a valid MST with a different (but equally correct) tie-break could be flagged as wrong by an edge-set-identity check even though its total weight is correct. This spec's mandatory gate is KaMSTa's weaker-but-actually-correct total-weight check; mst-weight-distribution-sensitivity's high-tie-density setting (c) makes this distinction concretely testable rather than theoretical.
  • KaMSTa reports MEAN of >=3 runs and explicitly does not report min/max/stdev; ECL-MST reports MEDIAN of 9 runs with explicit variance figures. This spec adopts ECL-MST's stronger convention (median + min/max/stdev) uniformly across all three variants, at reduced rep-count (4 instead of 9) only in mst-distributed-scaling where a single measurement point can already be extremely expensive at full cluster scale.
  • Neither paper sweeps weight DISTRIBUTION itself as a first-class reported experimental axis, even though ECL-MST's own random-seed study (a narrower, adjacent question — sensitivity to WHICH edges get sampled for a threshold, at a FIXED weight distribution) already demonstrates up to ~4x variance exists in this general space. This track's brief explicitly asks for weight distribution as a key axis; mst-weight-distribution-sensitivity is this spec's direct answer to that gap, generalizing ECL-MST's seed-sensitivity study into an explicit range/tie-density sweep neither paper ran.
  • A pure throughput-vs-algorithm-family framing structurally disadvantages Prim-family codes, which both papers' own related-work discussions describe as inherently serial (Prim relies on the cut property and builds one tree incrementally from a single growing frontier, unlike Boruvka's fully-data-parallel per-component step). This spec does not exclude Prim-family codes, but requires algorithm_family_disclosure precisely so a Prim-based result's lower throughput is legible as an expected structural property of the algorithm family, not silently penalized as if it were an implementation deficiency.
  • ECL-MST's MSF-vs-MST-only geomean split (excluding Jucele/Gunrock's single-connected-component limitation from unfairly penalizing them on multi-component graphs, or unfairly crediting MSF-capable codes with "harder" inputs those two can't even attempt) is preserved verbatim in mst-kernel-real-graphs rather than re-derived, since it is already a well-designed fairness mechanism in the source paper.
Open questions
  • Neither KaMSTa nor ECL-MST evaluates a graph with NATIVE (real, non-synthetically-inserted) edge weights — every graph in both papers' suites is either originally unweighted (weights inserted afterward) or weighted only in the sense of a synthetic integer range. This track's suite therefore has no genuinely real-weighted MST benchmark instance (e.g. a road network with real distances, or a network with real cost/capacity edge attributes); adding one is a candidate future extension not resolved here.
  • KaMSTa's exact core-vs-hardware-thread accounting for its "up to 65,536 cores" claim, and whether the paper's own reported numbers at that scale use 1 or 8 threads per MPI process, could not be disambiguated from the fetched text alone (see survey.md).
  • Whether ECL-MST's paper-reported numbers (Tables 2-5) used the exact same weight-generation scheme as the repo's demo `main.cu` hash formula, or a different (perhaps genuinely random) scheme, is unresolved; mst-weight-distribution-sensitivity's setting (a) uses a standard PRNG rather than replicating the repo's specific hash, on the assumption the hash was a demo convenience rather than the paper's actual methodology, but this assumption is not independently confirmed.
  • Whether KaMSTa's 6 real-world strong-scaling graphs (friendster, twitter, uk-2007, it-2004, wdc-14, US-road) use the same [1,254] synthetic weight range as its synthetic generators, or carry different (possibly native) weights, could not be confirmed.
astar-search1 papers2 variants

Single-pair shortest-path search (start -> goal) on an 8-connected 2D occupancy grid via GPU-parallel (bidirectional or unidirectional) bucketed A*, measured as search-phase wall time and nodes expanded, with path optimality (not approximation) as the correctness gate.

path = A*(grid[H,W] occupancy (0=passable,1=obstacle), start, goal, heuristic=octile/Chebyshev-consistent); 8-connected movement, integer- scaled edge costs (straight vs. diagonal); output is the minimum-cost path (or "unreachable") plus the parent chain from start to goal.
