Fairness notes
  • A* with an admissible, consistent heuristic (octile distance on a uniform-cost 8-connected grid) is exact, not heuristic-approximate — unlike most other tracks in this benchmark set, the correctness gate here is a strict equality check against an independent reference shortest-path cost, not a tolerance or approximation ratio. Any GPU implementation that trades optimality for speed (e.g. weighted A*, epsilon-admissible relaxations) must be reported as a DISTINCT variant, not folded into these numbers, since it changes the correctness contract.
  • The repo's `--repeats` flag on `demo.sh` defaults to 1, which is too few to report a meaningful median/min/max; both variants above fix a minimum repetition count (10 for named maps, 5 per grid cell for the procedural sweep) explicitly rather than inheriting the tool's single-run default.
  • "Compressed-grid" construction (`data/generated/*.bin`) is a real, separate cost the repo already treats as a distinct artifact from the search call — this spec keeps that separation explicit via preprocessing_reported rather than letting it silently inflate or deflate the reported search time depending on whether an implementation reuses a pre-built compressed grid.
Open questions
  • The paper's own MovingAI map selection (which named maps/categories, how many start-goal pairs per map) could not be confirmed — no arXiv preprint exists for this ICS 2026 paper and the ACM DL page was not fetched as fulltext. The recommended_subset above is a reasonable standard-corpus stand-in, not a reproduction of the paper's exact table.
  • The identity of the "prior GPU baseline" the paper reports 11.91x geomean / 43.33x peak speedup against (per a WebSearch summary of the abstract page, not independently verified) is unconfirmed — likely a massively-parallel-heap-based GPU A* (e.g. Zhou & Zeng, AAAI 2020 style), but this should be verified against the paper's related-work section before being named as a required baseline.
  • Exact largest grid size used in the paper's own scaling experiments (beyond demo.sh's default 1024) was not confirmed.
betweenness1 papers2 variants

Single-source dependency-accumulation betweenness centrality on hypergraphs (Brandes-style forward BFS + backward dependency phases, generalized from vertices/edges to vertices/hyperedges), measured as wall-clock running time and parallel self-speedup on a shared-memory multicore machine; hypergraph load time excluded from per-round timing.

dep[V] = HyperBC(H=(V,E) hypergraph, source in V); H is unweighted, undirected (symmetric) incidence structure between vertices and hyperedges; output is a per-vertex dependency/centrality score (double) accumulated via one forward traversal (shortest-hyperpath counting) and one backward traversal (dependency propagation) from a single source vertex — same scope as classical single-source Brandes BC, not an all-pairs/exact aggregate BC.

Fairness notes
  • The artifact the automated pipeline attached to this paper (github.com/DevSheth/prallel-hypergraph-algorithms) is a third-party CUDA course-project reimplementation of 4 of the paper's 8 algorithms and specifically does NOT include betweenness centrality or MIS. Had this spec been written against that repo, the "betweenness" track would have had literally no matching code to benchmark. This spec is instead grounded in the paper's own official repo (jshun/ligra) and its companion artifact-evaluation repo (jshun/ppopp20-ae), which do implement and time HyperBC exactly as described in the paper. This is exactly the "same-name-different-project collision" / "third-party reimplementation is not an artifact" trap this project's own CLAUDE.md already warns about, caught here for a case the automated artifact-finder missed.
  • The paper's own protocol reports the MINIMUM of 3 trials as its headline number, with no mean/median/max disclosed. Best-of-N is exactly the kind of one-sided reporting the fairness principles ask to avoid; this spec keeps min-of-3 as the headline (for direct comparability with the paper's own Table 2 numbers) but requires mean and max to also be reported, so a reader can tell whether the minimum is representative or a lucky outlier.
  • Unlike the bfs track (64 random roots), HyperBC here is timed from a single, unvaried source vertex — consistent with how the paper itself treats it (same convention as HyperBFS, HyperCC, etc. in Table 2, all timed once per dataset/thread-count cell, not averaged over multiple sources). This spec preserves that single-source convention rather than importing the bfs track's multi-root averaging, since importing it would make this benchmark's numbers incomparable to the one existing paper in this track for no fairness benefit (a single dependency-accumulation BC pass is not subject to the same root-dependent load-imbalance variance that motivates multi-root averaging for plain BFS).
Open questions
  • The exact default source vertex used by the paper's own scripts when "-r" is omitted (readECLgraph/Hygra loader default, likely vertex 0) was not directly confirmed by reading run_scalability's invocation lines byte-for-byte; this spec assumes source=0 and asks submitters to disclose otherwise.
  • Whether the paper's Table 2 HyperBC numbers used edge-aware parallelization or direction-optimization (mentioned in the AE README as used "for the Orkut-group, Web, and LiveJournal hypergraphs due to their highly-skewed degree distributions") specifically for BC, or only for the traversal algorithms (BFS/SSSP/CC), is not disambiguated in the available README text — flagged for direct source-code confirmation (HyperBC.C's use of EDGELIMIT-style thresholds) before treating direction-optimization disclosure as settled for this variant, unlike the bfs track where it is a REQUIRED disclosure field.
bipartite-matching1 papers2 variants

Exact maximum-cardinality matching in bipartite graphs on GPU via a deterministic initial-matching phase followed by parallel bidirectional augmenting-path search, measured as steady-state edges/s throughput with the two algorithmic phases (initial matching, augmenting-path search) timed and reported separately since the code itself already separates them rather than blending into one number.

match[V] = MaxBipartiteMatching(A[L,R] biadjacency (sparse, CSR, unweighted), L,R the two vertex partitions); output is a partial bijection between L and R such that every matched pair is an edge in A and no vertex is matched more than once; the algorithm returns a MAXIMUM-cardinality such matching (exact, not approximate).

Fairness notes
  • The paper's own code already separates phase-1 (initial matching) and phase-2 (augmenting-path search) timing rather than blending them — this spec's timing_scope directly mirrors that existing separation rather than imposing an external convention, and makes reporting BOTH phases mandatory (not just the flashier apSearchPhase_throughput number).
  • Because 21 of the 21 evaluation graphs are general SuiteSparse instances (web/road/citation/social/synthetic), NOT natively bipartite, this spec makes the bipartite-construction method a REQUIRED disclosure field. Silently choosing an easy row/column split vs. a harder bipartite-double-cover construction could make the "same-named" benchmark instance mean very different matching difficulty across two submissions without this being visible.
  • Maximum bipartite matching is exact — there is no approximation-ratio axis for this track, unlike several of this batch's other singleton tracks (MIS, spectral sparsification). The correctness gate is correspondingly a hard, binary maximality check (no augmenting path remains), not a quality score to be reported jointly with time.
Open questions
  • The exact numeric speedup factor vs. "fastest prior GPU code" was lost to inline MathML markup in the abstract text as extracted (`<tex...>$...$</tex>` placeholder with no resolvable value in the available `included.json` abstract field); the README's one_liner ("1.63x over fastest prior GPU code") was used as the parent benchmark_groups.json summary but was not independently re-derived from the paper's own fulltext (ACM DL paywalled, no arXiv found) — flagged for confirmation before treating 1.63x as authoritative.
  • The identity of "fastest prior GPU code" (which specific implementation/paper) was not confirmed from available sources; likely a predecessor GPU bipartite-matching kernel, possibly from the same lab given the ECL- naming convention, but not verified.
  • Whether the paper's own per-graph bipartite construction (row/column split vs. other) is uniform across all 21 instances or chosen per-instance based on the graph's natural structure was not resolved from the README's brief "input files in matrix market format" note.
dynamic-graph-kernel1 papers3 variants

Maintaining or computing a query-able result R over a graph G that evolves through a sequence of timestamped edge batches, covering two distinct problem shapes this track's own papers target: (1) genuine incremental MAINTENANCE of a live result (an SSSP tree) under a stream of edge insertions/deletions, where batch size and insert/delete mix are semantic choices that affect result staleness; and (2) one-shot STREAMING ANALYTICS over an already-complete historical temporal-edge log (temporal motif counting), where "batch"/chunk size is a pure performance-tuning knob with no effect on the (single, final) answer. The two are kept as separate variant families rather than forced onto one shared metric, per notes_on_fairness.

Family A (maintenance): R_i = Update(R_{i-1}, B_i) for a sequence of edge-change batches B_1..B_k (each B_i a set of (u,v,w,op) tuples, op in {insert, delete}), where R_i must be observably equivalent to Recompute(G_i) from scratch (G_i = G_0 with B_1..B_i applied), and a point query Q(R_i, s, t) = shortest-path distance/parent from s to t must be answerable after each B_i commits. Family B (streaming analytics): Count_M(G) = number of valid delta-temporal-motif matches for motif template M in a FIXED temporal edge multiset G = {(u_i,v_i,t_i)}, computed once by streaming G through memory in temporal-chunk order; G itself is never mutated during a run.

dgk-incremental-update-latencyupdate-latency and post-update query-latency of a maintained SSSP result under a stream of edge insertions and deletions, swept across batch size and insert/delete mix — the direct operationalization of this track's "update batch sizes, insert/delete mix, update-throughput vs. query-latency" axes, modeled on Khanda et al.'s incremental-SSSP-maintenance problem.
inputs
suitereal temporal-edge logs replayed in chronological order as an insertion stream — Khanda et al.'s own graph suite could not be confirmed from available sources (see survey.md), so this spec substitutes DTMiner's independently-verified real temporal-graph suite (same source data, different use: here the timestamps drive an actual insertion ORDER rather than a chunking scheme).
selectiongraphs with a real per-edge timestamp (so chronological replay is meaningful, not an arbitrary synthetic ordering), large enough that a single edge batch is a small fraction of |E| at the batch sizes below.
recommended_subsetwikitalk (SNAP, 1,140,149 v / 7,833,140 temporal edges) — small/medium control instance, stackoverflow (SNAP, 2,601,977 v / 63,497,050 temporal edges), temporal-reddit-reply (8,901,033 v / 646,044,687 temporal edges) — large instance, ethereum (66,323,478 v / 628,810,973 temporal edges) — large, real financial-transaction-graph instance, CollegeMsg (SNAP, 1,899 v / 59,835 temporal edges) — tiny debug/CI-size control instance, added since none of the above four are small enough for fast iteration
graph_typeundirected weighted (edge weights: real graphs above are unweighted natively — see weight assignment in protocol below); replayed as directed-then-symmetrized where the source technique requires undirected
dense_operandN/A
protocol
formatan initial snapshot G_0 is built from the first X% of each graph's chronologically-sorted edges (X in {50, 90}, i.e. two starting-point sizes), CSR/adjacency-list, construction timed once and reported separately (see e2e-preproc variant below); the REMAINING (100-X)% of edges are replayed as the update stream, grouped into batches per the sweep below, preserving their original relative chronological order within and across batches.
edge_weightsREQUIRED disclosure — this axis is not fixed to one value because neither surveyed paper's exact weight distribution was confirmable. Two settings must both be run and reported: (a) UNIT weights (every edge weight = 1, i.e. SSSP degenerates to unweighted-BFS-shortest-path, isolating pure algorithmic/data-structure overhead from weight-comparison cost), and (b) uniform-random integer weights in [1, 255) (matching the convention this repo's mst/spec.yaml documents KaMSTa using), assigned once at G_0 construction and inherited by inserted edges deterministically from a fixed-seed generator so re-runs are reproducible.
batch_size_sweepREQUIRED sweep, reported as a curve not a single point: batch size B in {1 (single-edge-at-a-time), 10, 100, 1000, 0.01%*|E|, 0.1%*|E|, 1%*|E|} edge-changes per batch. B=1 is the finest-grained/most-realistic "streaming" setting; the percentage-of-|E| points let large and small graphs be compared on the same relative axis.
insert_delete_mix_sweepREQUIRED sweep at EACH batch size above: insert:delete ratio in {100:0 (insert-only, the natural mode for a chronological-replay stream since these graphs have no recorded deletions), 90:10, 50:50, 10:90}. Deletions beyond insert-only are SYNTHETIC — edges are chosen for deletion uniform-randomly from among previously-inserted edges after a random delay (fixed seed=42) — and MUST be labeled as synthetic in any report, since none of the recommended_subset graphs carry real deletion timestamps. This directly operationalizes the "deletions are slower, needs tree repair" asymmetry noted in this track's survey.
warmup1 full batch-apply + query cycle (discarded)
reps20 repeated batch-apply-then-query cycles per (batch_size, insert_delete_mix) cell, same underlying edge sequence replayed with the same fixed seed for the synthetic-deletion selection
statisticmedian (report min/max/stdev alongside)
timerstd::chrono/CUDA-event bracket around (a) the batch-apply-to-consistency step alone, and (b) a point query issued immediately after (a) completes
timing_scopeupdate_latency_ms = time for R to become observably consistent with G_i after B_i is applied (i.e. time until Recompute(G_i) would agree with R_i, whether the implementation achieves this via full recompute or true incremental update — both are legitimate implementations of this variant and must be labeled which one was run, per algorithm_disclosure below); query_latency_ms = time to answer a single-pair distance query issued immediately after update_latency_ms elapses. Both are reported per batch, not just once.
algorithm_disclosureREQUIRED: report whether the technique under test performs true incremental maintenance (touches only the affected subgraph, per Khanda et al.'s "rooted tree" approach) or recomputes from scratch every batch — this variant exists precisely to make that distinction visible as a throughput/latency curve rather than a binary claim, since a from-scratch baseline is a legitimate (if slow) point of comparison, not a disqualified one.
snapshot_consistencyREQUIRED disclosure of the consistency model: this spec DEFAULTS TO AND REQUIRES batch-atomic consistency — a query issued between update_latency_ms measurements must never observe a partially-applied batch (either the full pre-batch or full post-batch graph state, never an intermediate one). If a technique only offers a weaker model (e.g. eventual consistency, individual-edge-level visibility mid-batch), that must be disclosed and the query_latency_ms measurement repeated at the START, MIDDLE, and END of batch application to characterize the staleness window, rather than silently reporting only the post-batch number as if it were representative throughout. Neither surveyed paper's artifact-level consistency model could be confirmed (see survey.md open_questions), so this default is this spec's own fairness-driven choice, not derived from either paper.
preprocessing_reportedG_0 construction time reported separately, once per (graph, X%) pair — see dgk-e2e-preproc
precisioninteger edge weights (both unit and [1,255) settings above); distances accumulated in a width sufficient to avoid overflow for the largest graph (>=64-bit for temporal-reddit-reply/ethereum scale)
metric
primaryupdate-throughput = batch_size / update_latency_ms (edge-changes/ms), reported as a curve over the batch_size sweep
secondaryquery_latency_ms (median, post-batch); update_latency_ms (median, min/max); staleness-window query_latency_ms at start/middle/end of batch application if snapshot_consistency is weaker than batch-atomic
correctnessMANDATORY ground-truth gate, stronger than what this spec could confirm either paper's own artifact actually does (see survey.md): after EVERY batch, R_i's distances/parents for a sample of >=1000 uniform-random (s,t) pairs (or all pairs if |V|<=1000) must exactly match (integer weights, so exact match is the correct bar, not a tolerance) an independently computed from-scratch reference (Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford, run once per checked batch on G_i). A technique whose own internal-consistency check (e.g. parent/distance-array agreement without an external reference) passes but whose values disagree with the from-scratch reference does NOT pass this gate — internal consistency alone is insufficient, since the unofficial reimplementation surveyed for this track uses exactly that weaker check and it would not catch a systematically-wrong-but-self-consistent update rule.
dgk-temporal-batch-throughputaggregate streaming throughput and end-to-end completion latency for a ONE-SHOT analytics query (temporal motif counting) over a fixed, complete historical temporal-edge log, with chunk/batch size swept as a performance-tuning knob (NOT a semantic insert/delete axis — no mutation occurs in this variant) — the direct operationalization of DTMiner's own evaluation shape, kept separate from dgk-incremental-update-latency because conflating "chunk size for cache locality" with "batch size for update semantics" would misrepresent what either paper actually varies.
inputs
suiteDTMiner's own real temporal-graph suite (verified from fulltext + repo scripts, see survey.md)
selectionsame 4 graphs DTMiner itself uses, all real, all with genuine timestamps spanning multiple years
recommended_subsetwikitalk (wi): 1,140,149 v, 7,833,140 temporal edges, delta=24h, stackoverflow (so): 2,601,977 v, 63,497,050 temporal edges, delta=24h, temporal-reddit-reply (re): 8,901,033 v, 646,044,687 temporal edges, delta=10h, ethereum (eth): 66,323,478 v, 628,810,973 temporal edges, delta=1h
motifs13 structurally diverse motifs (3-5 edges each), matching DTMiner's own M1-M13 set (Figure 11) exactly, since these are the only motif shapes independently confirmed via both the paper text and the repo's `motifs/M*.txt` files.
dense_operandN/A
protocol
formattemporal edge list, sorted by timestamp; loaded and index-structure-built once per (graph, chunk_size)
chunk_size_sweepREQUIRED sweep, reported as a curve: chunk size S_c as a fraction of the platform's LLC capacity — {25%, 50%, 100%, 200%} of LLC-per-core (DTMiner's own formula sizes S_c to exactly fit the LLC alongside index/reserved space; sweeping around that target, including deliberately-too-large settings, makes the claimed cache-locality benefit falsifiable rather than assumed). LLC capacity and per-core share MUST be reported alongside the sweep since the sweep is defined relative to it.
warmup1 full mining run per (graph, motif) pair (discarded)
reps5
statisticmedian (report min/max alongside; DTMiner's own paper does not report a repetition count for its headline numbers, which this spec's median-of-5 requirement fixes)
timerwall-clock (host-side) around the full streaming pass, plus a separate bracket around preprocessing (chunk-index construction) alone
timing_scopestreaming/mining time only for the primary number; preprocessing (locality-aware chunk partition + hierarchical index construction) is a one-shot cost per GRAPH (reusable across all 13 motifs, matching DTMiner's own "preprocessed once for different applications" framing) and is reported separately, see preprocessing_reported.
preprocessing_reportedstandalone (ms, once per graph, amortized note that it is reused across all 13 motifs) AND folded into an end-to-end number (preprocessing_time + mining_time for a single motif), both reported, matching DTMiner's own Table 2 / Figure 18 practice — one of the few places in either paper's evaluation this spec adopts wholesale rather than tightening.
numa_disclosureREQUIRED if the platform is multi-socket/NUMA: report whether the technique is NUMA-aware (thread/memory affinity, work stealing hierarchy) since DTMiner's own three-level work-stealing ablation (Figure 15) shows this accounts for a 3.6x-20x difference on its own, independent of the chunking idea itself — a NUMA-naive baseline run on a NUMA machine would otherwise look artificially bad for reasons unrelated to the paper's actual contribution.
precisionN/A (exact integer motif count)
metric
primaryedges/second = total temporal edges in the graph / streaming_time_seconds (aggregate throughput of the one-shot pass)
secondaryend-to-end completion time per (graph, motif) pair, ms (preprocessing + mining); LLC miss count or cache-reference count if measurable on the platform (matches DTMiner's own use of this as a mechanism-level metric, not just a speed number)
correctnessexact match of the reported motif count against an independently computed reference count (a straightforward, unoptimized brute-force temporal-subgraph-search on a SMALL held-out subgraph sample where brute force is tractable, e.g. the first 1% of edges of the smallest graph in the suite) — motif counting is a discrete, exact-answer problem, so "exact match" is the only valid gate, not a numeric tolerance.
dgk-e2e-preprocone-shot cost of building the initial data structure — either the SSSP rooted-tree/auxiliary-edge structure (Family A) or the chunk/hierarchical index (Family B) — from a static starting graph, reported standalone rather than folded silently into the first update or the first query, since both papers in this track build a nontrivial structure before any update/query timing begins and neither fully separates that cost from steady-state numbers in their own headline results.
inputs
suiteunion of dgk-incremental-update-latency's and dgk-temporal-batch-throughput's suites
selectionsame graphs, at G_0 = the full graph (100% of edges) for this variant, since construction cost is what is being isolated here, not update behavior
recommended_subsetunion of both variants' recommended_subset lists above
dense_operandN/A
protocol
formatraw edge list (CSR/temporal-sorted as appropriate); construction IS the timed operation
warmup1
reps10
statisticmedian (report min/max)
timerwall-clock around the full construction call
timing_scopeconstruction only; no updates or queries/mining performed in this variant
preprocessing_reportedthis ENTIRE variant IS the preprocessing report, matching benchspecs/bfs/spec.yaml's bfs-reordering-cost pattern of promoting a preprocessing cost to a first-class variant rather than a footnote
memory_reportedpeak memory usage during construction (MB), matching DTMiner's own Table 2 practice
metric
primaryconstruction_time_seconds (median of 10)
secondarypeak_memory_MB; construction_time as a multiple of a single downstream update_latency_ms (Family A) or a single motif's mining_time_ms (Family B), i.e. a break-even-style number analogous to benchspecs/bfs/spec.yaml's break_even_reps
correctnessthe constructed structure must pass the same correctness gate as the variant that will consume it (dgk-incremental-update-latency's ground-truth check, or dgk-temporal-batch-throughput's exact-count check, run once against the freshly-built structure before any timing counts)
Fairness notes
  • DTMiner's chunk size and Khanda et al.'s batch size are NOT the same kind of parameter — one is a pure cache-locality tuning knob with no effect on the final answer, the other is a semantic choice that determines how stale a query's view of the graph can be. Treating them as one shared "batch size" axis (as a naive reading of this track's brief might suggest) would misrepresent both papers. This spec keeps them in separate variants with separate sweep semantics.
  • The unofficial reimplementation surveyed for Khanda et al. validates updates via internal parent/distance-array consistency, NOT comparison against an independent from-scratch reference. Whether the original paper's own artifact does better is unconfirmed. This spec's correctness gate for dgk-incremental-update-latency requires the stronger ground-truth comparison regardless, since a self-consistent-but-wrong update rule is exactly the failure mode an internal-only check cannot catch.
  • Neither paper's own artifact fully discloses its snapshot/consistency model under concurrent query-during-update. This spec makes batch-atomic consistency the required default and mandates disclosure (plus a staleness-window measurement) for anything weaker, rather than silently assuming one model.
  • DTMiner's paper does not state a repetition count for its headline speedup numbers (Figures 12-18), unlike the very deliberate 9-repetition-median protocol this repo's mst/spec.yaml documents for ECL-MST in the same general problem space (graph algorithms with highly input-dependent runtime). dgk-temporal-batch-throughput fixes this with an explicit median-of-5 requirement (5 rather than 9, in recognition that a single mining run on the largest graph, e.g. ethereum, already takes minutes per Table 2, making 9 reps proportionally more expensive here than in the mst track).
  • None of this track's recommended real-graph datasets carry genuine deletion timestamps, so the insert/delete-mix sweep in dgk-incremental-update-latency necessarily uses SYNTHETIC deletions. This is disclosed explicitly in the protocol rather than presented as if the deletions were drawn from real data, unlike a benchmark that might silently synthesize deletions without flagging them as such.
Open questions
  • Khanda et al.'s own graph suite, exact batch-size values, and weight-distribution choice could not be confirmed (IEEE paywall, no arXiv preprint, no accessible preprint elsewhere found). This spec's dgk-incremental-update-latency substitutes a principled, independently verifiable suite (DTMiner's real temporal graphs, replayed as an insertion stream) rather than guessing at the original paper's unconfirmed choices, and this substitution should be revisited if the paywalled fulltext becomes available.
  • Whether DTMiner's hierarchical-index hash table (built for 30% of vertices by default, per its own load-factor formula) introduces seed-dependent performance variance analogous to ECL-MST's filter-threshold seed sensitivity (mst track) is untested by the paper itself and left as a candidate future addition to dgk-temporal-batch-throughput (a random-seed sensitivity sweep) rather than assumed absent.
  • Whether a single implementation could reasonably be evaluated under BOTH variant families (e.g. an incremental-SSSP-style structure applied to a temporal-motif-adjacent counting query, or a DTMiner-style chunked streaming approach applied to incremental SSSP maintenance) is an interesting cross-pollination question raised by surveying these two papers together, but is out of scope for this spec, which benchmarks each paper's own problem shape rather than proposing a new hybrid one.
graph-layout1 papers2 variants

GPU-accelerated 2D force-directed / Path-Guided Stochastic Gradient Descent (PG-SGD) layout of pangenome variation graphs, measured as wall-clock time to complete a fixed SGD iteration schedule, with layout quality (Sampled Path Stress) reported jointly with time since this is a non-convex optimization with no single correct output.

coords[V,2] = PG_SGD(graph G=(V,E,paths), iteration_schedule, step_size_schedule); minimizes sum over sampled (path, node_i, node_j) triples of (||coords_i - coords_j|| - path_distance(i,j))^2 / path_distance(i,j)^2; output is a 2D embedding of every node.

layout-kernel-hprc-chromosomessteady-state layout wall time on the complete HPRC Year-1 whole-chromosome pangenome suite; graph loading (.og deserialization) excluded but reported separately (one-shot, not amortized)
inputs
suiteHuman Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC) Year-1 pangenome graphs, odgi .og format
selectioncomplete set: chr1-chr22, chrX, chrY (24 graphs, no cherry-picking possible since it's the full chromosome set)
recommended_subsetchrY or chr21 (smallest, ~3.2x10^5 nodes) — small/dev instance, chr1 (largest, ~1.1x10^7 nodes, ~1.1x10^9 nucleotides) — large/scale instance, 3+ additional mid-size chromosomes for coverage (e.g. chr6, chr12, chr17)
dense_operandN/A (graph structure + path set is the sole input)
protocol
formatgraph loaded once from .og; loading NOT counted in layout time
warmup1 full layout run, discarded (stochastic algorithm — first run may pay one-time GPU context/JIT costs)
reps15 independent runs per chromosome (matches the paper's own repeatability-check convention), different RNG seed each run
statisticmedian wall time, report min/max; median SPS, report the 95% CI half-width from the SPS estimator itself
timerhost-side wall clock around the full PG-SGD iteration loop; device-side CUDA events optionally for per-iteration breakdown
timing_scopePG-SGD iteration schedule only; .og loading and any node-order/path-index preprocessing excluded
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once per chromosome: .og load time
iteration_schedule_disclosureREQUIRED: number of SGD iterations, step-size schedule (min/max step, decay), and node/path sampling scheme (data-reuse factor, step-reduction factor if the warp-data-reuse GPU variant is used) must be disclosed and held fixed across implementations under test — these directly trade quality for time
metric
primarylayout_time (median seconds, min/max across 15 runs)
secondarySPS (Sampled Path Stress, median + 95% CI), speedup vs. CPU baseline (odgi layout, 32-core)
correctnessno exact-value correctness (non-convex layout optimization); quality gate is SPS_GPU / SPS_CPU_baseline <= 1.15 (allows the paper's own observed 1.08x ratio plus margin) computed with sample size and CI disclosed; a run whose SPS ratio exceeds this threshold does not count as a valid submission regardless of speed, since a layout that is fast but visibly worse is not a legitimate win on this task.
layout-e2e-with-loadingend-to-end time including one-shot graph loading, for the case where loading cost is non-negligible relative to layout time on smaller chromosomes (loading is NOT amortized across multiple layout calls in real pangenome-analysis usage — each chromosome is laid out once)
inputs
suitesame recommended_subset as layout-kernel-hprc-chromosomes
selectionsame
recommended_subsetsame
dense_operandN/A
protocol
format.og file on disk to final coords/.lay file
warmup1
reps15, same seeds as layout-kernel-hprc-chromosomes for direct cross-reference
statisticmedian total_time (load + layout), report min/max
timerhost-side wall clock around the full pipeline
timing_scopeload + PG-SGD, no amortization (k=1, single layout per load, matching real usage)
preprocessing_reportedload_time reported standalone alongside total_time, never silently folded in without also being independently visible
metric
primarytotal_time_s (median, min/max)
secondaryload_time_s standalone, layout_time cross-reference to layout-kernel-hprc-chromosomes
correctnesssame SPS-ratio gate as layout-kernel-hprc-chromosomes
Fairness notes
  • Because PG-SGD is stochastic and non-convex, reporting only the fastest run (best-of-N) without a paired quality check would let an implementation "cheat" by cutting iterations short. Both variants require SPS to be reported jointly with time, and layout-kernel- hprc-chromosomes gates on an SPS ratio threshold rather than treating speed as free-standing.
  • The 24-chromosome HPRC suite is the complete natural population for this task (one graph per human chromosome) — unlike most kernel tracks there is no risk of an unrepresentative hand-picked subset, but recommended_subset still fixes named instances for reproducible reporting under a compute budget rather than requiring all 24 for every submission.
  • The paper's warp-level-data-reuse GPU variant is explicitly algorithm- changing (produces a different layout than the CPU baseline, per the repo README), unlike the "no algorithm changes" GPU variant. The iteration_schedule_disclosure field is REQUIRED specifically so this distinction is visible rather than silently blended into one number.
Open questions
  • The exact SGD iteration count / step-size schedule used for the paper's headline 57.3x number (vs. e.g. a reduced-iteration variant used only for the ablation study) was not confirmed from the fetched HTML fulltext excerpt.
  • Whether the reported 15-run repeatability check is also the N used to compute the headline speedup/SPS numbers, or a separate smaller-N measurement, was not fully disentangled from the available text.
knn-graph-construction1 papers2 variants

Distributed-memory construction of an approximate k-nearest-neighbor graph (KNNG) over high-dimensional points via a forest of sparse random projection trees (build + query), measured as construction throughput jointly with recall against an exact brute-force KNNG, since this is an approximate algorithm and speed alone is not a legitimate win.

KNNG[N,k] = ApproxKNN(X[N,D] point set, ntrees T, target_neighbors k, locality_mode); builds T sparse random-projection trees over X (each a recursive space partition via random sparse hyperplane projections), then queries the forest per point to emit its k approximate nearest neighbors as a directed graph.

knng-kernel-single-nodesteady-state single-node build+query throughput on standard ANN-benchmark-style point sets, at a fixed accuracy operating point; the common denominator most ANN/KNNG papers report on before addressing distributed scaling
inputs
suiteANN-benchmarks-style point-set corpus, ubyte/fbin format
selectionMNIST (confirmed used by this paper's own repo/README: 60,000 points, D=784) plus the standard higher-dimensional ANN-benchmarks staples for size/dimension coverage, since the paper's own full dataset list could not be confirmed from available sources
recommended_subsetMNIST (60,000 x 784) — confirmed paper/repo instance, Fashion-MNIST (60,000 x 784) — same shape, harder structure, standard ANN-benchmarks control, SIFT1M (1,000,000 x 128) — standard ANN-benchmarks large instance, GloVe-100 (~1,183,514 x 100, angular) — standard ANN-benchmarks text-embedding instance
dense_operandN/A (point set IS the input; no separate dense operand)
algorithm_paramsntrees in {8, 16}, k (target neighbors) in {10, 20}, locality-based data-gathering ON (the paper's stated contribution) — both settings disclosed and held fixed across implementations under test
protocol
formatraw feature vectors (ubyte/fbin), loaded once, not counted in build time
warmup1 full build+query pass, discarded
reps5
statisticmedian of (build_time, query_time), report min/max
timerwall-clock (MPI_Wtime or std::chrono) around build and query phases separately
timing_scopetree build + forest query (KNNG construction); input I/O and output-graph serialization excluded but reported separately
preprocessing_reportedinput load time, separately, once per dataset
metric
primarypoints_per_second = N / (build_time + query_time), median
secondarybuild_time_s, query_time_s (each standalone), speedup vs. baseline ANN method at matched recall
correctnessrecall@k >= 0.90 against an exact brute-force KNNG computed once per dataset (independent reference, no approximation); recall MUST be reported alongside throughput on every submission — a faster build at lower recall is a DIFFERENT, not better, result, and must be plotted/reported as a distinct (recall, throughput) operating point rather than compared directly to a higher-recall number.
knng-distributed-scalingdistributed-memory strong-scaling throughput of the SAME accuracy operating point as knng-kernel-single-node, since this track's paper's central contribution is scaling KNNG construction to thousands of MPI processes on a supercomputer via a communication- reduction (locality-based data-gathering) scheme
inputs
suitesame corpus as knng-kernel-single-node, largest 1-2 instances (SIFT1M, GloVe-100) for scale-sensitivity
selectionsame accuracy operating point (ntrees, k, recall target) as knng-kernel-single-node, fixed across all process counts
recommended_subsetSIFT1M, GloVe-100
dense_operandN/A
protocol
formatsame as knng-kernel-single-node; input distributed once across ranks, not re-timed per process-count point
warmup1
reps3
process_counts_required1 node baseline, then a strong-scaling ladder disclosed explicitly (e.g. 16, 64, 256, 1024+ MPI ranks) — the paper's abstract claims 'thousands of processes', so the top of the ladder should approach that scale for the claim to be checked, not stop at a token multi-node point
statisticmedian wall time per process-count point, report min/max
timerwall-clock (MPI_Wtime) around build+query, barrier-synchronized across ranks before/after timing region
timing_scopebuild + query only; MPI initialization and data distribution/partitioning are one-shot and reported separately
preprocessing_reporteddata distribution/partitioning time, separately, at each process-count point (this cost itself typically grows with process count and is part of the scaling story)
metric
primaryparallel_efficiency(P) = time(1_node) / (P/P_base * time(P)), and points_per_second(P)
secondarycommunication volume or time (isolating the locality-based data-gathering optimization's effect, since that IS the paper's contribution), recall@k held constant across all points on the scaling curve
correctnesssame recall@k >= 0.90 gate as knng-kernel-single-node, verified at EVERY process-count point (approximate algorithms can lose accuracy under different data partitioning, so this is not a one-time check)
Fairness notes
  • Approximate KNNG construction has a fundamental speed/recall tradeoff; a benchmark that reports only throughput (as a bare "two orders of magnitude faster than its peers" claim, echoing this paper's own abstract framing) without a fixed or disclosed accuracy operating point is not comparable across implementations. Both variants above fix recall>=0.90 as the reporting gate and require recall to be reported alongside every throughput number, not asserted once and assumed stable.
  • This track's one paper is explicitly a distributed-memory (MPI) method whose central claim is process-count scalability — a single-node-only benchmark would miss the paper's actual contribution entirely, which is why knng-distributed-scaling is kept as a first-class variant rather than folded into a footnote, unlike how some other singleton tracks in this benchmark set only need one variant.
Open questions
  • The paper's own full dataset list and exact accuracy metric definition (recall@k vs. some other approximation-ratio notion) could not be confirmed — IPDPS 2023 is paywalled and no arXiv mirror was found via WebSearch. recommended_subset above is a reasonable, disclosed stand-in (MNIST confirmed from the repo; the rest are standard ANN-benchmarks staples), not a reproduction of the paper's exact table.
  • The specific baseline methods DRPT is compared against ("two orders of magnitude faster than its peers") are unnamed in available sources; likely candidates are other distributed/parallel randomized- partition-tree or graph-based ANN methods, but this was not verified.
  • Exact process-count ladder used in the paper's own scaling experiments (beyond the bundled 16-rank SLURM example) was not confirmed.
lca-bridge-finding1 papers2 variants

GPU adaptation of the Euler-tour technique for two exact tree/graph problems, benchmarked separately: lowest common ancestor (LCA) batch queries on trees, and bridge-finding on undirected graphs; measured as wall time across a size/shape parameter sweep, with theoretically optimal Euler-tour methods compared against simpler heuristics on both adversarial (deep/bushy) and typical (shallow) synthetic instances.

(LCA) answer[q] = LCA(T=(V,E) tree, query batch Q subset of V x V); (bridges) isBridge[E] = Bridges(G=(V,E) undirected graph); both are unweighted, exact combinatorial problems (no approximation ratio applies to either).

lca-kernel-synthetic-sweepsteady-state batch-LCA-query wall time on synthetic trees, swept across size, tree-shape ("grasp"), and query-batch-size parameters, separately from ground-truth generation which is one-shot and excluded from timing
inputs
suitesynthetic trees from the paper's own generators (generateSimple.cpp: uniform-random attachment; generateScaleFree.cpp: scale-free attachment)
selectionsizes and grasp values matching the paper's own E1-E5 experiment definitions in test/lca/testVariables.sh, generator=simple (E1-E5's own default)
recommended_subsetE1 (size vs. algorithm): sizes {1M, 2M, 4M, 8M, 16M, 32M} nodes, grasp in {-1 (shallow/wide), 1000 (deep/bushy)}, 5 seeds each, E2 (batch size vs. cuda-inlabel/cpu-inlabel/multicore-cpu-inlabel): fixed size 8M nodes, 10M queries, batch size swept over {1, 10, 100, 1e3, 1e4, 1e5, 1e6, 1e7}, 5 seeds, E3 (grasp/tree-depth vs. cuda-inlabel/cuda-naive/multicore-cpu-inlabel): fixed size 8M nodes, grasp swept over {1, 3, 10, 33, 100, 333, 1e3, 3333, 1e4, 33333, 1e5, 333333, 1e6, 1e7}, 5 seeds
dense_operandN/A
algorithms_under_testcuda-inlabel, cuda-naive, cpu-inlabel, multicore-cpu-inlabel
protocol
formattree generated once per (size, grasp, seed) combination; ground-truth answers pre-generated ONCE via the cpu-rmq reference algorithm BEFORE any timed run — never inside the timed loop
warmup0 explicit discarded warmup (the paper's own script times the actual answer-computation run directly; this spec keeps that convention since ground-truth generation, the closest thing to a 'first touch' cost, is already isolated outside the timed region)
reps5 (paper's own E1-E5DifferentSeeds=5 — distinct RANDOM INSTANCES, not repeated timing of the same instance; this spec additionally requires 3 REPEATED timed runs per generated instance to separate instance-to-instance variance from run-to-run measurement noise, since the paper's own script does not appear to re-time a fixed instance multiple times)
statisticmedian across the 3 repeated timed runs per instance, THEN median across the 5 seed-instances (two-level median); report min/max at both levels
timersingleRunTimeout=120s cap; internal wall-clock timer wrapping only the query-answering call (test generation and ground-truth generation excluded by the script's own control flow)
timing_scopequery-answering (LCA computation) only; tree generation and ground-truth (cpu-rmq) computation are one-shot per instance and excluded
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once per instance: tree-generation time and ground-truth (cpu-rmq) generation time
metric
primarywall time in seconds/ms as a function of the swept parameter (size for E1, batch size for E2, grasp for E3) — matches the paper's own parameter-sweep framing rather than a single throughput number
secondaryspeedup of cuda-inlabel over cuda-naive and over multicore-cpu-inlabel, per swept-parameter point
correctnessexact problem: every implementation's per-query LCA answer MUST exactly match the cpu-rmq-generated ground truth for the same (tree, query-batch) instance. This is a hard, binary gate (no partial credit) — CheckAnswers=true is REQUIRED for every timed configuration in this variant, matching the paper's own default for all 5 of its experiments.
bridges-kernel-repeated-meansteady-state bridge-finding wall time on undirected graphs, averaged over a user-set repeat count — kept as its OWN variant (rather than merged with the LCA variant above) because the paper's own bridges harness uses mean-of-repeats rather than LCA's median-of-seeded-instances convention, and its correctness-check wiring is documented in the paper's own script as incomplete ("TODO do we want to have some tests to check correctness?")
inputs

recommended_subset1M, 2M, 4M, 8M, 16M, 32M node graphs, generator=simple, matching lca-kernel-synthetic-sweep's E1 sizes
dense_operandN/A
algorithms_under_testwhatever bridges_runner.cu exposes via its -a flag; disclose the exact algorithm identifiers tested (analogous to cuda-inlabel/cuda-naive for LCA, but the exact bridges-specific identifier set was not independently confirmed — see open_questions)
protocol

warmup1 full run, discarded (this spec's addition — the paper's own -r flag controls only the AVERAGED run count, with no separate discarded warmup, matching the LCA variant's stricter convention)
repsREQUIRED minimum 5 (paper's own default is repeats=1 via the -r flag if unset, which this spec treats as insufficient for a reportable benchmark number, matching the fairness principle of never reporting an unrepeated single measurement)
statisticthe paper's own harness computes the ARITHMETIC MEAN of the repeats (per bridges_test.sh's own help text: 'Repeat tests <times> times and get average results'); this spec keeps mean as the headline for continuity with the paper's own reporting, but additionally REQUIRES min/max/median to be reported alongside, since mean-of-N is more sensitive to a single slow outlier run than the median-based convention used elsewhere in this survey batch
timerrun_experiments.sh's internal wall-clock timer around the bridge-finding call
timing_scopebridge-finding computation only; graph generation excluded
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once per instance: graph-generation time
metric
primarywall time in seconds/ms, mean of >=5 repeats (paper's own statistic, strengthened repeat-count floor)
secondarymedian, min, max across the same repeats; speedup of the Euler-tour method over any naive/heuristic competitor tested
correctnessexact problem (a bridge is a bridge or it isn't — no ambiguity), but THE PAPER'S OWN HARNESS DOES NOT GUARANTEE an automated ground-truth check is wired in by default (its own script marks this a TODO). This spec REQUIRES an independent bridge-finding reference (e.g. a straightforward O(V+E) DFS-based bridge algorithm, run once per instance, untimed) to validate every timed configuration's output before it counts — closing the gap the paper's own artifact leaves open, per this project's principle that a correctness gate must exist before timing counts, full stop.
Fairness notes
  • LCA and bridges use materially different repeat/statistic conventions within the SAME paper's own artifact (median-of-5-seeded-instances with pre-excluded ground-truth generation for LCA; user-controlled mean-of-repeats, default 1, for bridges). Rather than forcing one convention onto both, this spec keeps them as separate variants and is explicit about which statistic each inherits from the paper's own scripts, so a reader is never misled into thinking "median" and "mean-of-1-by-default" are the same rigor level.
  • The bridges harness's own help text admits its correctness checking is an unfinished TODO. This spec does not treat "the paper's artifact lacks a check" as license to skip one — an independent untimed reference bridge-finder is REQUIRED before any bridges timing counts, consistent with this project's "correctness gate before timing counts" principle even where the source artifact itself falls short of it.
  • Both LCA and bridges are exact problems (Euler-tour techniques carry theoretical correctness guarantees per the paper's own framing) — no approximation-ratio or quality axis applies to either variant, unlike several other tracks in this survey batch (MIS, spectral sparsification).
Open questions
  • Hardware (GPU model, compute capability) used for the paper's reported numbers was not found in the inspected scripts (NVCCSM is a user-supplied Makefile variable) or in the arXiv abstract page (PDF/HTML fulltext fetch attempts for arXiv:2103.15217 both failed to yield readable text via available tools) — needs direct PDF text extraction before this spec's hardware baseline can be pinned down.
  • The exact bridges-specific algorithm identifiers passed to `-a` in bridges_runner.cu (analogous to LCA's cuda-inlabel/cuda-naive) were not independently confirmed — test/bridges/prepare.py and run_experiments.sh were not read in this pass; needed to fill in bridges-kernel-repeated-mean's algorithms_under_test precisely.
  • Whether the bridges harness's own test/bridges generation pipeline uses the same size ladder as LCA's E1 experiment, or an independently chosen set of sizes, was not confirmed — this spec's recommended_subset for bridges-kernel-repeated-mean borrows the LCA ladder for cross-comparability rather than reproducing a confirmed paper choice.
maximal-independent-set1 papers2 variants

Single-node multi-GPU maximal independent set (MIS) computation on undirected graphs too large for one GPU's memory, measured as steady-state throughput (Mnodes/s, Medges/s) jointly with MIS cardinality (since MIS is not unique and a smaller/degenerate output would be a false win); graph load and untimed verification excluded from per-run time.

status[V] in {in, out} = MIS(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, CSR, undirected, binary CSR/.egr), num_gpus); a valid MIS satisfies: no two adjacent vertices are both 'in', and every 'out' vertex has at least one 'in' neighbor. A is unweighted; only connectivity matters.

mis-kernel-oversized-graph500steady-state multi-GPU MIS throughput on synthetic Graph500 R-MAT graphs sized to deliberately exceed a single GPU's memory (the exact regime MG-MIS targets); graph generation, dedup, and CSR construction excluded but reported separately (one-shot, not amortized)

Fairness notes
  • MIS is not a unique output — an implementation could trivially trade MIS quality (cardinality) for speed by using a weaker priority scheme. The paper's own abstract already discloses this tradeoff (-2.6% average size vs. baseline), which is good practice; this spec makes that disclosure MANDATORY in both variants rather than optional, per the project's requirement that approximate/heuristic problems report quality jointly with time, not as an afterthought.
  • The paper's own artifact keeps graph-load (prepTimer), MIS computation (runtime), and validity verification (verifyTimer) in three separate, non-overlapping timers in the source code itself — this spec's timing_scope/preprocessing_reported split is not an invention imposed on the paper; it directly mirrors what the paper's own code already does, made explicit and mandatory for submissions.
  • Because the README gives no concrete real-world named-graph list (unlike ECL-MM/graphB+ from the same lab in this survey batch), this spec anchors its size classes to the paper's own organizing variable — "exceeds one GPU's memory" — using Graph500 R-MAT rather than fabricating a named real-world suite the paper never specified. This keeps the spec's inputs traceable to something the paper actually said, rather than presenting an invented list as if it were confirmed.
Open questions
  • Whether the paper's own reported numbers (17.73x, 22.88x geomean) average multiple external repetitions of the binary or are single-shot per graph could not be confirmed from the README or the inspected portion of MG-MIS_10.cu (no outer repeat loop was visible around the main OpenMP parallel region in the excerpt read). This spec's reps: 5 / median-of-5 requirement is this benchmark's own addition for robustness, not a confirmed reproduction of the paper's exact statistic — flagged so a full source read (or contacting the authors) could tighten this before treating the variant as bit-for-bit paper-reproducing.
  • Exact real-world graph names/sizes used in the paper (if any beyond Graph500-generated instances) were not confirmed — the ICS25 PDF (linked from the README as userweb.cs.txstate.edu/~mb92/papers/ics25.pdf) was not machine-readable via the tools available for this survey; a follow-up with direct PDF text extraction should check Table/Figure captions for named SuiteSparse instances before finalizing whether a third "real-world graphs" variant should be added alongside the two Graph500-based variants here.
signed-graph-balancing1 papers2 variants

Parallel discovery and balancing of all fundamental cycles in a large signed graph (edges labeled +/-) via linear-time vertex/edge labeling, measured as fundamental-cycles-balanced-per-second, with the number of edges flipped reported as a solution-quality metric since the algorithm is a linear-time heuristic, not a proven-minimum edge-flip solver.

(labels[V], flipped_edges[E']) = graphB_plus(G=(V,E,sign: E -> {+,-}), iterations); builds a spanning tree, computes vertex/edge labels via path-compressed union-find, enumerates all |E|-|V|+1 fundamental cycles from non-tree edges, and flips the minimum-weight edge per imbalanced cycle so the whole graph becomes sign-balanced (every cycle has an even count of negative edges).

balancing-kernel-signed-snap-graphssteady-state balancing-phase throughput (spanning tree + labeling + cycle detection/traversal/flip) on the union of real signed-graph datasets used by this track's paper; CSV parsing/graph read excluded but reported separately (one-shot, not amortized)

A result that is fast but leaves any cycle unbalanced does not count, regardless of throughput. Edges-flipped count is reported as quality (heuristic minimality), never as part of the correctness gate itself, since graphB+ does not claim to find the provably minimum flip set.

Fairness notes
  • The algorithm's `iterations` CLI parameter (internal balancing rounds per invocation) is a quality/time knob that could otherwise be tuned per-graph to produce a favorable cycles/sec number on a run that barely reduces total flips, or an unfavorable one on a run that does much more useful work. Fixing it at 100 (the paper's own real-graph usage example) and requiring disclosure prevents silent tuning.
  • The abstract's single headline number (0.85s / 14M+ cycles/s on one 10M-vertex/22M-edge Amazon graph on a Titan V) is a single-point best-case claim; the spec requires the full recommended_subset (spanning three real orders of magnitude: ~100K-scale Wikipedia votes up to 10M-vertex Amazon composite) so a submission cannot report only the most favorable single instance.
  • Because the repo ships both GPU and CPU implementations of the IDENTICAL algorithm, balancing-gpu-vs-cpu-scaling is kept as a first-class variant specifically to prevent conflating "the algorithm is fast" with "GPUs are fast" — the two are separable here and the paper's own artifact makes that separation cheap to measure.
Open questions
  • The paper's PDF (freely hosted at userweb.cs.txstate.edu) could not be parsed as text with tools available in this environment (no pdftotext/PyPDF/pymupdf), so exact per-dataset vertex/edge counts and the paper's own reps/statistic convention beyond what the source code reveals could not be independently confirmed — the recommended_subset and protocol above are reconstructed from the repo's dataset-fetch script and CUDA source's own timer structure, not the paper's results tables directly.
  • Exact composition of the paper's headline "10 million vertices and 22 million edges" Amazon graph (which product categories were merged to reach that scale) was not confirmed; the spec asks submitters to disclose their own composition rather than assuming a specific one.
spectral-sparsification1 papers2 variants

Incremental spectral sparsification of a large undirected weighted graph: nearly-linear-time initial sparsifier construction followed by O(log N)-time per-edge-batch incremental updates, measured as time jointly with the relative condition number between original and sparsifier Laplacians, since sparsification quality and edge-count reduction are an inherent tradeoff with no single correct answer.

H_0 = Setup(G_0=(V,E_0,w): Laplacian L_{G_0}) via low-resistance- diameter (LRD) decomposition into node clusters, selecting a spectrally -critical edge subset; H_i = Update(H_{i-1}, Delta E_i (new weighted edges)) in O(log N) time per update using low-dimensional resistance embeddings to score edge importance/redundancy; output H_i is a sparse weighted graph (subgraph, not necessarily edge-subset of G) whose Laplacian spectrally approximates L_{G_i}.

sparsify-kernel-setup-suitesparsesteady-state one-shot setup-phase time (initial sparsifier construction from scratch) on the SuiteSparse Matrix Collection suite used by this track's paper; this is the common denominator any spectral sparsifier must support before incremental updates are possible

suiteSuiteSparse Matrix Collection (sparse.tamu.edu), symmetric positive-semidefinite Laplacian-derived instances

dense_operandN/A (sparse weighted Laplacian is the sole input)

reps5

recommended_subsetsame as sparsify-kernel-setup-suitesparse
dense_operandN/A

Fairness notes
  • Density and spectral fidelity (kappa) trade off directly — reporting only edge-count reduction (density) without kappa, or only kappa without density, makes results incomparable across implementations that pick different density targets. Both variants require both to be reported together, and correctness gates are defined at MATCHED density, not matched time, so a submission cannot win by simply sparsifying more aggressively.
  • The paper's central contribution is the incremental update path (O(log N) per update vs. full O(setup) re-sparsification) — a benchmark measuring only one-shot setup time would completely miss this claim. sparsify-incremental-updates is kept as an equally weighted, separately-reported variant specifically to prevent that.
  • The 10-update-cycle protocol requires reporting the full sequence (not just an average), since a method whose per-update time or quality drifts upward over the sequence (e.g. as the sparsifier accumulates edges and its clustering structure goes stale) would look artificially good if only cycle 1 or an average were reported.
Open questions
  • Exact edge-batch size and edge-selection scheme used in the paper's own 10-update-cycle experiments (random vs. degree-weighted vs. domain-specific, e.g. circuit-netlist-driven incremental edits) was not confirmed from the fetched HTML fulltext excerpt — the spec's edge_batch_spec requires disclosure rather than assuming a specific scheme.
  • Whether the paper reports kappa as global spectral condition number or a related per-cluster/local resistance-diameter bound at each of the 10 update points individually, versus only a single final-state number, was not fully disambiguated from the fetched excerpt.
vertex-cover1 papers2 variants

Exact GPU-parallel branch-and-bound search for Minimum Vertex Cover (MVC) and Parameterized Vertex Cover (PVC, cover size <= k) on small-to-medium undirected graphs, measured as search-tree wall time on a fixed mixed suite of adversarial and real-world instances, with exact-optimum correctness (this is an EXACT combinatorial problem, not an approximation) as the hard gate before any timing counts.

cover[V] subset of V = VertexCover(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, undirected), mode in {MVC, k}); output is a vertex subset S such that every edge has at least one endpoint in S; MVC minimizes |S|, PVC decides/returns S with |S| <= k for a given k. A is unweighted, undirected, simple (no self-loops/multi-edges after preprocessing).

vertex-cover-mvc-kernelsteady-state GPU search-tree wall time to find the EXACT minimum vertex cover on a fixed mixed suite of adversarial and real-world graphs; the search-tree exploration itself is the entire timed region (there is no separable "preprocessing" phase for this problem beyond CSR/adjacency-list construction, which is one-shot and reported separately)
inputs

correctnessEXACT problem, not approximate: returned |S| MUST equal the known-optimal MVC size recorded in the suite's ground truth (from the paper's own MVCS table, itself derived from exact external solvers), AND S must be a valid cover (every edge has >=1 endpoint in S, checked by brute-force edge scan). Any mismatch invalidates that run entirely — there is no partial credit / approximation ratio for this variant, since MVC-exact admits none.
vertex-cover-pvc-kernelsteady-state GPU search-tree wall time to DECIDE, for a given parameter k, whether a vertex cover of size <= k exists (and return one if so) — the parameterized decision variant, timed separately from MVC-search because PVC's early-termination behavior (it can stop as soon as ANY size-k cover is found, or prove none exists) gives it a qualitatively different time profile than exhaustive minimization
inputs
suitesame suite as vertex-cover-mvc-kernel
selectionsame 20 named instances; k values derived as MVCS[graph] + offset for a spread of offsets spanning both 'yes' (offset >= 0) and near-threshold 'no' (offset < 0, if provable within a bounded search) cases
recommended_subsetsame as vertex-cover-mvc-kernel
dense_operandN/A
k_offsetsREQUIRED disclosure of the exact offsets tested per instance (paper's own script parameterizes K as a list of offsets added to the known-optimal MVCS value); this spec recommends at minimum offset in {0, +5, +20} to characterize the yes-instance time profile as slack increases
protocol
formatsame as vertex-cover-mvc-kernel
warmup1
reps3
statisticmedian of 3, report min/max
timersame as vertex-cover-mvc-kernel
timing_scopesearch-tree traversal only, same exclusions as vertex-cover-mvc-kernel
preprocessing_reportedsame as vertex-cover-mvc-kernel (shared across MVC/PVC runs on the same graph — do not re-time construction per k value)
version_disclosureREQUIRED, same as vertex-cover-mvc-kernel
metric
primarysearch wall time in milliseconds (median of 3), reported as a function of k-offset (time-vs-slack curve)
secondarymin/max time; yes/no decision correctness
correctnessEXACT decision problem: for offset >= 0 (a size-k cover is known to exist since k >= optimal), the returned cover must have size <= k and be valid; for offset < 0 tests, a correct implementation must report non-existence (verified against the exact known-optimal size, not by exhaustive re-verification, since MVCS gives ground truth).
Fairness notes
  • MVC/PVC are EXACT combinatorial problems on this track's chosen instance suite (the paper deliberately ships known-optimal answers for every graph via its own MVCS table) — unlike most of the other singleton tracks in this batch, there is no approximation-ratio or quality-tradeoff axis here; correctness is a hard binary gate, and this spec treats it that way rather than inventing a soft quality metric that would not reflect how the paper itself evaluates.
  • The paper's own test driver (test/runGraphs.py) does not discard a warmup run — all 3 repeats become data rows. For the shorter DIMACS-hat instances (300-1000 vertices), first-call GPU context/JIT overhead can be a non-trivial fraction of total time; this spec adds an explicit discarded warmup run the paper's own script lacks, applying the same fairness discipline used across the rest of this survey batch (bfs, betweenness, etc.) rather than reproducing an omission.
  • The paper's own USE_COUNTERS=1 build is explicitly documented in the README as "won't run efficiently" — i.e. it is a profiling-only mode that perturbs the timing it would otherwise help explain. This spec keeps per-SM load-balance instrumentation (NODES_PER_SM/Counters) as optional supplementary output, never as part of the primary timed variant, matching the paper's own documented caveat rather than silently conflating a profiling build with a benchmark build.
Open questions
  • Whether the paper's own reported headline numbers used all 5 BLOCK_DIM values and reported the best, or fixed a single block_dim across all instances, was not confirmed beyond the grid-search structure visible in runGraphs.py; this spec requires disclosing the full sweep to avoid ambiguity either way.
  • The exact provenance/exact-solver used to produce the MVCS ground-truth table (external ILP solver? a specific PACE-challenge submission?) was not confirmed from the repo; flagged since the correctness gate for this entire track depends on trusting that table.
  • Whether HusseinAmro/component-aware-vertex-cover-gpu (a later, related repo referencing this paper's problem, arXiv:2512.18334) is an appropriate external baseline for this track, or a separate contribution that should get its own track later, was not resolved — left as a candidate baseline rather than folded into this spec's variants.

primitives

sequence-alignment6 papers4 variants

Pairwise dynamic-programming sequence alignment (Smith-Waterman local / Needleman-Wunsch global-semi-global, exact or X-drop-approximate), plus the two end-to-end genome-mapping pipelines (BWA-MEM-class short-read mapping, LASTZ-class whole-genome alignment) that use a pairwise-alignment kernel as one stage of a larger seed/index -> filter -> extend pipeline. The surveyed literature splits along two axes that cannot be collapsed into one variant: exact-optimal vs. deliberately-approximate (X-drop) scoring, and kernel-only DP throughput vs. end-to-end pipeline throughput with a one-shot index/table build.

H[i,j] = max( H[i-1,j-1] + sigma(q_i, s_j), E[i,j], F[i,j], nu ) — the standard SW/NW recurrence over query Q (length n) and subject S (length m), sigma a substitution function (simple match/mismatch or a matrix such as BLOSUM62), E/F the linear- or affine-gap auxiliary matrices; variants 3-4 wrap this kernel inside seed -> filter/index -> extend pipelines.

seqalign-exact-pairwise-kernelsteady-state kernel throughput for EXACT optimal pairwise alignment (Smith-Waterman local / Needleman-Wunsch global / semi-global), preprocessing excluded. The common denominator of AnySeq, MASA-CUDAlign/MultiBP, and the futhark-mem-sc22 `nw` benchmark — all three compute a provably optimal score (MultiBP's block pruning is lossless by construction, not an approximation).
inputs

selectionDNA long-sequence pairs: real GenBank accessions named in >=1 code-verified surveyed artifact, capped so the small/medium tiers stay single-GPU/CPU tractable (<=50 Mbp); large tier is explicitly optional (chromosome-scale, needs a multi-GPU node or cluster). Short-read batch: fixed count and length from AnySeq's own methodology (regenerate with Mason or an equivalent read simulator, same reference chromosome and read length — exact Mason version/seed not recoverable from the source, see open_questions). Protein tier: synthetic random sequences at the exact sizes futhark-mem-sc22 ships (`row_length` in its compiled-script header).

primaryGCUPS_nominal = n*m / time, using the FULL unpruned matrix dimensions n*m so pruned methods (MultiBP) remain comparable to unpruned ones (AnySeq)

For pruning methods, the pruned result must equal the unpruned reference's score on every held-out instance where the unpruned reference is still tractable — pruning that changes the returned score fails the gate outright (does not qualify for this variant; would need to move to the heuristic variant below with a relaxed correctness definition).

seqalign-e2e-short-read-mappingend-to-end short-read mapping pipeline throughput (one-shot index build + align a full real read set), correctness gated by BIT-EXACT output match to a named reference tool. FastAlign's own stated bar ("100% identical output to BWA-MEM").

selectionFastAlign's own paper-scale dataset could not be recovered from any accessible source (no arXiv/OA, repo README only shows a quick-test example) — this spec substitutes a standard, independently reproducible public dataset: a public 30x Illumina WGS run of a well-characterized reference sample (e.g. NA12878 or HG002 from GIAB), explicitly flagged as a substitution rather than a reproduction of the paper's own numbers (see open_questions). A cheap smoke-test tier reuses the repo's own quick-test example (E. coli GCA_000005845.2 reference + SRA SRR2584863 reads) — small enough to run in CI, but explicitly NOT a substitute for the human-scale tier when comparing throughput claims.

alignmentsingle full run over the complete read set (a "big job" benchmark — repeated full-dataset runs are prohibitively expensive for the human-scale tier); repeat >=2x and report both numbers if compute budget allows, otherwise explicitly flag the single-run limitation in the report rather than silently presenting one number as if it were a stable median.

Extra alignments beyond LASTZ's set are allowed and must be reported as a count/percentage, but do not by themselves fail the gate.
Fairness notes
  • Exact-vs-heuristic correctness cannot be collapsed into one tolerance rule: papers 1/4/5 (AnySeq, MultiBP, futhark-mem-sc22) are exact DP, paper 2 (LOGAN) is a deliberate approximation validated against another approximation, papers 3/6 (SegAlign, FastAlign) validate an end-to-end pipeline against a reference TOOL's output rather than a DP optimum at all. Variants above are split precisely along this boundary rather than forcing a single "correctness: <tolerance>" line to cover all six.
  • GCUPS is not a single well-defined number once pruning/banding enters the picture. This spec requires BOTH a nominal (full/unpruned matrix or band) and an effective (actually-computed cells) GCUPS wherever pruning or X-drop banding applies, and forbids reporting only the flattering one — none of MASA-CUDAlign/MultiBP, LOGAN, or their surrounding literature disambiguates this in the sources available for this survey.
  • Cost-normalized ($/hour) metrics, used by both end-to-end papers (SegAlign, FastAlign), are demoted to non-gating appendix data because cloud pricing drifts over time and a number priced in 2020 cannot be fairly compared to one priced in 2026 without re-pricing both to the same date — which this spec cannot guarantee a harness will do.
  • MASA-CUDAlign's own README aggregates "best results in different scenarios" across five hardware generations spanning 2010-2021 in a single table. Variant 1 explicitly forbids this by requiring GCUPS_ nominal to be reported for the SAME fixed hardware class across the whole recommended_subset, not a best-cell-per-row pick.
  • SegAlign itself selected "the instance type that gave LASTZ its best throughput among those tested" for its own CPU baseline — a legitimate choice for showing SegAlign in its best light, but not a fair standing baseline for a benchmark spec. Variant 4 fixes ONE named CPU baseline configuration instead.
  • No surveyed paper discloses a warmup/repetition/statistic protocol except AnySeq's unqualified "median." All four variants above therefore IMPOSE a protocol (1 discarded warmup, 5 reps, median + min/max) rather than inheriting silence from the literature as an implicit "single-run" default.
Open questions
  • LOGAN's exact substitution-matrix and gap-penalty values used in its own evaluation were not recoverable from the accessible fulltext (ar5iv); variant 2 substitutes AnySeq's disclosed DNA scheme for cross-variant consistency, which may not match what LOGAN itself actually used.
  • LOGAN's exact synthetic-dataset generator (tool + random seed) for the 100K read-pair benchmark is not stated in the accessible text; exact byte-for-byte reproduction of their dataset is not possible, only parameter-matched regeneration (length range, error rate).
  • MASA-CUDAlign/MultiBP's exact match/mismatch/gap-open/gap-extend values used in the TPDS'21 paper were not found in any accessible source (README or abstract); the MASA-Core command line supports configurable scoring but the paper's chosen values are unknown.
  • FastAlign's (PPoPP'26) actual paper-scale evaluation dataset (species, real read counts, depth) could not be recovered — the paper has no arXiv/OA copy and the ACM DOI page is paywalled/forthcoming as of this survey. Variant 3's human-scale tier is an explicit substitution, not a reproduction of the paper's own numbers; if/when the paper text becomes accessible this should be revisited.
  • futhark-mem-sc22's default `RUNS` repetition count (used by its `benchmarks/Makefile` when not overridden) and the exact statistic computed by `benchmarks/result-table.py` were not read in detail (file contents not fetched beyond the Makefile help text) — worth confirming before treating this paper's own numbers as directly comparable to the spec's imposed 5-rep/median protocol.
  • Whether GCUPS as reported by MASA-CUDAlign/MultiBP and by LOGAN is nominal (full n*m or full band) or effective (actually-computed cells) could not be determined from the accessible sources for either paper — flagged in notes_on_fairness as a required BOTH-numbers policy going forward, but the two papers' OWN published numbers cannot retroactively be classified into one bucket or the other from what was read.
  • Exact accession/download source for LOGAN's E. coli and C. elegans "real-data" alignment counts (1.8M and 235M alignments respectively) was not confirmed — the paper states the counts but not a directly fetchable dataset URL beyond the general BELLA pipeline reference.
  • BLOSUM62 ambiguity-code handling (N/X characters, etc.) in the protein-synthetic tier of variant 1 is unspecified by futhark-mem-sc22's reference implementation as read; assumed to only ever emit the 20 standard amino-acid symbols in its synthetic generator, not verified.
string-regex-matching5 papers3 variants

Multi-pattern regular-expression / finite-automata matching over a byte stream, measured as steady-state matching throughput in Gbps with automaton compilation/preprocessing strictly separated (and, where the literature's own contribution IS compilation, amortized over an explicit k), plus a distinct single-match latency variant for architectures (e.g. FPGA DSAs) that are not naturally described by a corpus-throughput number.

matches[] = MATCH(automaton A (NFA | DFA | custom ISA, compiled from a ruleset of R regular expressions), input stream S (bytes)); output is the set of (pattern_id, end_position) pairs where A accepts a prefix of S ending at that position (standard automata-processing semantics — this is NOT single-pattern substring search, it is simultaneous multi-pattern matching, the shape every paper in this track actually benchmarks).

regex-kernel-throughput-precompiledsteady-state matching throughput over a fixed input corpus with the automaton supplied ALREADY COMPILED (RE-to-automaton compilation excluded from the timed region but reported once, separately) — the common denominator matching how ngAP, GSpecPal, and 0002PJ20 all actually benchmark (automata ship pre-converted in their artifacts)
inputs
suiteunion of ANMLZoo + AutomataZoo + "Regex" (Becchi et al., regex.wustl.edu) for the NFA-family path, PLUS GSpecPal's independently-sourced Snort/ClamAV/PowerEN DFA-table corpus for the DFA-family path — these two corpora are NOT merged into one list since they are packaged and sized differently despite overlapping ruleset names (see survey.md Divergence 3)
selectionNFA-family: named benchmarks confirmed reused by >=2 of {ngAP, 0002PJ20, MFSA} in this track, i.e. those with an exact benchmark- name match across their respective config files/tables; DFA-family: all pattern sets GSpecPal ships (Snort, ClamAV, PowerEN), at a fixed, disclosed automaton-size point per ruleset (not the full 20-23-way size sweep, which is a separate axis — see regex-automaton-size-scaling notes below)
recommended_subsetPowerEN (ANMLZoo/Becchi, ~300 REs, 10MB input `poweren_10MB.input`) — shared by ngAP, MFSA (PEN), and 0002PJ20, Bro217 (Becchi 'Regex' suite, 217 REs, 10MB depth-biased trace) — shared by MFSA (BRO) and 0002PJ20, Snort (AutomataZoo, real wrccdc2012.pcap network trace) — shared by 0002PJ20 and (different packaging) GSpecPal, ClamAV (AutomataZoo, `clamav.input`) — shared by ngAP and 0002PJ20, Dotstar (ANMLZoo, `backdoor_10MB.input`) — used by ngAP; TCP-ext.homenet (ANMLZoo) used by MFSA as the analogous entry, CRISPR_CasOFFinder and CRISPR_CasOT (AutomataZoo, 10MB DNA inputs) — shared by ngAP and 0002PJ20, EntityResolution (AutomataZoo, `1m_names.input`) — shared by ngAP and 0002PJ20, GSpecPal-Snort (DFA-table corpus, one fixed size id e.g. snort_DFA12771, 10MB input), GSpecPal-ClamAV (DFA-table corpus, one fixed size id e.g. clamAV_DFA1501, 10MB input), GSpecPal-PowerEN (DFA-table corpus, one fixed size id, 10MB AND 20MB inputs — the only pattern set with 2 input sizes in GSpecPal's own suite)
automata_family_disclosureREQUIRED, free-text not a binary DFA/NFA enum: NFA (explicit table/bitset representation), DFA (explicit transition table), or other (e.g. a custom non-backtracking ISA a la Cicero) — every submission must state which, since throughput numbers across families are not apples-to-apples without this disclosure
dense_operandN/A
protocol

corpus_size_sweep1MB, 10MB, 20MB (matches MFSA's fixed 1MB, GSpecPal/ngAP's 10MB, and GSpecPal-PowerEN's additional 20MB conventions respectively; report all three where feasible rather than picking one)

reps10 (fixed floor for this spec, between MFSA's own two disclosed-but-inconsistent counts of 15 and 30 for execution-throughput and compilation-time respectively, and above GSpecPal's 3-run shell-level warmup)
statisticmedian, report min/max
timerdevice-side events (CUDA/HIP events) for GPU implementations; host-side wall clock (std::chrono or clock_gettime) for CPU/FPGA implementations, wrapping ONLY the matching pass
timing_scopematching only; automaton load/deserialization from disk, input- stream H2D transfer, and any format conversion are excluded from the timed region and reported separately, once, following GSpecPal's/ngAP's/0002PJ20's own shipped-pre-compiled convention
preprocessing_reportedseparately: automaton load/deserialization time, H2D transfer time (if applicable), one-shot per benchmark
metric
primaryGbps = corpus_size_bits / matching_time_seconds / 1e9 — the single canonical unit this spec fixes across the whole track; ngAP's MB/s must be reported alongside its Gbps-converted value (x8), not substituted for it
secondaryms (median matching time), plus native unit if the implementation's own convention differs (e.g. MFSA's fold-improvement-vs-M=1 must ALSO report the M=1 baseline's own absolute Gbps, never only the fold number)
correctnessexact match-position-list equality (pattern_id, end_position pairs) against an independent single-threaded CPU reference automaton simulation over the same input stream and automaton; a run whose match list differs from the reference in any position is invalidated and excluded from the statistic, following ngAP's and GSpecPal's own "Validation PASS!" / per-block pass-fail gating practice.
regex-e2e-compilation-amortizedend-to-end throughput including one-shot RE-to-automaton compilation (parsing, FSA construction, any merging/optimization), amortized over k matching passes — for tracks where compilation IS the paper's contribution (MFSA's automata-merging, Cicero's MLIR compiler pipeline), following MFSA's own excellent practice of reporting compilation time as a detailed, separately-visible stage breakdown rather than folding it silently into a blended number
inputs
