recommended_subsetBro217 (217 REs), PowerEN (300 REs), Protomata (300 REs), Ranges1 (299 REs), TCP-ext.homenet (300 REs), Dotstar09 (299 REs)
dense_operandN/A

compilation_stage_breakdown_requiredREQUIRED: report front-end (lex/parse), automaton-construction (RE-to-FSA), single-automaton optimization, and any cross-automaton merging/optimization as INDEPENDENT numbers, not one blended "compile time" — following MFSA's own 4-stage breakdown (front-end 1.29ms, AST-to-FSA 1.33ms, single-FSA-opt 2.03ms, merging up to 6.65s at M=all, all averaged over 30 runs)
warmup1 (full compile+match pipeline pass, discarded)

statisticmean of the above rep counts (matches MFSA's own choice); report min/max alongside, which MFSA itself does not
timerhost-side wall clock around each compilation stage independently; same timer as regex-kernel-throughput-precompiled around the matching pass
timing_scopecompilation time and matching time are ALWAYS reported as two separate numbers, even though this variant's headline metric amortizes them together — never report only the blended number
preprocessing_reportedcompilation IS this variant's subject; reported both as the standalone per-stage breakdown AND folded into the amortized headline metric below
amortization_count_requiredTrue
metric
primaryamortized_Gbps = corpus_size_bits * k / (compilation_time_seconds + k * matching_time_seconds) / 1e9, where k is the number of matching passes the compiled automaton is reused for before being discarded/recompiled; k MUST be explicitly reported (not left implicit) — report at k=1 (worst case, compile-once-use-once) and at k=1000 (amortized-heavy-reuse case) as two bracketing points
secondarycompilation_time_ms broken down by stage (standalone, per the required breakdown above), kernel-only_median_Gbps (cross-reference to regex-kernel-throughput-precompiled on the same benchmark, to make the amortization argument checkable), compression_ratio (states_before / states_after, if the compiler performs automaton merging/optimization — matches MFSA's own 71.95%-states / 38.88%-transitions reduction figures)
correctnesssame match-position-list equality gate as regex-kernel-throughput-precompiled, applied after compilation; additionally, for any automaton-merging/optimization technique, a formal-or-empirical check that the compiled automaton accepts EXACTLY the union of the source REs' languages (no false-positive cross-pattern matches introduced by merging) is REQUIRED before throughput counts — following MFSA's own activation-function correctness discipline.
regex-single-match-latencyper-match latency and energy for a single regular expression against a bounded input, for architectures (FPGA DSAs, or any design not naturally described by a streaming-corpus-throughput number) whose own claimed contribution is latency/energy per operation rather than aggregate bytes/second — follows Cicero's own metric framing rather than forcing an artificial Gbps conversion onto a design that was never built for streaming-corpus throughput
inputs

selectionsingle REs (not full rulesets) exercised one at a time, each against a bounded input window sized to the implementation's natural operating point (e.g. Cicero's sliding-window architecture) rather than a multi-megabyte streaming corpus
recommended_subsetsame named rulesets as regex-kernel-throughput-precompiled, but evaluated RE-by-RE rather than as a merged ruleset

timerhighest-resolution timer available on the platform (e.g. on-chip cycle counter for FPGA/ASIC designs, device-side events for GPU, std::chrono for CPU), wrapping only the single-match operation

metric

Fairness notes
  • Automata family (DFA vs NFA vs non-classical custom ISA) is a first-class, REQUIRED disclosure field in every variant, not an afterthought — GSpecPal (DFA) is the only paper in this track using a classical DFA table, ngAP/0002PJ20/MFSA are all NFA-lineage (with confirmed shared code ancestry: 0002PJ20 defines GPU-NFA, ngAP reuses it verbatim as a baseline, MFSA extends the same iNFAnt algorithm 0002PJ20 also reimplements), and Cicero is neither. A benchmark that silently pooled DFA and NFA throughput numbers together would compare fundamentally different memory-access and parallelism profiles as if they were the same kernel.
  • Throughput UNIT is fixed to Gbps across the whole track specifically because the 5 source papers use 4 different, non-interchangeable unit families (ngAP's MB/s, MFSA's RE-count-weighted relative fold- improvement, GSpecPal's raw unreported elapsed seconds, Cicero's per-match microseconds+energy). Every variant requires the Gbps conversion to be computed and reported even when an implementation's own natural unit differs, specifically so results from different papers' artifacts become comparable for the first time.
  • Compilation/preprocessing cost is either a first-class contribution (MFSA, Cicero) or entirely shipped-pre-compiled-and-excluded (ngAP, GSpecPal, 0002PJ20) — never something silently amortized without disclosure in this track's own literature. The spec's split into regex-kernel-throughput-precompiled (compilation given, excluded) vs regex-e2e-compilation-amortized (compilation IS the subject, k disclosed) mirrors this real, paper-driven split rather than forcing one universal preprocessing policy.
  • MFSA's own inconsistency — 30 repetitions for compilation-time measurement but 15 for execution-time measurement, within the SAME paper — is preserved deliberately in regex-e2e-compilation-amortized's reps_compilation/reps_matching split rather than smoothed over, since it reflects a real methodological choice (compilation is cheaper and noisier per-call, hence more reps) worth keeping visible; the kernel-only variant instead fixes ONE count (10) since it has no compilation/matching split to preserve.
  • GSpecPal's two-level warmup (3 discarded shell-level runs on a FIXED automaton, plus an in-kernel warmup phase separately timed and reported) is the most rigorous warmup practice found in this track's artifacts and is adopted as the floor for regex-kernel-throughput- precompiled, rather than the weaker or undisclosed practices of the other 4 papers.
  • Correctness validation (exact match-position-list equality against an independent reference) is made mandatory in every variant even though 2 of 5 papers' reachable sources do not document one (Cicero, 0002PJ20) — following the two papers that DO (ngAP's "Validation PASS!" gate, GSpecPal's per-block CPU cross-check), on the principle that automata processing has no continuous-error-tolerance concept: a match list is either exactly right or it is a bug, the same reasoning applied to the BFS track's validation-level gate.
Open questions
  • 0002PJ20's and GSpecPal's exact paper-reported throughput units could not be confirmed from reachable sources (0002PJ20's "Table 3" script header wasn't inspected in enough detail; GSpecPal's reachable driver code prints only raw seconds, with no throughput normalization visible at all — the true unit, if any, may live in unreached post-processing scripts). The spec's canonical Gbps conversion should be cross-checked against these papers' own published tables once fulltext becomes reachable, rather than assumed correct from the artifact code alone.
  • Cicero's full paper fulltext (ACM DL, paywalled) was not reached; it is not confirmed whether the paper reports ANY aggregate corpus-throughput number that would make regex-kernel-throughput-precompiled directly applicable to Cicero, or whether per-match latency truly is its only reported performance framing as the AE.md checklist alone suggests.
  • ngAP's exact per-configuration repetition count and warmup protocol (in `launch_exps.py` / `exec_config_*` files, not inspected) were not confirmed; this spec's reps=10 floor for regex-kernel-throughput- precompiled is this spec's own choice, not derived from ngAP's actual practice.
  • The relationship between GSpecPal's numeric per-ruleset DFA-size identifiers (e.g. clamAV_DFA1104 through clamAV_DFA2042) and a human-meaningful automaton-size quantity (state count? source-pattern count?) is unconfirmed; regex-kernel-throughput-precompiled's DFA-family recommended_subset picks one arbitrary size id per ruleset pending this clarification, and a dedicated automaton-size-scaling variant (sweeping all 20-23 sizes GSpecPal ships per ruleset) is left as a natural future extension once the size semantics are confirmed.
  • Whether MFSA's paper reports any absolute (non-fold-relative) Gbps/MB/s throughput number anywhere beyond the extracted evaluation section is not fully confirmed; regex-e2e-compilation-amortized's requirement to report the M=1 baseline's own absolute Gbps is this spec's own reconstruction from Eq. 11's definition, not a number directly quoted from the paper.
hash-table3 papers3 variants

Concurrent/parallel hash-table performance under three distinct workload families found in this track's literature (bulk build-probe join, bulk counting/upsert, general dynamic CRUD), measured as operations per second at controlled load factor and key distribution, with memory overhead reported as a function of load factor rather than left implicit.

table[K] -> V; open-addressing (linear probing) or equivalent collision scheme; K, V fixed-width (integer or fixed-length byte string) unless a variant states otherwise; concurrent multi-threaded or single-GPU-kernel access as specified per variant.

Fairness notes
  • The track's three papers benchmark three non-interchangeable operation profiles (build-then-probe with no delete; upsert-only with no plain read; full CRUD) — collapsing them into one "op-mix ratio" parameter would misrepresent two of the three papers' actual workloads, so the spec keeps them as separate variants rather than one parameterized variant with an op-mix knob.
  • Load factor is swept and reported by only 1 of 3 papers (Clevel-Hashing) despite being cheap to measure and central to every hash-table design's memory/throughput tradeoff; the other two either fix it silently (ShovonGMK23: 0.4, undisclosed as a design choice in the paper text, only recoverable from the artifact's `main()`) or never compute it at all despite having the numbers to do so (DEDUKT). All three spec variants make a load-factor sweep mandatory, following Clevel-Hashing's 10K-insertion-interval sampling protocol.
  • Only Clevel-Hashing names a repeated-trial statistic (mean of 5 runs). ShovonGMK23's own reproducibility table shows single-run numbers diverging from its paper's published numbers by 10-60%+ on several datasets with no explanation offered — direct evidence that single-run GPU timing is unreliable for this class of kernel. The spec fixes 5 repetitions with median+min/max as the floor across all three variants, using Clevel-Hashing's repetition count since it is the only precedent, but reporting median (not the surveyed paper's mean) to reduce sensitivity to the kind of outlier runs ShovonGMK23's own numbers suggest are common.
  • Memory overhead is never reported as an absolute quantity by any of the three papers; Clevel-Hashing's load-factor curve is the closest proxy (memory overhead ∝ 1/load_factor - 1) and is adopted directly as the spec's memory-overhead definition, computed at each swept load-factor point in every variant, rather than left as a design detail invisible to the benchmark.
  • Key distribution is asserted but not shown for the uniform case in Clevel-Hashing ("results using uniformly distributed workloads are similar... but not shown"), and neither ShovonGMK23 nor DEDUKT runs a synthetic distribution at all despite DEDUKT explicitly measuring the downstream *effect* of its real data's skew (load-imbalance ratio). The spec requires both uniform and Zipfian(0.99) synthetic key sets in every variant that supports synthetic keys, specifically to test Clevel-Hashing's own unshown claim rather than assume it generalizes.
  • ShovonGMK23's build-only "Hashtable rate" and DEDUKT's counting-kernel- only "Gk-mers/s" (Fig. 9, explicitly excluding the exchange module) are both good practice — isolating the hash table's own cost from surrounding pipeline phases — and are adopted as the model for every variant's `timing_scope`/`preprocessing_reported` split, in contrast to the headline pipeline-speedup numbers both papers ALSO report, which must never be confused with the kernel-only numbers.
Open questions
  • DEDUKT's effective per-table load factor across its 6 datasets and varying node/GPU counts was never computed by the paper itself; this spec's load-factor-sweep protocol for hash-table-counting-upsert REPLACES DEDUKT's fixed undisclosed-ratio capacity constant with an explicit swept target, so results under this spec are not directly comparable to DEDUKT's own published numbers without also re-deriving what load factor DEDUKT's fixed constant implied for each dataset (roughly 2%-53% by back-of-envelope calculation from Table III, not independently confirmed).
  • It is not confirmed whether ShovonGMK23's in-paper published TC-pipeline numbers used the same load_factor=0.4 default found in the artifact's `tc_cuda.cu main()`, since the hash table there is rebuilt fresh (with a `load_factor` argument) on every one of up to 606 fixed-point iterations and only the top-level default was inspected, not every call site.
  • Clevel-Hashing's assertion that uniform-key results are "similar" to its reported Zipfian(0.99) results has no supporting numbers in the reachable fulltext; this spec's requirement to run both distributions (rather than only Zipfian, as the surveyed paper effectively does) is designed to test this claim for the specific implementations under benchmark, not to assume it holds in general.
  • No paper in this track runs its hash table on both a GPU and a CPU+persistent-memory platform, so the spec cannot fix one hardware baseline across all three variants; hash-table-build-probe-kernel and hash-table-counting-upsert default to GPU (matching their two source papers), hash-table-crud-mixed-ops defaults to CPU+PM-or-DRAM (matching Clevel-Hashing) — a genuinely cross-platform comparison would require new measurement infrastructure beyond what any surveyed paper attempts.
scan-reduction3 papers3 variants

Associative(-commutative) reduction of n input values, measured three ways this track's literature actually benchmarks: a flat reduction to one scalar (steady-state, memory-bound GB/s vs. achievable HBM bandwidth); a segmented/keyed reduction into H << n output bins (generalized histogram, H swept independently of n); and a cascaded/fused reduction whose running accumulator feeds a downstream consumer op inside one kernel launch (online-softmax-then-GEMM). No surveyed paper implements a literal Blelloch/Hillis-Steele all-prefixes scan; this gap is disclosed rather than papered over (see open_questions).

flat: out = reduce(op, A[n]) -> scalar. segmented: out[H] = reduce_by_key(op, A[n], key[n] in [0,H)) -> H scalars. fused: running_max[n]/running_sum[n] via an online recurrence over A[n], consumed by a downstream GEMM within the same kernel launch (no intermediate HBM round-trip for the reduction's own output).

scan-reduction-flat-kernelsteady-state throughput of a flat sum-reduction over a single GPU-resident array to one scalar output, single isolated call — Navarro's own benchmark shape, the only variant with a well-defined memory-traffic lower bound (read n elements once, write 1).

Two distributions: Normal (mean=0, var=1) and Uniform(0,1) (Navarro's own two, adopted verbatim).

ADDITIONALLY (a fix vs. all three surveyed papers, none of which reports this): run-to-run bit-identity is checked by repeating the SAME algorithm on the SAME input across all `reps` calls and confirming the output bit pattern is IDENTICAL every time; a non-deterministic algorithm (varying accumulation order across launches, e.g. from scheduling-dependent atomics) must be flagged as such rather than silently passing a tolerance-only check.

Genuinely a different kernel from scan-reduction-flat-kernel (contention profile and race-resolution strategy both depend on H, not on n alone).

scan-reduction-fused-cascadeda running/online reduction (running-max, running-sum recurrence across sequential input tiles — the structurally scan-like part of this operation) fused with a downstream consumer op (GEMM) inside one kernel launch, so the reduction's own intermediate output never round-trips through HBM — RedFuser's own benchmark shape (safe softmax -> GEMM, the attention/MoE-routing pattern). Measured as end-to-end latency/speedup vs. an unfused baseline, not raw reduction GB/s, since the claim is specifically about eliminating a round-trip, not about one kernel's isolated bandwidth.
inputs

MoE routing shape: gate logits [tokens=4096, experts in {4096, 8, 64}], fp16, top-k in {2, 8} (the repo's own codegen-example default is experts=4096, k=8; smaller expert counts added since production MoE routing typically has far fewer experts than 4096 and neither this paper's reachable text nor its example scripts confirm the real evaluation-table shapes, appendix-gated — see open_questions).
recommended_subsetflash-attention seq_len=2048 + MoE-routing experts=64,k=8 (both fp16/fp32-accum)
dense_operandfp16 compute / fp32 accumulate (code-confirmed default in both example shapes)
protocol
formatraw dense tensors, no preprocessing
warmup20
reps100
statisticmedian (report min/max/stdev alongside)
timerdevice-side events (CUDA events or equivalent)
timing_scopekernel-only, END-TO-END across the fused op (score computation + online softmax reduction + downstream GEMM in one launch) vs. the SAME computation as separate unfused kernels (naive PyTorch-eager-style: separate softmax kernel writing its output to HBM, then a separate GEMM kernel reading it back) — both timed under the identical protocol so the comparison isolates the fusion's HBM round-trip savings, not a warmup/rep-count mismatch (a fix vs. the source paper, whose own timing protocol could not be located at all in the reachable text/code — see open_questions).
preprocessing_reportedn/a
precisionfp16/fp32-accum primary; fp8-quantized secondary (paper's own case study, exact tolerance not locatable — see open_questions)
metric
primaryspeedup = unfused_baseline_time / fused_time
secondaryms (median, fused and unfused each reported separately, not just the ratio)
correctnessrelative error of the fused kernel's final output vs. the unfused reference computation (same precision, same op order as far as possible) < 1e-3 for fp16/fp32-accum (looser than the flat/segmented variants' fp32 tolerance, matching standard flash-attention-family practice for fp16 compute) — PLUS the same run-to-run bit-identity check as the other two variants, since the fused kernel's online/blockwise rescaling changes accumulation order relative to a single-pass reference by construction, making it a prime candidate for the kind of non-determinism this spec is designed to surface rather than hide.
Fairness notes
  • None of the three surveyed papers reports whether repeated runs of their OWN technique on the SAME input produce bit-identical output. Floating-point addition is non-associative, and all three techniques change accumulation order relative to a naive reference (tensor-core MMA reduction order, atomic race-resolution ordering, online/blockwise softmax rescaling) — this spec makes a run-to-run bit-identity check a REQUIRED reported field in all three variants' correctness sections, not an afterthought.
  • Navarro's own artifact documents a genuine baseline FAILURE (FP16 CUB overflowing on the Uniform-distribution correctness test) rather than silently omitting that data point. This spec's correctness section treats such a failure as a reportable result (the baseline fails this variant's gate), not as a reason to drop the config from the sweep.
  • Henriksen's released `genhisto` microbenchmark tests only an associative integer-count operator, even though the paper's own text claims support for "arbitrary associative and commutative operators" (which would include floating-point sums, where the associativity claim is only approximately true in finite precision). This spec adds an fp32 sum-histogram as an explicit secondary correctness case specifically to close this untested gap, rather than assuming the integer case generalizes.
  • RedFuser's own timing protocol (warmup, repetitions, timer identity) could not be located anywhere in the reachable paper text or repository code — the weakest-verified paper across both tracks in this delivery. Rather than guessing a protocol and attributing it to the paper, this spec applies the project's standing warmup=20/reps=100 convention uniformly and flags in open_questions that RedFuser's own practice remains unconfirmed.
  • No surveyed paper reports GB/s for a cascaded/fused kernel (RedFuser reports only latency/speedup, despite its operation being structurally memory-bound). This spec keeps speedup as the PRIMARY metric for scan-reduction-fused-cascaded specifically because the claim under test (round-trip elimination) is better captured by a fused-vs-unfused comparison than by an isolated bandwidth number, while still requiring both raw times (not just the ratio) to be reported.
Open questions
  • No paper in this 3-paper input set implements a literal Blelloch/Hillis-Steele all-prefixes scan (an output array of n partial sums, inclusive or exclusive). The three variants above are grounded in what these three papers actually measure (flat reduction, segmented reduction, fused/online reduction) rather than inventing an ungrounded fourth variant. A dedicated scan-array variant is a candidate future extension if a literal-scan paper is added to this track's input set.
  • RedFuser's Appendix A.5 (which the paper's own main text points to for exact benchmark shapes/configs) was not reachable through either arxiv.org/html or the equivalent fulltext-rendering path used for this survey; `scan-reduction-fused-cascaded`'s recommended shapes are therefore a mix of the repo's own codegen-example defaults (flash-attention: q/k/v=[128,16,512,64]; MoE routing: A=[4096,4096], k=8) and this spec's own extrapolation to smaller/more-realistic expert counts, NOT independently confirmed against the paper's actual evaluation table.
  • RedFuser's timing protocol (warmup count, repetition count, timer identity, correctness tolerance) could not be located in the reachable paper text or repository code at all — flagged rather than guessed; see notes_on_fairness.
  • Whether a float-sum generalized histogram (as opposed to the integer-count case Henriksen's own released artifact actually tests) remains fast under the paper's race-resolution strategies, and whether it is run-to-run deterministic, is untested by any surveyed paper. `scan-reduction-segmented-histogram`'s fp32 secondary case is this spec's attempt to close that gap, but has no paper-reported numbers to validate against.
topk-selection3 papers3 variants

Selecting the k largest elements from a set of n candidates, returned as (value, index) pairs; measured as steady-state exact-selection kernel throughput on a GPU-resident array (the shape this track's most systematically-benchmarked paper actually tests), plus two approximate-search variants — recall-gated ANN top-k over a billion-scale index, and ranking-quality-gated top-k under reduced-precision score computation — that this track's literature treats as genuinely different claims with different correctness models, not size variants of the same benchmark.

topk(scores[n], k) -> (values[k], indices[k]), values sorted descending

topk-array-kernel-exactexact top-k of a single GPU-resident array, steady-state kernel throughput, single isolated call. The only variant in this track with a mathematically well-defined single "correct" answer (up to tie ordering) — matches AIR Top-K/GridSelect's own benchmark shape, the most systematically-swept paper in this track.
inputs
suitesynthetic, generated on-device per call (curand)
selectionn (array length) swept as powers of two from 2^15 to 2^30 (32,768 to ~1.07B elements); k swept two ways per n: (a) a small-k regime k in {1, 10, 32, 100, 1000} matching realistic ML/DB top-k usage (beam search, MoE routing, sparse-attention top-k, DB TOP-N queries), and (b) a k-as-fraction-of-n sweep, k/n in {2^-12, 2^-8, 2^-4, 2^-2} (k roughly 8..2^28 at the largest n), always enforcing k < n. batch_size in {1, 32, 256} (single-query vs. batched-query regimes; AIR Top-K's own sweep uses {1, 100}).
recommended_subsetn in {2^20 (~1M, fits L2), 2^24 (~16M, exceeds L2, HBM-resident), 2^28 (~268M, large-HBM-resident)} x k in {10, 1000, n/100} x batch_size in {1, 256} x all 3 distributions below = 54 configs, a tractable subset of the full sweep for routine re-runs; the full n-power x k-power sweep is the reference for headline claims.
dense_operandinput array: fp32, one of three distributions selectable at generation time (AIR Top-K's own three, adopted verbatim): (1) Uniform(0,1] via curandGenerateUniform; (2) Normal(mean=0,stddev=1) via curandGenerateNormal; (3) "Unfriendly"/adversarial: all but the low 12 bits of each float's IEEE-754 bit pattern fixed to a common high-bit prefix (masks entropy a radix-select pass would normally prune on) — REQUIRED, not optional, since it is the only distribution in this track's literature documented to change which algorithm wins.
protocol
formatraw unsorted array; no preprocessing/format-conversion step exists for this kernel class
warmup20
reps100
statisticmedian (report min/max/stdev alongside)
timerdevice-side events (CUDA events or equivalent)
timing_scopekernel only; each of the `reps` timed calls uses freshly-generated random data (not the same buffer replayed), matching AIR Top-K's own practice, to avoid caching artifacts; H2D/D2H excluded (data generated device-resident).
preprocessing_reportedn/a — no preprocessing step in this kernel class
metric
primarymedian time (ms) per call, reported per (n, k, batch_size, distribution) point
secondaryelements/sec = batch_size*n/time, for cross-n comparability
correctnesssorted top-k value multiset must exactly match (bit-exact for fp32, no tolerance — the reference is computed from the SAME input array, so no rounding-order ambiguity exists) an independently-computed CPU ground truth (full sort or nth_element); every returned index must be < n and must map back to its claimed value in the input array; no duplicate indices in the returned k-set. Checked on EVERY timed repetition, not just the last (a fix vs. AIR Top-K's own practice of checking only the final iteration to save time) — required because the input changes every iteration in this spec (fresh random data per call), so a bug that only manifests on some distributions would be invisible under an only-check-once protocol.
topk-e2e-ann-approxend-to-end approximate-nearest-neighbor top-k query: coarse-quantizer (IVF) search + per-partition candidate scoring + top-k merge across partitions, over a billion-scale real embedding index — UpANNS's own benchmark shape, and the only variant where "n" means total DATASET size rather than a single call's candidate-set size.
inputs
suiteSIFT1B, DEEP1B, SPACEV1B (real embedding datasets: 128-dim, 96-dim, 100-dim respectively)
selectionall three, since each is used by exactly one branch of the only surveyed artifact and none is redundant with another (different dimensionality, different source domain).
recommended_subsetSIFT1M (1e6, quick smoke test) and SIFT1B (1e9, headline claim) at minimum; DEEP1B and SPACEV1B for the full reference sweep.
dense_operandquery set: the dataset's own held-out query file (10,000 queries for SIFT1B, standard ann-benchmarks convention); k in {1, 10, 100}; nprobe (search-width knob) in {32, 64, 128, 256}; batch_size (queries per search call) in {1, 10, 100, 1000}.
protocol
formatIVF-PQ index (product-quantized, KSUB=256 codebook rows), built ONCE offline (training + population, `train_*.cpp`/`demo_*.cpp`'s add step) — this one-shot index-build cost is measured and reported separately (see preprocessing_reported), never folded into per-query time.
warmup5
reps20 REPEATED runs of the SAME query batch — a fix vs. UpANNS's own practice of running the batch exactly once with no repeated-trial statistic at all.
statisticmedian (report min/max/stdev alongside)
timerwall-clock (std::chrono or gettimeofday), one bracket per named phase
timing_scopeper-phase breakdown REQUIRED (matching UpANNS's own instrumentation, made mandatory rather than incidental): coarse-quantizer search, data transfer to accelerator, on-accelerator search, result transfer back, host-side merge/sort. Total end-to-end query time is the sum; index build/train/add is excluded from this number.
preprocessing_reportedindex build (train + populate) wall time reported separately, once, per dataset — NOT amortized into per-query time, since it is a one-shot cost paid once per dataset regardless of query volume (unlike a per-call format conversion).

metric
primaryQPS (queries/sec) at each recall@k operating point (a recall-QPS curve across the nprobe sweep, not a single number)

correctnessRecall@k (k in {1,10,100}) against an exact brute-force nearest-neighbor ground truth, computed once per dataset and shipped/cached. Recall is not gated pass/fail before timing counts (recall IS the accuracy metric here, unlike the other two variants' hard correctness gates) — but a technique's QPS number is INVALID to report standalone without its recall at the SAME nprobe operating point (fixes UpANNS's own practice, and the wider ANN-benchmarking literature's common practice, of quoting a headline QPS number without pinning the recall it was measured at).
topk-approx-precisionapproximate top-k over per-query similarity scores computed under REDUCED-PRECISION fixed-point arithmetic (the scores themselves are approximate, not just the search coverage) — Top-K SpMV's own benchmark shape, distinct from topk-e2e-ann-approx because the approximation source is numerical precision of the score computation, not index/search-space coverage, and distinct from topk-array-kernel-exact because correctness is a ranking-quality metric, not exact value-set equality.

dense_operandK fixed at 100 (matches the only surveyed paper's own choice)

warmup10
reps30
statisticmedian (report min/max/stdev alongside)
timerdevice/accelerator-side event or on-board invocation counter

preprocessing_reportedpacket-wise CSR compression + precision quantization, once, separately
precision20-bit (Q1.19), 25-bit (Q1.24), 32-bit fixed (Q1.31), 32-bit float — all four reported side by side, not just the fastest
metric

secondaryGB/s attained vs. peak HBM bandwidth (roofline-style)
correctnessranking-quality metrics vs. an exact fp64 CPU reference — Precision@k, Kendall's tau, NDCG@k — REQUIRED to pass a minimum threshold (NDCG@100 >= 0.95) before a precision configuration's speed number counts as reportable (a fairness FIX: the source paper plots quality and speed as separate curves without gating one on the other, which lets a reader quote a low-bit config's raw speed without its accuracy caveat attached).
Fairness notes
  • AIR Top-K/GridSelect checks correctness only on the LAST of 100 timed iterations (each of which uses freshly-generated random data) to save time. Since a correctness bug could be data-dependent and the data changes every iteration, this spec requires checking every repetition, not just the last.
  • UpANNS's public artifact runs its entire query-batch benchmark exactly ONCE per configuration — no warmup, no repeated trial, no statistic beyond a single wall-clock number per phase. This is the weakest timing protocol of any paper surveyed across this project's topk-selection AND spmv tracks combined. The spec fixes reps=20 for the ANN variant specifically because UpANNS's per-query time is dominated by network/PIM-transfer latency (not a cheap microsecond-scale kernel), so 20 reps of a whole query batch is tractable without the multi-hour cost concerns that apply to, e.g., AlphaSparse's format-search in the SpMV track.
  • Top-K SpMV plots ranking-quality (Kendall's tau/NDCG) and speed as independent curves with no stated pass/fail threshold connecting them — a reader can cite the paper's fastest (lowest-bit) configuration's speed without also citing its (potentially much worse) ranking quality. This spec adds a mandatory NDCG@100 >= 0.95 gate before a precision configuration's speed number is reportable at all.
  • No surveyed paper reports a QPS number explicitly pinned to a recall operating point in its headline claim (UpANNS's abstract states "4.3x QPS vs Faiss" without stating at what recall). This spec requires every topk-e2e-ann-approx QPS number to carry its recall@k alongside it, never standalone.
Open questions
  • A value-only (no-index) output mode is not benchmarked by any surveyed paper — all three return (value, index) pairs since the index is the actually-useful output in every real use case here. Whether a value-only variant would show meaningfully different performance (e.g. enabling algorithmic shortcuts that skip index bookkeeping) is left as an untested extension.
  • The three variants' "n" axes are not directly comparable (single-array size vs. per-row candidate count vs. total dataset size behind an index) — see survey.md's Divergences. A unified cross-variant normalization (e.g. "effective candidates examined per top-k call") was considered but not adopted, since it would require assumptions about IVF partition-selectivity and per-row nnz that neither UpANNS nor Top-K SpMV's artifacts expose cleanly enough to compute reliably.
  • Top-K SpMV's exact host<->FPGA DMA inclusion could not be confirmed from the reviewed harness (the same open question already flagged in the spmv track's survey for this paper) — `topk-approx-precision`'s "reported separately" requirement is a specification choice to force clarity going forward, not a confirmed fact about the paper's own number.
  • UpANNS's PIM (Processing-in-Memory / UPMEM DPU) hardware is not reproducible on commodity GPU/CPU hardware — the `topk-e2e-ann-approx` variant's protocol is designed to be hardware-agnostic (any accelerator implementing the same IVF-PQ pipeline), but re-running UpANNS's OWN numbers specifically requires UPMEM DPU access (7 PIM boards, 128GB, per the paper's abstract), which most benchmarking setups will not have.
dp-dynamic-programming1 papers2 variants

All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) on large sparse graphs via a hybrid dynamic program: dense Floyd-Warshall recurrence tiled within METIS-partitioned subgraphs, combined with global Dijkstra (SSSP) sweeps across subgraph boundaries, run distributed across multiple MPI ranks / GPUs, to avoid the all-to-all communication a naive blocked-Floyd-Warshall APSP requires.

Given a graph G=(V,E) (weighted or unweighted, directed or undirected), compute shortest-path distance (and predecessor) between every pair of vertices: d(k)[i][j] = min(d(k-1)[i][j], d(k-1)[i][k] + d(k-1)[k][j]) applied locally per METIS partition, reconciled globally via per-boundary-vertex Dijkstra sweeps across the k=1..|V| recurrence.

dp-apsp-partition-count-sweepsteady-state solve throughput as a function of graph size and METIS partition count K, one-shot METIS partitioning + sparse-format load excluded from solve time and reported separately, since preprocessing cost (partitioning) does not amortize the same way across problem sizes and the paper's own contribution is specifically about avoiding per-partition global communication at solve time.
inputs

namehugebubbles-00020, hugetrace-00020
noteSuiteSparse large planar-mesh graphs, |V| >10M, approaching the paper's own 11.5M-vertex headline scale
partition_countK in {8, 32, 128, 512} (METIS -k; the artifact's own README example uses K=128, the SLURM script uses K=8), swept independently of graph size to isolate the paper's partitioning-communication tradeoff

reps5

timerwall-clock (std::chrono or MPI_Wtime) wrapping the solve call only, e.g. G.solve() / G.solveSubGraph(); NOT recovered from the artifact's own source (fap.cpp contains no timing instrumentation) -- this protocol is this survey's own specification, not the artifact's confirmed default. See open_questions.

correctnessMANDATORY pre-timing gate, matching the artifact's own confirmed mechanism (fap/utils/checkResult.h): for each solved subgraph, sample 20 source vertices and, for each, 10 random destination vertices (200 pairs total); recompute the true shortest distance via a reference Dijkstra implementation and require exact match (unweighted graphs: integer hop-count equality; weighted graphs: floating-point distance equality within 1e-5 relative, accounting for summation order differences between the DP recurrence and the reference Dijkstra walk). This is a SAMPLING-based check (200 of |V|^2 pairs), not exhaustive -- recommended strengthening (not in the artifact): full APSP cross-validation against a reference all-pairs Dijkstra on small instances (|V| <= 2000) as an additional, exhaustive gate.
dp-apsp-graph-property-matrixsolve throughput across the four structural graph-property combinations (directed x weighted) the artifact's own codebase treats as first-class cases, since the DP recurrence and the Dijkstra cross-check both behave differently on each (directed graphs require asymmetric distance matrices; unweighted graphs reduce Dijkstra to BFS-style hop counting).

Fairness notes
  • The artifact's own core solve path (fap.cpp) contains no timing instrumentation; this spec's protocol (warmup/reps/statistic/timer) is therefore a REQUIREMENT this survey imposes for reproducibility, not a description of a confirmed existing default -- flagged explicitly rather than presented as the paper's own practice.
  • The correctness mechanism the artifact does confirm (200-pair random Dijkstra spot-check) is real and unusually well-documented among this project's singleton-track artifacts, but is sampling-based; this spec keeps it as the practical default (matching the artifact's own convention and avoiding an expensive full-APSP recompute at scale) while recommending an additional exhaustive check on small instances, so a bug confined to untested vertex pairs is not silently missed at the scales where full verification is affordable.
  • The paper's own headline 11.5M-vertex / 2048-GPU result uses a dataset not identified in the sources fetched; this spec's recommended_subset instead uses SuiteSparse-named graphs at comparable or smaller scale so the benchmark is runnable without needing the paper's exact (unidentified) largest input.
Open questions
  • The paper's own timing protocol (warmup/repeat/statistic/timer, and precisely what code region is wrapped) was not recoverable from the sources fetched -- fap.cpp has no time/clock/MPI_Wtime calls in the portion read, meaning timing lives in an external driver not present in the surveyed repo tree.
  • The specific dataset name used for the paper's own 11,548,845-vertex / 2048-GPU headline result was not identified from the fetched README or scripts.
  • Whether the sampled correctness check (check_ans, 200 pairs) is run by default in the artifact's benchmark scripts, or is only available as an opt-in debugging call, was not confirmed beyond seeing it invoked from app/singleNodeExample.cpp's main().
hausdorff-distance1 papers2 variants

Hausdorff Distance (HD) between two point sets, computed via GPU ray-tracing-core-accelerated k-NN search with spatial-grid and provably-exact branch-and-bound pruning (X-HD), measured against an exact brute-force reference and an industrial-standard baseline (ITK), across three structurally different point-set domains the artifact treats as first-class (medical imaging, geospatial, 3D graphics).

HD(A,B) = max(h(A,B), h(B,A)); h(A,B) = max_{a in A} min_{b in B} dist(a,b); A, B are point sets in R^n_dims (n_dims in {2,3}). X-HD reformulates the inner min_{b in B} dist(a,b) as an RT-accelerated k-NN query, adding a spatial grid (reduce BVH traversal intensity), HD estimators (provably-exact early-termination bounds on the running max-min), and CUDA-kernel offload of distance computation from RT shaders to fix a grid-induced load-imbalance.

hd-exact-kernelsteady-state kernel time to compute the EXACT Hausdorff distance for a point-set pair, across four algorithm choices exposed directly by the artifact's own CLI (-variant eb/nn/itk/rt) and an execution-target axis (-execution cpu/gpu, GPU-only for rt); eb is treated as this benchmark's ground-truth reference, matching the artifact's own apparent design (see survey.md)
inputs
suitethree domains exposed as first-class CLI options (-input_type image/wkt/ply): medical-imaging point sets (MRI segmentation-mask-derived), WKT geospatial point/polygon data, PLY 3D graphics point clouds/meshes -- required to be exercised as sub-cases of this ONE variant (not three separate variants, per survey.md Divergences: the algorithm and its correctness/timing protocol are domain-agnostic, only input format and typical scale differ)
selectionthe paper's own exact dataset list was not recoverable from the sources fetched in this survey (README gives only the CLI signature, flags.cc returned compiled usage text not raw flag definitions) -- this spec therefore specifies known public sources per domain as a disclosed, reasonable stand-in rather than leaving the suite unspecified, flagged in open_questions
recommended_subsetmedical (image): a public MRI-segmentation mask pair (e.g. Medical Segmentation Decathlon or comparable public set), 2D slice instances ~1e3-1e5 points and a 3D volume instance ~1e5-1e7 points, matched to HD's standard role as a segmentation-quality metric, geospatial (wkt): OpenStreetMap-derived polygon/point extracts at three size classes: small ~1e3 points, medium ~1e5 points, large ~1e6 points, graphics (ply): Stanford 3D Scanning Repository models as small/medium/large -- Bunny (~35K vertices), Dragon (~437K vertices), Lucy (~14M vertices)

statisticmedian wall time, report min/max

timing_scopekernel only: point-set file parsing and any BVH/grid index construction are preprocessing, excluded from the timed region but reported separately, one-shot
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once per point-set pair and per variant: file-parse time; BVH-build time (nn/rt variants); grid-build time (rt variant's specific spatial-grid optimization, since this is one of X-HD's three named contributions and must be visible on its own, not folded into query time)
metric

secondaryspeedup vs. eb (exact reference) and vs. itk (industrial baseline) -- matches the paper's own reporting convention (abstract: 5.3x over ITK on average, up to 6.4x over a GPU-optimized prior HD solution)
correctnessrt and nn MUST return the same HD value as eb (the exact reference) within floating-point tolerance (relative error < 1e-6 at matched precision, or exact match if inputs/outputs are integer/quantized). This track's problem is NOT an accuracy-for-speed approximation the way ANN or spectral sparsification are: X-HD's grid and HD-estimator optimizations are described as provably-exact search-space pruning (branch-and-bound style early termination that never discards the true max-min point), so there is no legitimate quality-vs-speed operating-point tradeoff here -- only a pass/fail exactness gate. A variant that returns a materially different HD value is not "faster at lower quality," it is incorrect, and must be excluded from the timing comparison rather than reported alongside it.
hd-e2e-preprocessingend-to-end throughput including one-shot index construction (BVH for nn/rt, spatial grid for rt specifically) amortized over k=10 point-set-pair queries against the same reference structure -- relevant when one point set (e.g. a fixed reference mesh/anatomical atlas) is queried against many others, a realistic batch-scoring usage this track's single-pair kernel variant does not capture

Fairness notes
  • The artifact's own timing protocol (warmup count, repetition count, statistic, timer placement) could not be recovered from the sources fetched in this survey -- the README exposes only a bare CLI usage example, and flags.cc's raw flag-definition source was not obtained (only compiled usage text). This spec's protocol section is therefore explicitly specified from this project's general convention rather than lifted from the paper/artifact, flagged here and in open_questions per the fairness principle that a spec must not silently assume methodology it cannot cite.
  • Because X-HD's three domains (medical/geospatial/graphics) share one algorithm and CLI, this spec keeps them as required sub-cases of a single variant rather than three separate variants -- splitting them would let a submission cherry-pick the domain where X-HD performs best without ever reporting the other two.
  • eb is treated as ground truth on the strength of the CLI's own naming and the paper's framing of nn/itk as baselines and rt as the contribution; this was not independently confirmed from a methods section (none was fetched) and should be verified against the paper's own text if it becomes available, per open_questions.
Open questions
  • The artifact's exact evaluation dataset list (specific medical imaging cohort, specific WKT source, specific PLY models) was not recoverable from the fetched README/abstract -- recommended_subset above is this spec's own disclosed stand-in using standard public sources per domain, not a reproduction of the paper's own table.
  • Whether "eb" stands for "exact brute-force" or some other exact-bound method, and whether it is itself GPU- or CPU-only or both, was inferred from the CLI's variant-naming convention and the paper's framing, not confirmed from fulltext (no arXiv/OA link recorded for this paper).
  • Timer implementation, warmup, and repetition convention actually used by the artifact's benchmark scripts (if any exist beyond the bare CLI example) were not found in the portion of flags.cc retrieved; if raw source becomes available this should be re-verified against the protocol specified here from general convention.
  • Whether the "GPU-optimized HD solution" the abstract claims up to 6.4x speedup over is the same as the -variant nn baseline exposed by the CLI, or a distinct prior work not present in the artifact at all, was not disambiguated.
json-parsing1 papers1 variants

Fully GPU-offloaded JSON parsing (UTF-8 validation, tokenization, nesting-structure/structural-index recognition) measured as throughput over standard JSON corpora, covering both a single large deeply-nested document and many independent JSON-Lines records with an explicit chunking-strategy axis, with RFC 8259 validation strictness reported as a first-class disclosure alongside speed.

Given a raw JSON byte buffer of size N: produce a structural index — for every structural character (`{`, `}`, `[`, `]`, `:`, `,`, string quotes), its byte offset, plus a `pair_pos` array mapping every opening bracket/brace to its matching closer — sufficient to support O(1)-ish key/array-index navigation via a query iterator without a full recursive-descent re-parse. Standard-JSON mode processes one such buffer as a single document; JSON-Lines mode processes C independent single-object buffers (one per line), optionally pre-split into K chunks for coarse-grained parallel dispatch.

json-parse-throughput-gpusteady-state GPU parsing throughput (GB/s) for the full 3-phase pipeline (UTF-8 validate + tokenize + nesting-recognition) as one measured region, H2D input transfer and D2H structural-index transfer EXCLUDED and reported separately (device-resident timing is the meaningful number for a GPU-resident downstream-query pipeline; a candidate that must round-trip to host per query is a different, worse-case claim that should be reported as a distinct number, not silently substituted).
inputs
suitestandard JSON-benchmarking corpora (the field's common denominator, used by simdjson/Pison-class CPU parsers this artifact itself compares against) plus the artifact's own Twitter-derived sample family, covering both input modes.
selection(a) Standard-JSON: large single-document files with varying nesting depth and array/object density; (b) JSON-Lines: large multi-record files with varying per-record size, to separate "many tiny records" from "few large records" parallelism regimes. Both required per candidate; a submission reporting only one mode is incomplete (see notes_on_fairness).

correctnessMANDATORY pre-timing gate, exact match required (JSON structure recovery is a discrete/exact problem, no floating-point tolerance applies): the recovered structural index (`structural` byte offsets + `pair_pos` matching-bracket map) must exactly reproduce a reference recursive-descent CPU parse (e.g. against Python's `json` module or simdjson's own structural index, cross-checked at the level of "same set of structural byte offsets, same bracket pairing") on every file in the suite before any speed number for that file counts. validation_strictness: > report explicitly, as a REQUIRED disclosure alongside every speed number: does the parser (1) fully validate per RFC 8259 (reject malformed UTF-8, trailing commas, unescaped control characters, etc. — matching simdjson's strict mode) or (2) assume well-formed input and skip some/all validation for speed (a legitimate but DIFFERENT claim). A malformed-input test set (5-10 deliberately invalid JSON files covering common malformed classes: truncated document, invalid UTF-8 byte, unescaped control char, mismatched brackets) must be run through the parser and its accept/reject behavior reported — a parser that silently returns garbage instead of rejecting invalid input is NOT comparable on speed to one that validates, and this variant requires the validation-strictness disclosure precisely so that substitution can't happen silently.
Fairness notes
  • The paper's own repo splits Standard-JSON and JSON-Lines into entirely separate binaries/entry points with no single combined benchmark; a candidate reporting only one mode's throughput (typically the easier, larger-document Standard-JSON case) would be an incomplete comparison against simdjson/Pison/cuDF/GPJSON, all of which handle both. Both modes are required in this spec's single variant precisely to prevent that omission.
  • GPU JSON parsers have an unusually large H2D-transfer-to-compute ratio compared to compute-bound GPU kernels elsewhere in this project (parsing itself is closer to memory-bandwidth-bound than compute-bound); this spec excludes H2D/D2H from the primary kernel-only number specifically because for a GPU-resident downstream pipeline (e.g. GPU dataframe ingestion, cuDF-style), the transfer cost is amortized/irrelevant, but requires it reported separately since a CPU-baseline (simdjson) comparison that ignores the GPU's transfer cost would be unfair to simdjson.
  • No source found in this survey states cuJSON's own RFC 8259 conformance/validation-strictness policy; validation_strictness is added as a mandatory disclosure specifically because 'branch-minimal for maximal parallelism' (the paper's own framing) is a design space where skipping validation checks is a natural and legitimate speed/safety tradeoff that must not be hidden inside an unqualified throughput number.
Open questions
  • paper_reproduced/scripts/readme.md (claimed by the top-level README to hold 'all the scripts' for reproducing the paper's figures) was not fetched in this survey -- it is the authoritative source for cuJSON's actual timing protocol (warmup/reps/timer) and should be read directly before finalizing warmup=5/reps=20 above as anything more than this spec's own placeholder.
  • The large (~1GB-class) datasets used in the paper's actual performance evaluation are hosted externally (Google Drive link in the README) and were not inspected; recommended_subset's exact file identities (twitter-large-record, twitter-small-records) are inferred from the repo's own naming convention, not confirmed against the paper's literal Table/Figure data.
  • Whether cuJSON validates RFC 8259 strictly or assumes well-formed input by default could not be determined from the fetched sources -- this is exactly the gap validation_strictness's mandatory disclosure is meant to force a future measurement pass to resolve empirically.
membership-filter1 papers1 variants

GPU approximate-membership-query (AMQ) filter data structures (GQF, TCF, RSQF, SQF, Bloom, Blocked Bloom) benchmarked for insert/query/ delete throughput, with false-positive rate reported as a MANDATORY joint measurement alongside every throughput number (never speed alone), swept across filter capacity and across uniform vs. skewed key-frequency distributions.

A filter F of target capacity N and target false-positive rate epsilon supports: insert(key) -> void (adds key to F, using B bits/key of storage, B a function of epsilon and the filter's design); query(key) -> bool (returns true if key was inserted -- REQUIRED, zero false negatives -- or, for a key never inserted, returns true with probability <= epsilon, a false positive); delete(key) -> void, where supported (GQF, SQF, TCF only -- Bloom/Blocked-Bloom/RSQF as specified here do not support delete).

filter-insert-query-fpr-gpusteady-state GPU throughput for insert, positive query, and random/false-positive query, reported JOINTLY with the empirically measured false-positive rate at each capacity -- the common denominator across all six filter types this artifact implements, matching the artifact's own point-test range (2^22 to 2^30 items).

metric

correctnessMANDATORY dual gate, jointly required with every throughput number (never reported separately, per this track's brief): (1) ZERO false negatives -- every one of the N inserted keys' positive queries MUST return true, checked exhaustively (not sampled) for every (filter, capacity, distribution) configuration before its speed number counts; (2) empirical false-positive rate on the random-query test must not exceed the filter's DOCUMENTED target epsilon by more than 20% relative (e.g. a filter targeting epsilon=1/256 must measure FPR <= 1/256 * 1.2 on a random-query set of at least 10x the filter's capacity, for statistical reliability of the FPR estimate itself). A throughput number reported without its paired FPR measurement from the SAME run is INCOMPLETE and must not be cited alone.
Fairness notes
  • This track's brief explicitly requires false-positive rate reported JOINTLY with throughput, never as an afterthought; this spec makes that mandatory as a dual gate (zero false negatives + FPR-within-tolerance) rather than a display convention, since a filter could otherwise report a large throughput number while silently exceeding its target FPR under high load or at large capacity (a known failure mode for hash-based AMQ filters as they approach full occupancy).
  • The released artifact's own README explicitly does NOT reproduce a Zipfian/skewed key-frequency test locally (the dataset is available only by emailing the author); this spec still requires a skewed-distribution sub-case since real-world key-frequency distributions are rarely uniform and a filter's collision/eviction behavior (for cuckoo-style or bucketed designs) can differ materially under skew -- but flags the substitution explicitly rather than silently reusing the paper's own unreproducible dataset claim.
  • Only GQF/SQF/TCF among the six filter types support delete; this spec does NOT force RSQF/Bloom/Blocked-Bloom into an incomplete delete comparison, avoiding the apples-to-oranges trap of penalizing filters that never claimed delete support.
  • The bulk-TCF path's pre-sort workaround at capacity 2^30 (needed to fit within GPU memory) is a real, reportable cost of that specific insertion strategy relative to the point-TCF path's presumably-unsorted insertion; this spec requires it reported separately as a preprocessing cost rather than silently absorbed into either the insert throughput number or ignored entirely.
Open questions
  • No stated warmup/repeat/statistic convention was found at the run_full_battery.sh orchestration level; each sub-tool (GQF/SQF/RSQF's run_all_tests.sh, the pog_warp_tests binary, the bulk-tcf batched_template_tests binary) may have its own internal convention not inspected in this survey -- the protocol specified here is this spec's own construction, not confirmed against the artifact's literal internals.
  • Whether the released harness enforces the zero-false-negative / FPR-within-tolerance gate automatically, or only reports raw counts for manual inspection, was not determined from the fetched top-level scripts (run_tests.py orchestrates test binaries but does not itself appear to assert pass/fail).
  • The Warpcore external-baseline comparison is documented only for the point-TCF path (pog_warp_tests); whether a comparable external baseline exists (or is fair to construct) for GQF/RSQF/SQF/Bloom/Blocked-Bloom was not determined -- left as an optional extension rather than forced into this spec's required variant.
morphology-image-kernel1 papers1 variants

Generated-code throughput for an image-processing pipeline (Harris corner detector: grayscale -> Sobel gradients -> structure-tensor sum -> corner response) on mobile ARM CPUs, comparing a domain-extensible rewrite-rule compiler (Rise/Shine, and Lift) against Halide (default schedule) and OpenCV, with a mandatory per-pixel-error + PSNR correctness gate before any timing counts.

Given an RGB image, compute the Harris corner-response map: convert to grayscale, compute Sobel x/y gradients, form the local structure tensor via a windowed (3x3) weighted sum of gradient products, and compute the corner response R = det(M) - k*trace(M)^2 (k=0.04) per pixel.

morph-harris-kernel-throughputsteady-state per-image kernel throughput across implementations and target CPUs, matching the artifact's own confirmed protocol (30 timing iterations, median/min/max), with the timer-mechanism asymmetry between implementations (wall-clock vs. OpenCL device-side events) explicitly reported rather than hidden, since it is a real methodological difference found in the source.
inputs
suitethe artifact's own two bundled images: rgb.png (Halide's demo image, 'small') and venice_wikimedia.jpg (PolyMage's demo image, 'big'); exact pixel dimensions not independently re-verified in this survey

targets4 ARM CPU targets from the artifact's own shipped configs: Cortex-A7, Cortex-A15 (Odroid XU4), Cortex-A53, Cortex-A73 (Odroid N2); an x86 Intel-i7-7700 config is also shipped as a portability example
implementationsOpenCV (cv::cornerHarris, CPU reference/baseline), Halide (default schedule), Rise/Shine (SHINE_VERSIONS OpenCL-kernel variants -- exact count not enumerated in this survey), Lift (OpenCL-kernel variant)
protocol
warmup0 (matching the artifact's own confirmed behavior: all 30 iterations are recorded, no discarded warmup iteration; median is taken over all 30, which is somewhat but not fully warmup-robust)
reps30
statisticmedian (report min/max), matching the artifact's own time_stats()/ocl_time_stats() convention exactly
timerTWO mechanisms, per implementation, matching the artifact's own confirmed asymmetry: std::chrono::high_resolution_clock wall time (Halide, OpenCV -- includes host dispatch/queueing) vs. OpenCL device-side profiling events (Rise/Shine, Lift -- CL_PROFILING_COMMAND_START/_END, excludes host-side overhead). Report BOTH the raw numbers under each implementation's own native timer AND flag that the two are not directly comparable without a host-overhead correction (see notes_on_fairness).
timing_scopekernel-only per iteration (image already resident in memory, output write not timed); code generation (Halide/Rise/Shine AOT compilation) and image I/O are excluded from the timed loop and are one-shot setup costs, not reported per this artifact snapshot
metric
primarymedian wall/device time, ms, per (image, target CPU, implementation)
secondaryspeedup vs OpenCV and speedup vs Halide-default, dimensionless x, matching the paper's own headline framing (up to 16x over OpenCV, up to 1.4x over Halide)
correctnessMANDATORY pre-timing gate, matching the artifact's own confirmed error_stats() check exactly: every non-reference implementation's output is compared pixel-by-pixel against the Halide default-schedule output (the artifact's own designated gold reference) on the SAME image; max per-pixel absolute error, normalized by the gold image's own dynamic range, must be <= 0.01, AND PSNR must be >= 100 dB. Both conditions must hold (the artifact enforces both, aborting the run on failure of either) before that implementation's timing numbers for that image count.
Fairness notes
  • The artifact uses two different timer mechanisms for different implementations in the same benchmark run: CPU wall-clock (std::chrono, includes host-side dispatch/queueing overhead) for Halide and OpenCV, vs. OpenCL device-side profiling events (excludes host-side overhead) for Rise/Shine and Lift. This asymmetry systematically favors the OpenCL-timed implementations' reported numbers over the wall-clock-timed ones. This spec requires both numbers be reported under their native timers AND flags that a fair head-to-head speedup claim needs either a host-overhead-inclusive OpenCL wall-clock measurement or a device-side-only Halide/OpenCV measurement -- the artifact's own headline speedup claim (up to 16x over OpenCV) crosses this asymmetry and should be read with that caveat.
  • The Halide auto-scheduled variant's timing loop was found commented out in the exact artifact snapshot read (only its correctness check against the default schedule remains active); this spec does not include auto-scheduled-Halide as a confirmed-active timed implementation, and a re-measurement pass should confirm whether a newer artifact revision re-enables it.
  • The 2-image evaluation set (one small, one big) is small by the standards of most tracks in this project; this spec keeps it as-is (following the artifact's own convention) rather than inventing additional images, since expanding the suite would no longer be measuring what this specific paper's own artifact evaluates.
Open questions
  • Exact pixel dimensions of rgb.png and venice_wikimedia.jpg were not independently re-verified (would require fetching the binary image files from the Halide/PolyMage git submodules, out of scope for this survey pass).
  • The exact number and identity of SHINE_VERSIONS (the Rise/Shine OpenCL-kernel variants swept in the timing loop) was not enumerated from the source read -- only that the loop iterates 'for (int version = 0; version < SHINE_VERSIONS; version++)'.
  • Whether a corrected, timer-symmetric comparison (both implementations under the same timer mechanism) is available anywhere in the paper's own text was not checked (no arXiv/OA fulltext was fetched for this paper in this survey pass, only the GitHub artifact).
set-intersection1 papers2 variants

Per-edge sorted-adjacency-list set intersection (Jaccard-weight computation: |N(u) intersect N(v)| / |N(u) union N(v)| for every edge (u,v) in a graph), swept across list-length/degree skew and intersection selectivity, comparing a degree-aware binned kernel (tuned search-group-size/assembly-size per degree bin) against fixed-configuration GPU baselines and a CPU multi-core algorithm, all from the same codebase for an apples-to-apples comparison.

Given graph G=(V,E) in CSR (sorted neighbor lists per vertex): for every edge (u,v) in E, compute J(u,v) = |N(u) intersect N(v)| / |N(u) union N(v)|, where N(u), N(v) are u's and v's sorted neighbor-id arrays (list-merge-style intersection, O(deg(u)+deg(v)) per edge naively). Output: one Jaccard weight per edge, in CSR edge order.

setisect-degree-binned-kernel-gpusteady-state GPU kernel throughput for the degree-aware binned intersection kernel (edges bucketed by endpoint degree, each bin run with a search-group-size g / assembly-size a configuration), compared against fixed-(g,a) GPU baselines from the SAME repo (naive one-thread(-team)-per-edge, cuGraph) -- binning/ML-model- inference (choosing g,a per bin) counted as one-shot preprocessing, reported separately.

selectionSNAP/Network-Repository-class graphs (undirected, real-world), chosen for a 100x-plus spread in max/mean degree ratio across the set; both directed and undirected variants tested since the artifact supports both via _DIRECTED.

timerstd::chrono high_resolution_clock, wrapping the full per-edge intersection loop across all threads
timing_scopekernel only; CSR construction/sort excluded, reported once (see preprocessing_reported)
preprocessing_reportedseparately, once per graph: CSR construction/sort
metric
primaryMEdges/s
secondaryspeedup vs. single-thread CPU baseline (parallel efficiency), and vs. setisect-degree-binned-kernel-gpu's GPU number (cross-device comparison, clearly labeled as CPU-vs-GPU not same-hardware-class)
correctnessidentical exact-match gate as setisect-degree-binned-kernel-gpu
Fairness notes
  • The paper's own timing convention (-a averages -> mean, no stated warmup) is replaced here with median + discarded warmup, since raw-mean-of-N without a warmup discard is the same class of bias this project's other specs correct (see benchspecs/attention-kernel's notes on PAT/MEATTEN/ByteTransformer).
  • The paper's contribution is specifically about degree SKEW; a benchmark suite of only low-skew graphs would trivially favor the degree-aware kernel's baseline-parity case or, worse, only high-skew graphs would hide any overhead the binning/ML-inference step adds on well-behaved inputs. recommended_subset therefore spans low to extreme skew explicitly, including a near-uniform-degree control (roadNet-CA).
  • Binning + ML-model inference is a real one-shot cost the paper does not appear to isolate from kernel time in its own reported numbers (not stated either way in the fetched README); this spec makes it a mandatory separately-reported preprocessing cost so the degree-aware kernel's speedup is not silently inflated by hiding that cost inside an amortization argument that was never stated.
  • cuGraph and the repo's other compiled-in baseline variants (_SIMPLE_GPU_EDGE, _DONGARRA, _INHOUSE_CUGRAPH) exist in the same codebase; this spec names cuGraph and _SIMPLE_GPU explicitly as the required comparison baselines since they are the two named in the paper's own claimed 12x/35x speedup context, and leaves the others as optional additional comparisons (see open_questions).
Open questions
  • The exact algorithm behind the repo's _DONGARRA CMake option (a third GPU baseline) could not be identified from the fetched README alone -- if it corresponds to a specific named prior publication, it should be added as a required baseline rather than left optional.
  • Whether the paper's reported 35x-max / 12x-avg speedup was measured against _SIMPLE_GPU, _CUGRAPH, or some other configuration in this same repo could not be confirmed from the fetched README -- this spec requires reporting against BOTH named baselines to avoid ambiguity, but the paper's own headline number's exact baseline is unconfirmed.
  • No graph suite (named, with sizes) is bundled in the artifact's top-level listing; recommended_subset above is this spec's own standard SNAP/Network-Repository selection for degree-skew coverage, not the literal graph set used in the paper's own evaluation (not recoverable from the fetched README).
spatial-join1 papers1 variants

GPU spatial join: line segment intersection (LSI) and point-in-polygon (PIP) testing between two real geospatial polygon/polyline datasets, measured with index (BVH/grid) BUILD time reported separately from QUERY time, across a uniform-grid baseline, a software-BVH baseline, and an RT-hardware-accelerated implementation all sharing one codebase, plus an external GPU-library baseline, with full double-precision-equivalent correctness required despite RT hardware's native precision limits.

LSI: given two sets of polyline chains R (base map) and S (query map), find every pair of segments (r in R, s in S) that geometrically intersect, and the intersection point. PIP: given a point set P and a polygon set (represented as R's chains), determine for each point p in P which polygon (if any) of R contains it. Polygon overlay: combine LSI+PIP results to compute the full overlay of R and S (every resulting face and which R-polygon/S-polygon pair it came from).

spatial-join-lsi-pip-querysteady-state LSI and PIP query throughput across three index strategies sharing one codebase (uniform grid, software LBVH, RT-hardware-accelerated BVH), with index BUILD cost reported separately from query time -- since BVH build is explicitly the paper's own second stated bottleneck alongside precision recovery, collapsing build+query into one number would hide exactly the tradeoff the paper's contribution targets.

statisticmean (report min/max) -- RayJoin's own -warmup/-repeat flags directly implement this convention (average time over N repeat rounds after N warmup rounds); retained as-is since it is the artifact's own explicit, well-documented protocol, one of the more complete protocols found across this project's singleton-track surveys
timerdevice-side timer wrapping query_exec's query call only (the artifact's own internal timing, not independently re-verified in this survey)
timing_scopequery only; index BUILD (grid-cell assignment for mode=grid, LBVH construction for mode=lbvh, OptiX BVH construction for mode=rt) is a SEPARATE, REQUIRED-reported cost, since it differs by orders of magnitude in character between modes (RT-hardware BVH build is the paper's own stated second bottleneck) and pooling it into query time would erase exactly the tradeoff this track's brief asks to be measured (index build vs. query).
dataset_serializationreport separately, once per dataset pair: CDB-to-binary serialization time (polyover_exec's own -serialize option), a one-shot format-conversion cost distinct from both index build and query
