Fairness notes
  • GE-SpMM's and MaxK-GNN's correctness checks are compiled out / commented out by default in the shipped benchmark path (survey.md Divergence 3); this spec makes the correctness gate mandatory and pre-timing in every variant, never opt-in.
  • GE-SpMM (single CUDA-event pair around a 200-call loop) and MaxK-GNN (4 warmup + 4 measured samples) cannot report median/min/max from their own protocols. This spec requires per-iteration device timestamps and a >=100-sample measured window in gnn-agg-kernel-f32 specifically so those statistics are always computable.
  • No surveyed paper states an explicit dataset-inclusion criterion; every suite is inherited by citation from GNNAdvisor/SNAP popularity, and no two papers' suites are identical (survey.md Divergence 5). This spec fixes one explicit union-based criterion and a single named subset instead of letting each reproduction pick its own convenient graphs.
  • EPPGCN is the only surveyed paper reporting both a with-preprocessing and a without-preprocessing end-to-end number, and they differ materially (1.05-1.37x vs 1.03-1.35x). This spec's gnn-agg-e2e-preproc-f32 variant makes that split, with an explicit amortization count (k=200), a REQUIRED report for every artifact, not an optional extra the way EPPGCN alone currently provides it.
  • CAGNET's coarse end-to-end timer starts at epoch 1 with no warmup exclusion, which risks inflating the reported per-epoch time with first-touch/allocation overhead. gnn-agg-epoch-training-e2e explicitly forbids counting the first measured epoch, regardless of what a given artifact's own harness does.
  • MaxK-GNN's backward SSpMM (structured top-k sparsity) and QGTC's sub-8-bit quantized aggregation are NOT pooled into the fp32 dense-N metric above — they measure genuinely different arithmetic (fewer nonzeros per row by construction; integer MACs instead of FMAs) and reporting them on the same GFLOP/s axis as e.g. GE-SpMM would imply a false apples-to-apples comparison. Left as open questions below rather than forced into one of the four variants.
  • FASTEN's segmented matmul for heterogeneous GNNs and CAGNET's distributed 1D/1.5D/2D/3D decompositions are structurally different problems (grouped-by-relation-type GEMM; communication-bound multi-GPU/multi-node scheduling) from the single-adjacency-matrix, single-device aggregation this spec's four variants target. Neither is folded in; see open_questions.
Open questions
  • Whether a 5th "heterogeneous segmented aggregation" variant should be added to cover FASTEN's relation-type-grouped GEMM — its inputs (AIFB/ MUTAG/BGS/AM/DBLP/Freebase) and operator shape (segmented/grouped GEMM, not a single sparse adjacency @ dense) don't fit any of the four variants above without stretching "aggregation" past its usual meaning in this track's other 10 papers.
  • Whether a 6th "distributed-scale" variant (communication volume + weak/ strong scaling vs. GPU count) should be added to cover CAGNET's 1D/1.5D/ 2D/3D decompositions, given Phase 2's measurement machine is not fixed to a single node. Left out here since it needs a fundamentally different metric (words moved / comm time, not GFLOP/s) and multi-GPU access most of this track's artifacts (single-GPU/single-CPU kernels) don't require.
  • StraGCN's actual timing protocol (warmup/rep counts, timer) was not extracted — the README documents only how to launch full training (`python gcn.py`), and the timing loop presumably lives inside `StraGCN/gcn.py`/`dgl/gcn.py`, which was not read within this survey's scope. Needs a follow-up code read before StraGCN's artifact can be slotted into gnn-agg-epoch-training-e2e with confidence.
  • QGTC's exact warmup/repetition counts for its epoch-level "Epoch (ms)" table and its raw-GEMM TFLOPs table were not extractable from the README alone (arXiv fulltext 404'd); would need `0_7a_eval_QGTC_cluster_GCN.py` and `2_7c_QGTC_GEMM_INT8.py` read directly.
  • CBM's own harness reports raw seconds, not GFLOP/s or a normalized throughput metric — this spec's gnn-agg-kernel-f32 requires GFLOP/s, meaning a CBM reproduction needs an added normalization step (2*nnz*N, trivial, but CBM's artifact does not do this itself).
  • TC-GNN's dense-tile graph-translation preprocessing latency (as opposed to the resulting tile COUNT, which IS reported by `3_cnt_TC_blk_SpMM.py`) was not found in any shipped script; unclear whether it is measurable from the artifact as-is or requires instrumenting the translation code directly for gnn-agg-e2e-preproc-f32.
attention-kernel9 papers3 variants

Fused scaled-dot-product attention (the softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d))V core of transformer models), measured as steady-state kernel throughput with preprocessing (QKV projection, RoPE, KV-cache paging/block-table setup) reported separately, split into prefill/full-sequence, decode/KV-cache, and CPU-multicore variants that the surveyed literature treats as genuinely different claims — plus a causal-vs-bidirectional mask axis and an fp16/bf16 precision axis within each GPU variant.

O[B,H,Sq,d] = softmax( (Q[B,H,Sq,d] @ K[B,Hkv,Sk,d]^T) / sqrt(d) + mask ) @ V[B,Hkv,Sk,d] (GQA when Hkv < H; MHA when Hkv == H; Sq == Sk for prefill, Sq == 1 for decode)

attn-prefill-kernel-fp16bf16steady-state fused forward-pass attention kernel throughput for prefill/training-style workloads (all of Q attends over all of K,V in one call; no incremental KV cache), preprocessing (QKV projection, RoPE application, mask/bias construction) excluded and reported separately. This is the common denominator ByteTransformer, E.T., Hexcute's `benchmark_attention.py`, and FlashAttention-T's Figure-8 comparison all actually measure, and what RedFuser's MHA/MLA cascaded- reduction fusion and MetaAttention's generated softmax-attention kernel are drop-in candidates for.

This spec closes that gap.
Fairness notes
  • PAT, MEATTEN, and ByteTransformer each measure a single latency number per config with either no reported spread (ByteTransformer) or too few repetitions to compute one meaningfully (MEATTEN's REPEAT=3). This spec requires median + min/max from >=20 per-iteration device-side timestamps for every variant, following the same fix applied in benchspecs/spmm/spec.yaml to RoDe/GE-SpMM/SMaT's batched-mean timing.
  • MEATTEN's own correctness check (compareTensor, abs diff < 1e-3) exists in the repo but is disconnected from the performance benchmark driver — the perf loop never calls it. This spec makes the correctness gate mandatory and part of the SAME run as the timed measurement, for every variant.
  • PAT's benchmark script hard-codes batch=1134 specifically to saturate one A100's SM count and avoid tail-effect bubbles; this is a legitimate steady-state-throughput choice but is NOT representative of small-batch interactive decode latency (the metric users usually care about for chat). This spec keeps PAT's saturating-batch shapes in the recommended_subset for throughput comparability with PAT's own numbers, but adds small-batch (B=1, 16) shapes so latency-sensitive candidates aren't penalized for not saturating.
  • Prefix-sharing bandwidth accounting is not standardized anywhere in the surveyed literature: PAT reports latency reduction %% without publishing a bytes-moved formula, so a prefix-unaware kernel and a prefix-aware kernel are compared only by wall-clock, which conflates algorithmic reuse with raw kernel efficiency. This spec requires reporting bandwidth against BOTH a naive (per-query, no dedup) and a deduplicated (unique-block) byte count, so the two effects are separable — see attn-decode-kv-cache-kernel's metric section.
  • Causal and bidirectional attention are pooled into a single wall-clock number by no paper surveyed (each paper picks one mask and stays there); this spec adds mask as an explicit required sub-case within attn-prefill-kernel-fp16bf16 so the ~2x FLOP difference is visible rather than silently baked into a single reported number.
  • RedFuser, Hexcute, and MetaAttention (the 3 compiler/codegen papers) are treated as candidate SUBMISSIONS to attn-prefill-kernel-fp16bf16 or attn-decode-kv-cache-kernel (whichever shape they report), not as a separate 'compiled kernel' variant — the fusion boundary between softmax and the surrounding GEMMs is an implementation strategy, not part of this benchmark's operation definition, so pooling them with hand-written kernels (FlashAttention, MEATTEN) under the same variant is the correct comparison, not a category error.
  • No fp8 attention variant is defined: none of the 9 papers benchmarks full QK^TV attention in fp8 (RedFuser and Hexcute's 'FP8' benchmark categories are quantized GEMM/MoE-routing, not attention). Adding an fp8-attention variant without literature grounding would violate the same-standard-as-the-track principle this spec otherwise follows; left as an open question.
Open questions
  • FlashAttention-T's exact warmup/repeat count inside its compiled fp16-fwd-bench CUDA/C++ binary was not visible from the README alone (only that it writes a CSV report); the binary's source was not fetched.
  • RedFuser's repo is a fork of Apache TVM/Relax with generic apps/tests boilerplate; no attention-specific benchmark driver distinct from the general TVM test harness was located in the top-level listing within this survey's time budget — Appendix A.5 of the paper (not machine-extractable from the fulltext render used) likely has the exact shapes.
  • MetaAttention's 'operator-specific tolerances' for its GPU correctness suite (tests/functional) were not given as concrete numbers in the README; this spec's 1e-2/1e-3 values for the GPU variants are NOT independently confirmed against MetaAttention's own thresholds.
  • E.T.'s (SC'21) timing protocol and correctness tolerance could not be extracted from the top-level README within this survey's time budget — only the kernel source (kernels/attention.cu, confirming fp16 + tensor-core MMA) and the 3 example-encoder test targets were read. A deeper pass would read test/encoder_*_test source directly.
  • LightSeq2's SC'22-specific evaluation section (as opposed to the monorepo README's mixed v1/v2/v3 numbers) was not independently retrieved; the arXiv abstract page (2110.05722) did not expose fulltext evaluation detail through the fetch tool used. The recommended_subset's BERT/GPT2/Transformer shapes are this spec's own choice, not lifted from a confirmed LightSeq2-specific table.
  • Whether Phase 2 wants a 4th variant specifically for the MLA (multi-head latent attention, DeepSeek-style) structural variant that RedFuser and (approximately) this spec's deepseek-v2-lite-mla-approx shape gesture at: MLA's low-rank KV compression changes the memory-traffic formula in attn-decode-kv-cache-kernel's metric (bytes moved is NOT simply 2*L*Hkv*d, since K and V are reconstructed from a shared latent), and none of the 9 papers surveyed publishes an MLA-specific byte-accounting formula. Left as a todo rather than guessed.
convolution9 papers4 variants

Forward 2D convolution (NCHW) for CNN-inference-shaped workloads, covering four legitimately different algorithm classes found in the surveyed literature — dense direct/im2col-implicit-GEMM, sparse structured-pruned, sub-8-bit/binary quantized, and autotuning-search cost — each measured with a fixed protocol so GFLOP/s numbers across algorithm classes stay comparable rather than being inflated by a smaller executed-op count.

Y[N,Cout,Hout,Wout] = conv2d(X[N,Cin,Hin,Win], W[Cout,Cin/groups,Kh,Kw], stride=(Sh,Sw), pad=(Ph,Pw), groups=g); groups=1 for standard conv, groups=Cin=Cout for depthwise. Reference (algorithm-invariant) FLOP count used for the primary GFLOP/s metric in every variant: flops_ref = 2 * N * Cout * (Cin/groups) * Kh * Kw * Hout * Wout — this is the "problem size" FLOP count (same formula regardless of whether the implementation is direct, im2col-GEMM, Winograd, FFT-conv, or sparse/pruned), so an algorithm that does fewer *executed* multiply-adds (Winograd, sparse) can legitimately show GFLOP/s above the executed-op rate; that is expected and must not be hidden — see metric definitions per variant below.

conv-dense-kernel-fp32Steady-state kernel throughput of a dense conv (direct, im2col-implicit-GEMM, Winograd, or FFT-conv — algorithm class must be disclosed), fp32, single layer, preprocessing (schedule search / weight-layout transform) excluded from timed calls and reported separately, once.

Fairness notes
  • Tetris's own artifact times ALL REPEAT=100 calls inside one aggregate CUDA-event bracket (elapsedTime/REPEAT = mean, no distribution) — this spec requires per-rep timestamps instead, so median/min/max (the instructions' preferred statistic) can actually be computed, not just a single mean.
  • Tetris applies the same post-pruning Cout to every baseline (including dense cuDNN) before computing FLOPS, which is fair among those baselines but conflates 'is my sparse kernel fast at this small shape' with 'did pruning+sparse-kernel actually help the end user' — conv-sparse-pruned-kernel-fp32 requires both a same-shape GFLOP/s number and a speedup-vs-original-unpruned-shape number to separate these.
  • ASPLOS_artifact (0033XSRS21) is the only CPU-relevant paper in the survey that explicitly states a cache-flush policy (100M-float flush before every one of 50 iterations) — adopted as the CPU-variant default here, generalized to >=32MB, rather than left unspecified as in the other CPU-adjacent papers.
  • No paper in this survey reports median or min/max — Tetris and ASPLOS both report only a mean, cgo reports mean+std-dev. Per the instructions' fairness principle, this spec fixes median (report min/max) as the required statistic across all variants, which is a strictly stronger disclosure than any paper's own practice.
  • Ansor-AF-DS's entire contribution is autotuning-search wall-clock time to match (not beat) plain Ansor's steady-state kernel quality — folding this into conv-dense-kernel-fp32's per-call GFLOP/s would erase the paper's actual claim, so it gets its own variant (conv-tuning-cost) instead.
  • cgo-artifact-2020's own repo already separates kernel-only (convolutions.sh) from end-to-end (end_to_end.sh, with a --nokernel ablation) — this split is the direct precedent for keeping conv-dense-kernel-fp32 (and its siblings) kernel-only while requiring preprocessing/synthesis time to be reported, never silently amortized in.
  • DSXplore's own artifact (main.py) has no isolated forward-conv timing path — it is a 350-epoch training loop. This spec does not treat DSXplore's artifact as directly reproducible evidence for any kernel-only number; it is cited in the survey but not load-bearing for any protocol value in this spec.
  • Odyssey's reported numbers are an HLS/AutoSA cost-model estimate from a design-space search, not a profiled wall-clock run — it is excluded from the GFLOP/s-based variants entirely rather than being force-fit into the same units as the GPU/CPU papers; see open_questions.
Open questions
  • Tetris's exact numerical tolerance inside TensorEqual (the CPU-reference correctness gate in cudnn_test.cc) was not recoverable from the code excerpt read — the 1e-3 relative tolerance in this spec is this survey's own choice, not copied from Tetris.
  • Ansor-AF-DS's actual per-call timing implementation lives inside its forked TVM's time_evaluator runtime, which was not read in full; the exact warmup/repeat/statistic TVM uses by default (and whether Ansor-AF-DS changes it) is unconfirmed — conv-tuning-cost's protocol is this spec's own design, not extracted from their code.
  • TCBNN's per-kernel timing loop (in the 36KB kernel.cuh and the per-network .cu drivers) was not read in full — the 5.6K images/sec headline number's exact warmup/repetition/statistic is unconfirmed; conv-quantized-kernel's GPU protocol numbers are carried over from the Tetris precedent (WARM=30/REPEAT=100 pattern), not extracted from TCBNN itself.
  • Hidet and VeGen were surveyed at abstract level only (their repos' current HEAD is a post-paper product / general-purpose vectorizer without an accessible original-artifact benchmark script); neither contributed a protocol value to this spec.
  • No paper in the 9-paper track input targets 3D/stencil/PDE-style scientific convolution, despite the track's general framing mentioning it — this spec covers only CNN-inference (2D, image-shaped) convolution, since that is what every surveyed paper actually does. A scientific-conv variant (3D grid, larger stencil radius, likely FFT-conv-dominant regime) is left as a genuinely open gap, not fabricated from unsupported assumptions.
  • Odyssey's FPGA HLS-cost-model numbers are excluded from all four variants above (see notes_on_fairness) rather than converted into a comparable GFLOP/s figure — whether/how to fold FPGA systolic-array conv into a future variant (measured against actual bitstream execution, not the AutoSA cost model) is unresolved.
  • Exact GPU model used in TCBNN's paper-reported evaluation (vs. just the sm_75 compute-capability floor in the Makefile) was not confirmed from the files read.
ann-search7 papers2 variants

Nearest-neighbor search over a fixed vector/point database, split into two variants that the 7 surveyed papers treat as genuinely different claims: high-dimensional APPROXIMATE search over the standard SIFT/DEEP/SPACEV billion-scale suite (recall@k vs QPS Pareto curve as THE metric, never QPS alone), and low-dimensional (2D/3D) EXACT (or tightly error-bounded) spatial k-NN over real point-cloud/geometric data where recall@k is meaningless (search is exact by construction) and correctness is instead a measured exact-match rate or bounded error rate. Index-build time/memory and batch-vs-single-query latency are always reported separately from steady-state search throughput in both variants.

high-dim variant: for each query q in Q[Nq,D], return the (approximate) top-k indices of X[N,D] minimizing dist(q, x_i) under a fixed distance metric (L2 by default), N up to 10^9, D in [96,128]; low-dim/exact variant: for each query q in Q[Nq,D], return the EXACT top-k (or all points within a fixed radius r) of X[N,D], D in {2,3}, N up to 10^7

ann-highdim-recall-qps-paretosteady-state approximate nearest-neighbor search throughput (QPS) at FIXED recall@k targets, reported as a recall-vs-QPS curve (never QPS alone), with index-build time and peak memory reported as separate, one-shot numbers (not amortized into per-query time). This is the common denominator PathWeaver, DRIM-ANN, UpANNS, and FANNS all actually target (all 4 evaluate on the SIFT/DEEP/SPACEV billion-scale family and an IVF-PQ-or-graph-based index), and is the standard ann-benchmarks.com-style framing this track's papers only partially realize on their own (see Divergences: only FANNS sweeps multiple recall targets by construction; the other 3 report at most one fixed recall floor or none at all in their released scripts).
inputs
suiteunion of the standard billion-scale ANN benchmark datasets named across the 4 high-dim papers: SIFT1B/SIFT100M (texmex/BIGANN corpus, 128-dim), DEEP1B/DEEP100M (Yandex benchmark, 96-dim), SPACEV1B (Microsoft SPTAG, 100-dim); plus PathWeaver's `sift-128-euclidean` (ann-benchmarks-convention SIFT, presumed SIFT1M scale) for a million-scale comparison point none of the billion-scale papers provide.
selectionfix the 3 billion-scale bases at both their native 10^9 scale and the 10^8 (100M) sub-scale DRIM-ANN and FANNS already use for GPU-memory-constrained comparisons, so GPU and non-GPU (CPU/FPGA/PIM) candidates are both representable; add SIFT1M (the classic small- scale sanity-check size, PathWeaver's own dataset) so a candidate that cannot yet scale to billions still has a comparable submission point. 10,000 queries per dataset (the convention all 4 papers already share).

warmup10
reps20 minimum per (dataset, recall-target, batch-size) cell — raising every one of the 4 papers' own (unstated or unenforced) repetition counts to this project's general >=20-sample floor; none of the 4 released scripts states a per-config repetition count explicitly in the fetched excerpts.
statisticmedian QPS/latency (report min/max); mean recall@k across reps (recall is a ratio over the fixed query set, not a per-iteration timing sample, so mean is the correct statistic there — matching PathWeaver's own convention of mean-recall + median-latency)

batch_and_single_queryMANDATORY: report BOTH a large saturating batch (10,000 queries, matching FANNS's own throughput-oriented convention) for peak-QPS numbers AND single-query (batch=1) latency with a full distribution (report p50/p95/p99, matching FANNS's 100,000-individual-query latency-distribution practice) — closing the gap where UpANNS fixes a small batch (BS=10) throughout with no single-query mode, and PathWeaver/DRIM-ANN don't state batch size at all in the fetched excerpts.
metric
primaryrecall@k vs. QPS Pareto curve, k in {1, 10, 100} (FANNS's own 3 recall-report points, adopted as the standard here since it is the most complete framing surveyed), swept across enough index/search parameter settings (nlist/nprobe or graph search-width) to trace a curve, NOT a single (recall, QPS) point — a bare "N QPS" or "Nx speedup" number without an accompanying recall value is NOT an admissible submission under this spec, correcting UpANNS's own released script (which exposes NPROBS/TOPK as run parameters but never gates or reports the resulting recall in the same file).
secondarysingle-query p50/p95/p99 latency (ms) at the fixed recall targets; index build time (s) and peak memory (GB) as standalone numbers, per protocol.index_build
correctnessrecall@k computed against exact ground-truth top-k (brute-force L2, computed once per dataset/query-set and cached — the standard ann-benchmarks convention; ground-truth files ship with SIFT/DEEP/SPACEV already). A candidate's recall@k at its OWN chosen operating point must be measured and reported in the SAME run that produces the QPS number for that point (not read from a separate offline accuracy script) — closing DRIM-ANN's/UpANNS's gap where recall is either a hard-coded assumption (>=0.8 floor, not re-verified per run) or absent from the reproducibility script entirely.
exact-spatial-knn-kernelsteady-state EXACT (or, if the candidate is RTNN-style radius-relaxation approximate, tightly error-bounded with the error rate measured and reported as a first-class number, not assumed) k-nearest-neighbor or fixed-radius search over low-dimensional (2D/3D) point data, preprocessing (spatial index/BVH/grid construction) excluded and reported separately. This is CLOVER's and RTNN's own claim, and what X-HD's internal RT-accelerated k-NN routine (not its end-to-end Hausdorff-distance computation, which is a different operation) is a valid candidate submission for. Recall@k does not apply here — accuracy is binary exact-match (or a measured approximation-error rate for RTNN-style candidates), not a ratio against an approximate baseline.

selectionkeep all of CLOVER's 17 synthetic sizes (it is the only paper with a genuine size sweep in this family) plus one real dataset per source domain, so both the controlled-synthetic and real-world-distribution axes are covered.

batch_and_single_queryreport both all-points-as-queries (CLOVER's and RTNN's own convention: search points double as the query set) and a held-out single-query-at-a-time mode, since the former amortizes index-build benefit across N queries in a way a truly single-query interactive workload would not
metric
primarythroughput: queries/second (or points/second, for the all-points-as-queries mode), median over reps
secondarywall time (ms); index-build time and peak memory as standalone numbers, per protocol.preprocessing
correctnessMANDATORY, connected to the SAME run as the timed measurement (not a separate, possibly-dead-code sanity script — CLOVER's own `run_test()` has an unconditional early `return true;` before its real assertions, making it structurally unable to fail regardless of correctness, and X-HD ships every reproducibility run with `-check=false`; both are closed by this requirement): exact top-k / radius-set match against a brute-force O(N^2) CPU or GPU reference for at least one small size per dataset family (CLOVER's N<=10000 sizes are cheap enough to brute-force-check every run). For an RTNN-style approximate candidate (relaxed-radius query partitioning), report the MEASURED fraction of queries with an incorrect/incomplete result set against the same brute-force reference — RTNN's own practice (<0.001% at its default setting), adopted here as the required reporting format rather than a fixed numeric gate, since "exact" and "bounded- approximate" are both legitimate submissions to this variant as long as the error rate is measured and disclosed, not assumed.
Fairness notes
  • This track's own papers split cleanly into two families that do not share a benchmark, input suite, or accuracy notion: high-dimensional approximate search (SIFT/DEEP/SPACEV, recall@k) vs. low-dimensional exact spatial k-NN (point clouds, exact-match). Pooling them into one variant would force a meaningless recall@k onto exact search or force high-dimensional billion-scale data onto algorithms (CLOVER's grid/hub structures, RTNN's RT-core BVH) designed and only evaluated at 2D/3D. Kept as two fully separate variants, matching this project's precedent of splitting on genuinely different input-suite/accuracy axes (see attention-kernel's GPU-vs-CPU split, sparse-attention-kernel's structured-mask-vs-graph-adjacency split).
  • A bare QPS or speedup number without an accompanying recall value is explicitly disallowed for the high-dim variant (see metric.primary) — this directly implements the task's own stated key axis ('recall@k vs QPS Pareto curve as THE metric, never QPS alone') and fixes UpANNS's released run.sh, which exposes nprobe/topk as tunable parameters but never surfaces or gates the resulting recall in the same script.
  • Index-build time and memory are reported separately from search throughput in BOTH variants as a hard requirement — none of DRIM-ANN's, UpANNS's, FANNS's, CLOVER's, or X-HD's released reproducibility scripts do this cleanly (PathWeaver's script structure does it implicitly by running build once outside the search-parameter sweep, but never reports the number); this directly implements the task's own key axis.
  • Batch vs. single-query latency is made an explicit, mandatory dual report in both variants, generalizing FANNS's own practice (the only paper in the track that already does this) to every candidate, and closing UpANNS's small-fixed-batch-only gap.
  • Correctness/recall verification is made mandatory and connected to the SAME timed run for every candidate in both variants, closing gaps ranging from 'unstated' (DRIM-ANN, UpANNS's recall-gating) to 'disabled by default' (X-HD's -check=false) to 'structurally unfalsifiable' (CLOVER's dead-code early-return in run_test()).
  • X-HD's own end-to-end deliverable (a Hausdorff distance VALUE between two point sets) is explicitly OUT of scope for exact-spatial-knn-kernel — only its internal RT-accelerated k-NN routine is a valid candidate submission, since the end-to-end HD computation is a different operation (a max-min reduction over k-NN results), not itself a k-NN search implementation.
Open questions
  • PathWeaver: the multi-GPU headline claim (3.24x geomean over unspecified 'SOTA') and its recall/QPS behavior were not independently confirmed — only the single-GPU harness (single_pathweaver_one.py) was read in depth; the multi-GPU script (multi_pathweaver_one.py) was not fetched.
  • DRIM-ANN and UpANNS: neither paper's actual algorithm-level source (the DRIM-ANN/ and dpu/ subdirectories respectively) was read in depth within this survey's time budget — only top-level READMEs and run.sh/citation content were fetched, so exact warmup/repetition/statistic protocol for either paper's own released scripts remains unconfirmed (this spec's protocol section does not inherit either paper's practice as a result, and imposes its own floor instead).
  • RTNN: no warmup/repetition/statistic protocol was recoverable from the fetched arXiv fulltext excerpt; the repo's own benchmark/timing driver source (as opposed to README) was not read in depth.
  • X-HD: hardware (GPU model) was not confirmed from the fetched scripts; the internal JSON log schema (what exactly `-json $log` records) was not inspected, so it's unconfirmed whether X-HD's own scripts already separate k-NN-only time from full Hausdorff-distance compute time, which matters for extracting a fair exact-spatial-knn-kernel submission from its rt variant.
  • Whether a distance metric other than L2 (cosine similarity, inner product) should be added to the high-dim variant is left open — no paper in this 7-paper track attests a non-L2 metric, so adding one now would be ungrounded in this track's own literature, per the same principle applied to the sparse-attention-kernel track's fp8 decision.
  • CLOVER's mesh-sweep dataset (files under a `meshes/` directory, k=128) — the actual mesh identities/sizes were not enumerated from the source read; recommended_subset's clover-mesh entry uses a generic placeholder rather than named files.
dnn-operator-fusion5 papers4 variants

Fusing a chain of DNN subgraph operators (elementwise / reduction / GEMM combinations pulled from attention, normalization, MoE routing, and quantized-GEMM building blocks) into as few kernel launches as legally possible, measured separately at single-fused-kernel, subgraph, and full-model granularity, with compile/autotuning search time reported as its own axis rather than hidden inside any of those three.

Generic: given an operator chain op1 -> op2 -> ... -> opk drawn from the canonical pattern set below, produce a fused kernel (or minimal kernel set) computing the same function as the unfused sequential execution of op1..opk, and compare launch count / latency / bandwidth against the unfused baseline and against the best available hand-written reference.

fusion-single-kernelsteady-state latency/bandwidth of ONE fused kernel in isolation (synthetic harness, decoupled from any specific model), i.e. the "single-fused-kernel" granularity that RedFuser's four subgraphs and SumMerge collapse into by construction, and that LightSeq2 reports per-operator (10 reps).

gemm-gemmFFN shapes: [batch*seqlen in {2048,8192,32768}, hidden in {768,1024,4096}, ffn_mult=4]

Fairness notes
  • RedFuser reports subgraph-level numbers only and never a whole-model number; STOF and LightSeq2 both report a model-level number. This spec forces all three granularities (single-kernel, subgraph, model) to be requested and reported as separate variants specifically so a RedFuser-style submission can't be compared directly to a LightSeq2-style model-level claim without the gap being visible.
  • Only STOF quantifies compile/search time (Table 4, vs. MCFuser/Bolt); RedFuser has an autotuner but reports no search-time numbers at all. fusion-compile-search-time is made mandatory for any autotuning/codegen entrant so this gap can't recur silently; hand-written systems correctly report 0.
  • STOF's own kernel-level (10 warmup/20 reps) and end-to-end-level (10 warmup/10 reps) scripts already use two different rep counts for two different granularities — this spec keeps that distinction rather than forcing one rep count across levels, since the code (not the paper prose, which had incorrectly said '100' for the kernel level) is the ground truth for what STOF actually measured.
  • No paper in the track directly names cuDNN or TensorRT as a baseline; this spec does not invent numbers for them but requires torch.compile/Dynamo-Inductor (used by RedFuser and STOF) and PyTorch Eager (used by all three well-documented papers) as the mandatory minimum baseline pair, with hand-written per-pattern references (FlashAttention2-class) and a general compiler (TVM, RedFuser's own choice) as recommended additions.
  • LightSeq2 uses a different baseline system per model family (Fairseq+Apex / HuggingFace / DeepSpeed) rather than one fixed set; this spec's fusion-e2e-model variant instead fixes PyTorch Native + PyTorch Compile as the common baseline pair across all models, with framework-specific baselines allowed as bonus comparisons rather than replacements.
  • Fusion-single-kernel's unfused-baseline timing scope deliberately keeps per-kernel-launch overhead IN (not excluded), unlike a typical 'kernel-only' spec variant elsewhere in this project — because launch-overhead reduction is precisely operator fusion's mechanism of benefit; excluding it would make every fusion framework look like it has zero benefit at large shapes where compute time dominates launch overhead.
  • SumMerge and the CGO'25 RISC-V-backend paper only fit the taxonomy at the single-fused-kernel / quant-gemm and elementwise-chain corners respectively, and neither could be verified past abstract level (ACM 403, arXiv fulltext unreachable across 3 mirrors, and the RISC-V paper's listed artifact repo turned out to be an unrelated protobuf-acceleration project). They are represented in canonical_fusion_patterns for taxonomy completeness but contribute no concrete numeric defaults to the variants above.
Open questions
  • RedFuser's evaluation summary obtained does not state a single fixed precision for the non-FP8 workloads (MHA/MLA/MoE-routing) — likely fp16/bf16 given the model scales (LLaMA-65B, DeepSeek) but not confirmed in the text obtained.
  • STOF's correctness check (correct_verify_attn.py) computes max_diff/mean_diff against a PyTorch reference but the printed/enforced tolerance threshold was not visible in the code slice read; the 1e-2 (fp16) gate above is this spec's own default, not confirmed against STOF's actual pass/fail threshold.
  • SumMerge's shapes, baselines, and timing protocol are entirely unconfirmed (stub artifact repo, paywalled paper) — the quant-gemm pattern's inclusion of SumMerge in canonical_fusion_patterns is a taxonomy placement based on the abstract's description, not a benchmarked data point.
  • The CGO'25 RISC-V-backend paper's actual benchmarked kernel list, baseline set, and warmup/rep protocol could not be recovered at all from sources reachable in this environment; its 'up to 90% FPU utilization' headline number has no shape/baseline context attached and is not used anywhere in the variants above.
  • Whether RedFuser's per-pattern search-time is genuinely negligible (hence unreported) or simply omitted from the evaluation section is unresolved — the amortization_count_k metric in fusion-compile-search-time is designed to force this to be answered by any future RedFuser-class submission.
embedding-ops4 papers3 variants

Embedding-table gather/pooling kernels as used by DLRM-style recommendation models and by single-index gather workloads (knowledge-graph embeddings, word embeddings), measured under both uniform and power-law-skewed row access, with pooling-factor/batch axes matched to production-scale tables.

DLRM-style pooled: Y[b, :] = Pool_{j in bag(b)}( Table[idx_j, :] ) for b in [0, batch), Pool in {sum, mean}, |bag(b)| = pooling_factor (may be per-batch variable). Single-index (KGE/W2V-style): y[b, :] = f( Table1[i1(b), :], Table2[i2(b), :], ... ) for a fused elementwise/bilinear function f (e.g. TransE: Eemb[h]-Eemb[t]+Remb[r]).

Fairness notes
  • cuKE, RecFlex, EL-Rec, FULL-W2V each report a different timing granularity (single kernel / kernel-vs-e2e split / full training step / full training epoch) — no paper's own number is directly comparable to another's. embed-dlrm-pooled-kernel-f32 and embed-single-index-gather fix a common kernel-only denominator; embed-dlrm-e2e-preproc gives the honest end-to-end number RecFlex already separates but EL-Rec/FULL-W2V do not.
  • None of the 4 papers reports GB/s; all are memory-bound. This spec makes GB/s primary and requires reporting the unique-rows-touched count under skew so the number isn't inflated by silently double-counting cache-hit rows as fresh traffic.
  • EL-Rec runs its 1000-iteration timing loop with zero warm-up iterations, which the spec explicitly does not carry over (warmup=25 / 10 mandated instead).
  • None of the 4 papers reports a numeric max-rel-err correctness gate for the raw gather (EL-Rec/FULL-W2V substitute downstream task/embedding-quality metrics instead) — added here as a precondition orthogonal to any downstream-quality claim a paper wants to make separately.
  • RecFlex's power-law alpha=3.0 is adopted as the default skew parameter since it is the only paper in the track to parameterize skew explicitly; papers/systems claiming skew-robustness should also report at least one more skewed (alpha<3.0) and one less skewed (alpha>3.0 / near-uniform) point.
Open questions
  • No paper reports a cache/row-hit-rate number directly (cuKE and EL-Rec both build reuse/reordering optimizations around it but don't quantify it in the artifact scripts read); the row_hit_rate metric above is therefore a spec-level addition, not something validated against a paper's own reported number.
  • cuKE's benchmark scripts (test_cuke.py) show no explicit numeric-tolerance correctness check; whether one exists elsewhere in the repo (e.g. in test files not read) is unconfirmed.
  • RecFlex's end_to_end.py shows no explicit warm-up; whether warm-up is handled elsewhere (e.g. CUDA context/JIT warm-up before the timed script starts) was not confirmed by reading tune.py in full.
  • FULL-W2V's exact timer implementation (which clock/library) beyond 'mean and std of 5 runs' was not visible in the fulltext excerpt obtained.
moe-kernel1 papers2 variants

Fused mixed-precision Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) FFN kernel for LLM inference: token-to-expert routing/permutation + per-expert grouped GEMM with a quantized weight operand + gate-weighted un-permute/combine, measured at steady state with routing/permutation cost reported separately, swept across expert-count/top-k configurations and both uniform and realistically-skewed token-to-expert load.

For a token batch X[T,H] and router logits producing top-k expert assignment per token: Y[T,H] = sum_{e in topk(t)} gate[t,e] * (X[t,:] @ W1_e[H,I] -> activation -> @ W2_e[I,H]), where W1_e/W2_e are per-expert weight matrices stored in a low-precision format (e.g. INT4/AWQ or FP8, "mixed-type" in Hexcute's own terminology) and X is bf16/fp16. Routing requires building a per-expert token permutation (gather tokens assigned to each expert into contiguous grouped-GEMM operand blocks) and an inverse permutation + gate-weighted combine on the output.

moe-grouped-gemm-kernelsteady-state fused/grouped-GEMM MoE-FFN kernel throughput at fixed GPU clock, matching Hexcute's own "mixed-type MoE operator" claim (6.46x vs Triton) — token routing/permutation excluded from the timed kernel region and reported separately, since the paper itself keeps this kernel-level number distinct from its end-to-end vLLM serving numbers.

Fairness notes
  • This track's sole source (Hexcute/CGO'26) reports only an average kernel speedup (6.46x) and two end-to-end points, with no visible breakdown across expert-count/top-k configurations or token-distribution skew. moe-grouped-gemm-kernel's uniform-vs-skewed token_distribution sub-case is this spec's own addition (not lifted from the paper) to prevent a kernel from being credited only under the easy uniform-load case, which real trained routers rarely produce.
  • The paper conflates a kernel-only claim (Triton comparison) and a real-serving claim (vLLM DeepSeek-R1-AWQ) under the same headline MoE result; this spec's two-variant split (kernel vs e2e) makes that distinction explicit and prevents readers from citing the 2.60x e2e number as if it were the kernel's own speedup.
  • GPU-clock locking (nvidia-smi -lgc) is the one timing-protocol detail directly confirmed in the artifact and is carried over verbatim into moe-grouped-gemm-kernel; most other kernel tracks in this project only recommend clock locking, this one can mandate it with direct evidence.
Open questions
  • The artifact's actual MoE benchmark shapes live in hidet/examples/cute/test_moe.py (referenced by scripts/run_moe.sh) which was not fetched in this survey -- recommended_subset above is this spec's own construction from public MoE model configs, not confirmed against the artifact's literal test shapes. A follow-up pass should fetch that file directly.
  • No stated warmup/repeat count or correctness tolerance was found for the MoE-specific benchmark path (run_moe.sh) in the fetched README; the warmup=20/reps=100/1e-3 values in this spec are carried over from this project's quantized-gemm precedent, not confirmed against Hexcute's own MoE test harness.
  • Whether Hexcute's MoE kernel handles the shared-expert component of DeepSeek-V2/V3-style architectures (n_shared_experts in recommended_subset) as part of the same fused kernel or as a separate dense-GEMM call is unknown from the fetched sources.
spiking-neural-network1 papers1 variants

GPGPU simulation of a Leaky-Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) spiking neural network over a fixed simulated biological duration, measuring wall-time throughput (real-time factor) as a function of network topology (population count/size, local-vs-remote connectivity mix), simulated timestep count, and activity sparsity (firing rate), with a spike-train correctness gate against a reference (non-GPU or higher-precision) simulation required before any speed number counts.

For a network of P populations of N_p LIF neurons each, connected by weighted/delayed synaptic projections (dense within-population, sparse cross-population — the paper's own topology fixes ~80% of projections to front/rear-neighbor populations and ~20% to arbitrary remote populations): simulate T timesteps of dt=0.1ms each, where each timestep updates every neuron's membrane potential V_i(t+dt) = V_i(t)*decay + I_syn_i(t), emits a spike (and resets V_i) when V_i crosses threshold, and propagates that spike's synaptic current to all post-synaptic neurons after the projection's configured delay.

snn-lif-sim-throughputsteady-state simulation throughput (simulated-ms of network activity per wall-clock-second, i.e. real-time factor) for a fixed LIF network topology and firing-rate regime, network-construction / IR-compilation excluded and reported separately once. Matches BSim's own test/gpu/standard_test.cpp harness and its GeNN comparison points.

metric
primaryreal-time factor = simulated_duration_ms / wall_clock_ms (dimensionless; >1 means faster than biological real time)

correctnessMANDATORY pre-timing gate (BSim's own release build logs firing rate/membrane voltage but does not appear to wire an automated pass/fail check into the benchmark driver -- this spec closes that gap): per-neuron spike-train match against a reference simulator (GeNN, or BSim's own double-precision build as an internal reference) over the same simulated duration and identical random seed -- required tolerance: aggregate firing-rate relative difference < 5% AND per-neuron spike-count difference < 10% for at least 95% of neurons (spike TIMING match to the exact timestep is not required across different simulators/precisions, since discrete LIF dynamics are chaotically sensitive to floating-point order of operations at threshold-crossing boundaries — firing-rate/count statistics are the field's practical correctness proxy).
Fairness notes
  • BSim's own README states no warmup/repeat/timer convention and no automated correctness gate wired into the benchmark driver (release build only logs firing rate/voltage for manual inspection). This spec's protocol (1 discarded warmup run, 5 seeded repeats, median+min/max, mandatory firing-rate correctness gate) is this project's own construction from SNN-simulator field convention, not extracted from the artifact -- flagged explicitly rather than presented as if sourced.
  • BSim's reported speedup (1.41x-9.33x vs GeNN) spans a wide range with no visible per-configuration breakdown of which topology/firing-rate combination produces which end of the range; recommended_subset's 3-firing-rate x 2-size grid is designed so a re-measurement can attribute the range to specific (topology, activity) axes rather than reporting one cherry-pickable number.
  • Chaotic sensitivity of discrete LIF spike timing to floating-point order-of-operations means a bit-exact or tight-tolerance spike-train match across different simulators (BSim vs GeNN) is not a meaningful correctness bar; this spec uses aggregate firing-rate/spike-count tolerances instead, an explicit deviation from a naive 'exact output match' correctness convention.
Open questions
  • BSim's exact timing methodology (which timer, single-run vs averaged) for its own reported 1.41x-9.33x GeNN comparison could not be recovered from the top-level README; the protocol specified here is this spec's own design, not a reproduction of BSim's literal benchmarking script (test/gpu/standard_test.cpp's internal timing code was not fetched).
  • Whether BSim's release build's GFire.log/g_v.data outputs are suffient to reconstruct a full per-neuron spike train for the correctness gate above (as opposed to only aggregate firing rate) was not confirmed from the README alone.
  • The paper claims a general fine-grained IR that could in principle support neuron models beyond LIF, but the fetched README states 'the simulator only integrates the LIF model' -- whether other TPDS-paper-described optimizations (sparsity-aware load balance) generalize to non-LIF models is untested in this survey.
transformer-inference-fused1 papers2 variants

Fully fused transformer encoder layer (QKV projection, multi-head attention, feed-forward network, layer-norm, activation, all in one measured region) for variable-length inputs, executed padding-free so no compute is wasted on pad tokens -- distinct from benchspecs/attention-kernel, which isolates the MHA core alone; this track measures the WHOLE fused layer and requires explicit disclosure of which sub-ops are inside vs. outside the fusion boundary.

For a variable-length batch of B sequences with per-sequence lengths L_i <= S_max: Encoder(X)[B,S,H] = LayerNorm(X + FFN(LayerNorm(X + MHA(QKV_proj(X))))), where MHA is computed padding-free (each sequence's real L_i tokens only, no wasted work on padding up to S_max), QKV_proj and FFN are dense GEMMs + bias, and the whole N-layer stack (default N=12, BERT-base) is the timed unit unless a single-layer sub-variant is requested.

fused-encoder-layer-padfree-fp16steady-state latency of the padding-free fused BERT-base encoder (12 layers, all sub-ops -- QKV, MHA, FFN, LN -- inside one measured forward pass), fp16, swept across the batch x sequence-length grid that separates memory-bound small-batch decode-adjacent regimes from compute-bound large-batch/long-sequence regimes. Matches ByteTransformer's own bert_bench.sh sweep.

Fairness notes
  • ByteTransformer's own bert_bench.sh reports one latency number per (batch, seqlen) cell with no visible repeat/median at the shell-script level -- this spec requires >=20 device-side-timed repetitions with median + min/max reported, the same fix already applied to this paper's attention-only number in benchspecs/attention-kernel.
  • The paper's headline numbers mix a kernel-only MHA claim (6.13x vs PyTorch, out of scope here -- see benchspecs/attention-kernel) with an end-to-end 12-layer encoder claim (the 55-138% faster-than-framework numbers); this track's variants are scoped strictly to the full fused encoder layer to avoid re-litigating the attention-only comparison under a different track name.
  • fusion_scope_required_disclosure is added because 'fused transformer kernel' claims in this literature commonly differ in how many separate kernel launches are actually being called 'fused' -- ByteTransformer's own README does not itemize this per sub-op, so a candidate implementation could otherwise silently claim fusion credit for what is really 6 back-to-back unfused launches.
  • ByteTransformer's released correctness check (bert_transformer_test.py --export_data + bin/bert_transformer_test) is a separate binary from the timed benchmark path (bert_bench.sh); this spec makes the correctness gate mandatory and part of the SAME run as the timed measurement.
Open questions
  • Whether ByteTransformer's internal bert_transformer_test.py driver (invoked by bert_bench.sh) itself performs multiple internal iterations before printing the final latency line was not determined from the fetched shell script alone; the source of bert_transformer_test.py was not fetched.
  • No stated correctness tolerance value was found in the fetched README for the padding-free vs. padded numerical comparison; the 1e-2 abs-error gate here is carried over from this project's attention-kernel precedent for the same paper's MHA-only correctness check, not independently confirmed for the full-encoder case.
  • The paper's applicability claim to ALBERT/DistilBERT/DeBERTa is not accompanied by a released benchmark script for those architectures in the fetched top-level listing; fused-encoder-single-layer-kernel's cross-architecture comparability is this spec's own design intent, not a reproduction of a paper-reported ALBERT/DistilBERT/DeBERTa number.
winograd1 papers3 variants

Latency and throughput of Winograd/Cook-Toom fast convolution for 3x3 stride-1 layers, measured with an algorithm-invariant flop convention and with the numerical error the transform introduces reported as a first-class result rather than left unstated.

Y = A^T [ (G g G^T) (*) (B^T d B) ] A for output tile F(m,r): filter g is r x r (r = 3), input tile d is (m+r-1) x (m+r-1), (*) is element-wise multiply. Direct-equivalent output: standard 3x3 stride-1 convolution over NCHW input.

winograd-kernel-fp32steady-state convolution-layer throughput of a Winograd implementation at a disclosed tile size, comparable against direct/im2col/FFT convolution because the flop convention is algorithm-invariant

Fairness notes
  • Winograd changes the arithmetic performed, so GFLOP/s is meaningless unless the flop convention is pinned. This spec fixes flops_ref to the direct convolution count for every algorithm class, and requires the true multiply count to be reported alongside rather than substituted for it.
  • F(6,3) is the largest commonly deployed tile and the least numerically accurate. FeatherCNN, the track's only artifact, ships F(6,3) exclusively and contains no accuracy test for it. This spec makes an error bound a hard gate and adds a frontier variant, deliberately diverging from the artifact's practice.
  • Filter-transform placement can move a large fraction of the reported win at batch 1. It is excluded from the timed window here but must be reported; a hoisting choice left implicit makes two submissions incomparable.
  • Cold-cache is the mobile-inference reality and hot-cache flatters transform-heavy methods. Both are required.
  • The artifact commits no timing harness (measurement is delegated to wiki guides), so no protocol could be inherited; the constants here are set to match benchspecs/convolution/spec.yaml so the two tracks stay comparable.
Open questions
  • FeatherCNN's own layer list, warmup/repetition counts, and reported metric could not be recovered — the TPDS paper is paywalled with no arXiv mirror and the repo ships no benchmark script. The required_shapes above are taken from the shared convolution suite, not from this paper.
  • Whether FeatherCNN's ARM path uses the generic winograd_kernels.cpp or the F63-specialized file for a given layer is not documented; submissions using it should state which path executed.
  • Single-implementation track. Candidate external baselines for a real comparison: ARM Compute Library, NCNN, oneDNN, cuDNN's Winograd algorithms, and the classic Lavin-Gray reference.

codegen / tuning

autotuner-multi-kernel11 papers4 variants

Unlike the other tracks in this project, the "kernel" under test here is a compiler/autotuner SYSTEM, not a single fixed operation: the system is given a fixed, named multi-kernel suite (dense DL/HPC linear algebra, sparse linear algebra, and PolyBench affine loops) plus a search budget, and is scored on BOTH the wall-clock cost to reach a schedule/kernel AND the steady-state performance of the kernel that schedule produces — since the surveyed literature reports these two axes with wildly inconsistent rigor (see survey.md "Divergences"), and this track's own name ("multi-kernel") signals that suite breadth, not single-kernel depth, is the point.

system-under-test S (a compiler, autotuner, or scheduling-language instance) is given each kernel k in the fixed suite K below, as source/IR, plus a wall-clock search budget; S produces optimized executable code for k; both the search trajectory (time -> best-found performance) and the final produced code's steady-state performance are measured. K spans three disjoint kernel families (dense/sparse tensor ops, PolyBench affine loops) because the surveyed papers target genuinely different substrates and optimizing across them is not a single comparable operation.

tensor-kernel-steady-state-f32post-tuning steady-state kernel throughput of the dense+sparse tensor kernel suite, fp32, using whichever schedule the system under test found within the tensor-kernel-tuning-cost variant's 3600s checkpoint (search time is EXCLUDED from this number but its cap is enforced — unlike GMC/PrecTuner/WACO/FlexTensor, which report post-tuning numbers with no reported/bounded search budget at all).

l2_cacheflushed between iterations on GPU (matches the two most rigorous surveyed protocols: SparseTIR, CuAsmRL)
timing_scopekernel only; H2D/D2H, format conversion, and any JIT/codegen dispatch overhead excluded
deviation_from_surveyed_practicePruner's own reported latencies come from a 500-iteration PyTorch-level mean that includes Python dispatch overhead; this spec requires a pure device-side per-iteration timer instead, since dispatch overhead is not part of "kernel throughput" and would penalize systems that don't emit a PyTorch custom-op wrapper.
metric

correctnessmax relative error vs. fp64 CPU reference < 1e-4 (matches this project's spmm/sddmm track convention for cross-track comparability)
tensor-kernel-tuning-costthe search/tuning cost required to reach the steady-state variant's result, reported as a Pareto curve (time -> best-found performance) at fixed checkpoints — mandatory and primary as WALL-CLOCK time, because the track's own papers use incommensurable units (Pruner: trial count; TPP-mlir: wall time; CuAsmRL: "one-time training cost"; WACO/GMC: unreported despite search/model-solve being their core contribution).
inputs

protocol
budget_checkpoints_seconds60, 600, 3600
devicesingle reference device, same as tensor-kernel-steady-state-f32 (see notes_on_fairness on hardware scope)
measured_at_each_checkpointbest-found kernel performance so far (GFLOP/s, per tensor-kernel-steady-state-f32's protocol), AND number of trials/candidates evaluated so far (secondary, non-comparable across systems but reported for context)
final_reporttime-to-within-5%-of-best (interpolated from the checkpoint curve) as the single headline number, plus the full 3-point curve
deviation_from_surveyed_practiceOnly Pruner (matched n-trials table) and TPP-mlir (explicit wall-time comparison) report anything resembling this today, and neither uses fixed checkpoints — this spec fixes 60s/600s/3600s so a closed-form solver (GMC, PrecTuner) that finishes in well under 60s and an RL-based search (CuAsmRL) that needs hours are both placed on the same curve rather than compared via cherry-picked, differently-sized budgets.
metric
primarywall-clock seconds to reach within 5% of best-found GFLOP/s
secondaryGFLOP/s at each of the 3 checkpoints (Pareto table); trial/candidate count at each checkpoint
baselinesAnsor/AutoTVM at the same 3 checkpoints, as the common enumerative-search reference every DNN-operator paper in this track already baselines against
correctnesssame gate as tensor-kernel-steady-state-f32, applied to the checkpointed best-found candidate, not just the final one (a candidate that fails correctness does not count as 'best-found')
polybench-affine-kernel-f64steady-state execution time of the PolyBench/C 4.2.1 suite (fixed 30-kernel list, LARGE_DATASET), the one input family this track's literature is directly and confirmably anchored to (PrecTuner/LnLAMP) — kept as its own variant rather than folded into the tensor-kernel variants because PolyBench's kernels (stencils, DP recurrences like nussinov/floyd-warshall, solvers) are not FLOP-throughput-comparable to GEMM/conv, and PolyBench papers customarily report raw time + speedup, not GFLOP/s.
inputs

dataset_sizeLARGE_DATASET (PolyBench's standard research-paper convention; EXTRALARGE optional/reported if the system supports it)
precisionPolyBench default (fp64) EXCEPT as swept in polybench-affine-mixed-precision below

reps20

deviation_from_surveyed_practiceGMC (the closest analogue, though not itself a PolyBench paper) states only "median of 10, no stated warmup." This spec adds explicit warmup and raises reps to 20 for a tighter median, since polyhedral-compiler papers' own timing protocols were the least specified of any cluster surveyed (see Divergences).

primarywall-clock ms per kernel
secondaryspeedup vs. -O3 baseline
baselines-O3 (gcc/clang, no polyhedral transformation) — the floor, Pluto (state-of-the-art polyhedral CPU optimizer, PrecTuner's own baseline), PPCG (GPU polyhedral baseline, for systems that target GPU)
correctnessmax relative error vs. -O3 unoptimized reference < 1e-6 (tight: same architecture, no atomics/reduction-order nondeterminism expected at fp64)
polybench-affine-mixed-precisionprecision-vs-speed Pareto frontier for the subset of PolyBench kernels amenable to mixed/reduced precision (PrecTuner's own target: nussinov, fdtd-2d, heat-3d, seidel-2d, plus any kernel the system under test chooses to lower) — reported as a FRONTIER, not gated by a single fixed tolerance, because PrecTuner's own design explicitly trades accuracy for speed under a tunable error budget, unlike the fixed-dtype half-precision variants used elsewhere in this track (Pruner/CuAsmRL/ TPP-mlir simply run a kernel in fp16; PrecTuner tunes A CONTINUOUS precision-selection parameter).
inputs
suite[nussinov, fdtd-2d, heat-3d, seidel-2d] mandatory (matches PrecTuner's own confirmed test set); remaining PolyBench kernels optional
error_budgets_swept1e-2, 1e-4, 1e-6
protocolsame timing protocol as polybench-affine-kernel-f64
metric
primaryspeedup vs. fp64 -O3 baseline at each error budget

baselinesPluto/PPCG at fp64 (same as polybench-affine-kernel-f64), LuIs (fixed 16-bit fixed-point competitor, single-threaded only — reported where the system under test supports single-threaded comparison)
correctnessrelative error <= the swept budget, measured against a fp64 -O3 reference; this IS the metric, not a pass/fail gate (see metric above)
Fairness notes
  • PolyBench is confirmed as the target suite for only 1 of 11 papers (PrecTuner/LnLAMP). A spec that made PolyBench the ONLY kernel family, as this track's naming might suggest, would misrepresent 10/11 papers' actual practice. This spec keeps PolyBench as two dedicated variants and adds the dense/sparse tensor-kernel suite (three variants) as the dominant real practice in this track.
  • Search/tuning cost is reported by only 3 of 11 papers (Pruner, TPP-mlir, CuAsmRL), each in a different unit (trial count, ad-hoc wall-time comparison, 'one-time cost' framing). This spec makes wall-clock time at 3 FIXED checkpoints (60s/600s/3600s) mandatory and primary for every system, with trial/candidate count reported only as non-comparable context — this is the single biggest fix relative to current practice, since it is the axis the task brief explicitly flagged as crucial.
  • WACO and GMC's core contribution is a fast/cheap search strategy (ANN retrieval; closed-form performance-model solve) that largely sidesteps the 'expensive search' problem other autotuners have, yet neither paper reports a quantified search-time number. Forcing them through the same 3-checkpoint budget table as an RL-based search (CuAsmRL) or enumerative search (Ansor) makes their near-zero search cost directly visible and verifiable, rather than left as an unquantified design claim.
  • Several surveyed protocols never state warmup counts (GMC, Gensor, WACO, Ivanov, Exo 2 as read) or batch many iterations behind a single timer call (Pruner's 500-iteration PyTorch-level mean, which includes framework dispatch). This spec fixes per-iteration device-side timers with explicit warmup for every variant, and explicitly excludes framework dispatch overhead from the kernel-only timing scope.
  • Correctness gates are undocumented for 4 of 11 papers in the accessible sources (GMC, Gensor, WACO, FlexTensor). This spec makes a numeric correctness check mandatory before any timing counts, and — for the tuning-cost variant specifically — applies the gate to EVERY checkpointed candidate, not just the final reported one, so a system cannot 'find' a fast-but-wrong kernel early and let it count toward the Pareto curve.
  • PrecTuner treats precision as a continuously tuned parameter under an error budget, a fundamentally different claim from 'run this kernel in fp16' (Pruner/CuAsmRL/TPP-mlir's fixed-dtype half-precision runs). This spec keeps PrecTuner's frontier framing for the PolyBench mixed-precision variant, while the dense/sparse tensor-kernel suite's precision is fixed at fp32 (a separate fp16/bf16 variant is left as an open question below rather than forced into this version, to keep the spec to 4 variants per the instructions).
  • Hardware portability claims range from a single A100 (CuAsmRL) to 4 CPU microarchitectures (TPP-mlir) to cross-vendor GPU (Ivanov) to GPU+CPU+FPGA (FlexTensor). This spec designates ONE reference GPU (A100-class) and ONE reference CPU (current server-class x86 with AVX-512, matching TPP-mlir's SPR node) as mandatory; additional platforms are optional/reported-if-available rather than required, since matching every paper's full portability claim is out of scope for a reproducible single-lab benchmark run.
  • The SpMM/SDDMM matrix subset intentionally reuses benchspecs/spmm's recommended_subset (cora, citeseer, pubmed, amazon, youtube, pdb1HYS, cant, consph, dc2, rma10) rather than inventing a new list, so results for a system that appears in both tracks (e.g. a sparse tensor compiler tested here and a hand-written SpMM kernel tested in the spmm track) are directly comparable within this project.
Open questions
  • Exact timing/warmup/repetition protocol for Exo 2, Ivanov/Polygeist, WACO, FlexTensor, PrecTuner/LnLAMP, and Gensor could not be confirmed from accessible sources (ACM paywalls, corrupted PDF extraction for WACO, no arXiv preprint located for FlexTensor, HTML mirror 404s for Exo 2). The protocol values in this spec for those systems' likely kernel families are this spec's own fixed choice, not verified against what those specific papers did — flagged per-variant above via 'deviation_from_surveyed_practice' where a comparison was possible.
  • Whether a dedicated fp16/bf16 variant of the dense/sparse tensor-kernel suite (distinct from PolyBench's continuous-budget mixed precision) should be a 5th variant given Pruner/CuAsmRL/TPP-mlir all test fixed half precision; left out to keep the spec to 4 variants per the task instructions, but is the most likely candidate for a 5th if Phase 2 wants finer precision coverage.
  • Whether the 3 fixed tuning-budget checkpoints (60s/600s/3600s) are well-calibrated across ALL system types in this track once real runs are attempted — a closed-form solver may finish in well under 60s (making the curve mostly flat/uninformative for it) while an RL-based search may need hours of training before its FIRST valid candidate; checkpoint spacing may need revisiting after a pilot run.
  • Whether FPGA (FlexTensor) and AMD-GPU (Ivanov's retargeting target) platforms belong in this spec at all, given the project's Phase 2 hardware constraint is 'any machine' but FPGA/AMD-GPU access may not be available on the eventual measurement machine — left as optional rather than mandatory.
  • GMC and Exo 2 primarily perform compile-time multi-versioning / library generation rather than an online search loop; whether their code-generation time should count toward the tuning-cost variant's budget checkpoints, or should be reported as a separate near-instant 'compile time' outside the search-cost framing entirely, is unresolved — this spec currently asks for it to be reported if measurable, without asserting which bucket it belongs in.
  • WACO's exact 726-sparsity-pattern dataset (cited only in secondary sources) was not found checked into the public repo in full — only ~20 example .csr files are present. Its exact provenance (which SuiteSparse selection criterion, if any) was not traced and could not be cross-checked against this spec's own SpMM/SDDMM matrix subset.

other

hamiltonian-simulation1 papers2 variants

Classical (non-quantum-hardware) time evolution e^{-iHt}|psi_0> of sparse quantum Hamiltonians via Trotterization, benchmarked both end-to-end (diagonal-budgeted step-count search + repeated propagator application) and as an isolated diagonal-sparse SpMV/matrix-exponential kernel, gated by state fidelity against a dense NumPy reference where memory permits (system size in {qubits}, matching the parent task's suggested axis directly -- see survey.md Divergences #4).

Given Hamiltonian H (sum of Pauli-string terms, read from a HamLib HDF5 file) and final time T: (1) [diaq method only, one-time preprocessing] binary/exponential-search the smallest step count r such that num_diagonals(exp(-i*H*(T/r))) <= D_max (a user-set diagonal budget); (2) compute the per-step propagator U = exp(-i*H*(T/r)) once (dense matrix exponential over the Hamiltonian's sparse/diagonal representation); (3) apply U to the initial state vector r times via repeated diagonal- sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV): psi_r = U^r psi_0.

hamsim-e2e-hamlib-diagonal-budgetend-to-end wall-clock time for full Hamiltonian time evolution (diagonal-budget step-count search, included as reported one-time preprocessing, PLUS r repeated propagator applications), across HamLib's 4 problem families and the paper's own qubit-count range, compared against 6 baselines run in the SAME driver script (fair, same-harness comparison per survey.md)
inputs
suiteHamLib (Sawaya et al. 2024), hosted on the NERSC public portal (portal.nersc.gov/cfs/m888/dcamps/hamlib/), same HDF5 files the paper itself downloads (paper-confirmed wget commands in README)
selection4 families, all instances the paper evaluates (Table 3, confirmed from fulltext, not a further-subsampled cherry-pick): TSP (8-16 qubits, 6 instances, purely diagonal), MaxCut (10-16 qubits, 8 instances, purely diagonal), Heisenberg (6-14 qubits, 7 instances, ~19 active diagonals at 10 qubits), TFIM (7-16 qubits, 6 instances, ~21 active diagonals at 10 qubits); diagonal counts 1-33 and sparsity 93.75%-99.9985% across the full instance set (Table 3)
recommended_subsettfim: graph-1D-grid-pbc-qubitnodes_Lx-10_h-6 (paper's own README usage example), tfim, heisenberg, maxcut, tsp: smallest instance per family (paper's own low end, ~6-10 qubits) for a fast correctness+performance sanity pass, tfim, heisenberg, maxcut, tsp: largest instance per family (paper's own high end, 14-16 qubits) for the paper's headline speedup regime, fidelity check skipped by construction above 15 qubits (see correctness below)
dense_operandN/A -- state vector of dimension 2^num_qubits (complex128), Hamiltonian as a sum of Pauli-string terms converted to DiaQ's diagonal-sparse layout
diagonal_budgetPERCENT_DIAGONALS swept in {10, 30, 50} (percent of 2*dim-1 maximum possible diagonals), matching the CLI argument's own semantics (confirmed from app2_hamlib_latest.py: max_d = max(1500, PERCENT_DIAGONALS * (2*dim-1) // 100)); the paper's README usage example uses 10 -- this spec's 30/50 points are its own addition for a budget-vs-speed/fidelity tradeoff curve the paper's own Table 3 does not fully sweep, flagged as not individually paper-verified
final_timeT=1.8 (script's own default, matches the README usage example exactly)
protocol
timestep_countNUM_TIMESTEPS is NOT an independent input for the diaq method -- it is the OUTPUT of the diagonal-budget search (estimate_min_timesteps_diaq(), confirmed read from source) run once per (Hamiltonian, PERCENT_DIAGONALS) pair; all baseline methods in the same run use the SAME resolved NUM_TIMESTEPS (confirmed: all methods share one `exact_times` list built after the search resolves), so step count is held fixed across methods within one comparison, per survey.md Divergences #3
warmup1 discarded iteration -- a benchmark-spec ADDITION: the artifact's own script (app2_hamlib_latest.py, confirmed read) times and PRINTS the first iteration (no discard) before running ITRS-1 more; this spec inserts an explicit untimed warmup call before the first recorded iteration, since a first-call-included measurement risks conflating one-time JIT/cache/allocator warmup with steady-state cost, per this project's standing fairness principle
reps10 -- matching the PAPER'S OWN reported protocol ("averaged over 10 runs," fulltext), NOT the script's bare CLI default of ITRS=5 (survey.md Divergences #1); a reproducer must pass ITRS=10 explicitly on the command line to match the paper
statisticmedian, report min/max and standard deviation (paper's own fulltext reports mean +/- stddev via bar-chart whiskers; this spec adds median/min/max per the standing project fairness principle, without dropping the paper's own stddev reporting)
timertime.perf_counter() (confirmed directly from source: `from time import perf_counter`, used to bracket each method call)
timing_scopeper-method total wall time for r propagator applications ONLY; the one-time diagonal-budget search (preprocessing) and the one-time propagator-matrix computation (U = exp(-i*H*dt), computed once before the repetition loop for diaq/csr/dia/csc methods, confirmed from run_diaq()/run_sparse() source) are explicitly OUTSIDE the ITRS-repeated timed region for those methods -- but for qiskit-aer and expm_multiply, EACH repetition reconstructs/re- applies the operator from scratch inside the timed loop (confirmed from run_qiskit()/run_expm_multiply_csr() source: no U is precomputed and reused across the loop for these two methods). This asymmetry is a REAL property of the compared methods, not a spec artifact: Qiskit's PauliEvolutionGate-based circuit construction and expm_multiply's action-without-forming-the- operator design do not have an equivalent one-shot-U-then-reapply structure the way DiaQ/CSR/DIA's explicit matrix exponential does.
preprocessing_reporteddiagonal-budget search time and one-shot propagator-matrix construction time reported SEPARATELY, once, not amortized into the per-iteration ITRS measurements (matches the paper's own "one- time preprocessing...negligible compared to the overall simulation cost" framing, and is structurally confirmed from the script as described above)
metric
primaryspeedup vs. Qiskit-Aer = median(T_qiskit-aer) / median(T_method), per Hamiltonian family and qubit count (paper's own primary comparison axis)
secondarywall time (s) per method, speedup vs. each of the 5 other baselines (expm_multiply, CSR, DIA, NumPy dense, Qiskit-Aer-GPU), diagonal-budget-search time (one-time), propagator-construction time (one-time)
correctnessstate fidelity (Qiskit's state_fidelity()) between each method's final state and a NumPy-dense reference computed via scipy.linalg.expm applied to the FULL (untrotterized) Hamiltonian -- matches the paper's OWN correctness check exactly, not invented (survey.md Divergences #4). Threshold: fidelity >= 0.999 required to count as a valid timed result (paper's own reported HamSim fidelities are ~1.0; Aer's own fidelity is reported as low as 0.03-0.18 on some instances, which the paper treats as a BASELINE FAILURE, not a tolerance to relax -- this spec preserves that framing rather than loosening the threshold to make Aer "pass"). SCALE LIMIT, inherited directly from the artifact's own guard (confirmed from source): the dense reference, and therefore this correctness gate, is automatically SKIPPED for num_qubits >= 16 "to avoid memory issues" -- at that scale only the performance numbers are reportable, with no independent correctness check, exactly as in the paper's own artifact.
hamsim-microbench-diagonal-spmvisolated diagonal-sparse SpMV kernel throughput, separating the core linear-algebra primitive from Trotter-step orchestration and HamLib I/O overhead the end-to-end variant also pays -- included because the parent task's "per-step time" axis is most directly answered by this isolated kernel, not the end-to-end application number
inputs
suitesynthetic diagonal-sparse matrices generated by the repo's own microbench_spmv.py generator (confirmed present in repo), not drawn from HamLib HDF5 files directly
selection--qubits swept in {8, 10, 12, 14, 16}, --diag-frac (diagonal density) swept in {0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.3} (fractions bracketing the 93.75%-99.9985% SPARSITY range Table 3 reports for real HamLib instances, i.e. diag-frac in [0.00015, 0.0625]-equivalent -- this spec's own choice of representative points, flagged as not individually paper-verified), --format in {diaq, dia, csr, numpy} (all 4 formats the script itself supports, confirmed from README)
dense_operandstate vector of dimension 2^qubits, complex128
protocol
warmup1 discarded call per (qubits, diag-frac, format) combination -- benchmark-spec addition, not confirmed present in the microbenchmark script (not read in as much depth as app2_hamlib_latest.py; flagged as unconfirmed)
reps10
statisticmedian, report min/max
timertime.perf_counter(), consistent with the end-to-end script's own choice (not independently confirmed for this specific microbenchmark file, since only its CLI-flag interface was read from the README, not its full source)
timing_scopesingle SpMV call only (U applied once to the state vector), matrix construction/format-conversion excluded and reported separately
preprocessing_reportedmatrix generation and format conversion (e.g. dense-to-DiaQ, dense-to-CSR) reported once, separately, not amortized into the per-SpMV time
metric
primaryGFLOP/s = 2 * nnz(U) * 2^qubits (complex mul-add, counted as 2 real flops each way, standard complex-GEMV flop count) / spmv_time_seconds
secondarywall time (ms) per SpMV call, speedup of diaq format vs. dia/csr/numpy at matched diag-frac
correctnessoutput state vector compared to a numpy dense matmul reference at the same (qubits, diag-frac) point, relative error < 1e-10 (double precision, exact SpMV has no approximation error beyond floating-point rounding, so this is a bit-level correctness check, not a quality/speed tradeoff)
Fairness notes
  • The artifact script's own CLI default (ITRS=5) undercounts relative to the paper's own reported protocol (10 runs, fulltext) -- this spec uses 10 explicitly and flags the discrepancy so a naive re-run with no arguments does not silently diverge from the paper's own numbers.
  • The artifact's timing loop does not discard a first-iteration warmup (confirmed from source); this spec adds one, per the project's standing fairness principle, while preserving the paper's fidelity/threshold framing (see correctness field) rather than loosening it.
  • The one-shot-U-then-reapply vs. reconstruct-every-iteration asymmetry between diaq/csr/dia/csc and qiskit-aer/expm_multiply (protocol, timing_scope) is a genuine structural difference between the compared methods' own APIs, not a spec choice to favor one side -- reported explicitly rather than papered over, matching this project's "be an engineer, not a diplomat" instruction.
  • The correctness gate is automatically unavailable above 15 qubits, inherited directly from the artifact's own memory-driven guard; this spec does not invent a substitute large-scale correctness check (e.g. a cheaper approximate fidelity estimator) since the paper's own artifact does not have one either -- flagged as a genuine scale limitation of the track's evaluation methodology, not just of this spec.
Open questions
  • Exact diag-frac / qubit sweep points used in the paper's own microbench_spmv.py / microbench_spgemm.py / microbench_expm.py results (referenced in the README and file listing, but their source was not read in the same depth as app2_hamlib_latest.py -- only the CLI-flag interface is confirmed, not the internal generator/timing-loop structure).
  • Whether the paper's own reported 10-run protocol used a discarded warmup iteration that simply isn't visible in the current public script state (e.g. if the paper's actual experiment used a since-modified version of app2_hamlib_latest.py) is unconfirmed.
  • Exact PERCENT_DIAGONALS values swept in the paper's own Table 3 / speedup figures (only the README's single usage example, 10, is directly confirmed; the paper likely sweeps more values given the "diagonal-budget" framing, but the exact set was not extracted from the fulltext).
  • Whether DiaQ's SpMV kernel selection (CPU SIMD/multithreaded vs. CUDA) is automatic or requires the separate diaq_gpu Python module + a different build flag for the microbenchmark scripts specifically (confirmed required for the end-to-end diaq-gpu method from README, not independently confirmed for microbench_spmv.py).

Built by Claude Code. Specs are grounded in per-paper surveys (benchspecs/<kernel>/survey.md); each spec's evidence field maps claims back to individual papers. Numbers here describe intended measurement methodology — nothing has been executed yet.
